## Pagina 2

Presentation
| GRI 2-1 |
Banco de Occidente is a publicly traded company with securities 
listed on the Colombian Stock Exchange for ordinary and 
subordinated bonds. As of December 31, 2025, $3.20 trillion has 
been issued and $3.10 trillion has been placed, of which $1.41 
trillion of Series B bonds linked to the Consumer Price Index 
(CPI) remain outstanding, with average issuance and maturity 
terms of 2017 and 2029, respectively. As of the close of 2025, the 
current issuance and placement program stands at $12.00 trillion, 
with an available quota of $6.00 trillion to meet funding needs. 
Additionally, Banco de Occidente’s shares are listed and traded 
on the Colombian Stock Exchange as common stock.  
Main place of business: 
Santiago de Cali, Valle del Cauca.  
Main address:
Carrera 4 # 7-61

A
Absenteeism: occurs when an employee fails to 
report to work or leaves their workplace, whether 
with or without justification. 
ADL Digital LAB: a digital services provider. 
Agile Scaling: a methodology for carrying out 
projects in a flexible, dynamic, and rapid manner 
to enhance team productivity. 
Artificial Intelligence (AI – ARI): This is the technology 
that enables machines to learn, reason, and perform 
tasks that normally require human intelligence. 
B
Balanced Scorecard: a management tool that 
applies predictive and balanced performance 
indicators from the financial, people, process, and 
customer perspectives within the company. 
Banking Correspondent: a channel that provides 
collection services through third-party partners, 
under the full responsibility of Banco de Occidente, in 
order to reach regions where the presence of branches 
is limited, thereby offering greater availability for 
customers to make their payments. 
Basel: These are the international agreements or 
recommendations on banking supervision issued by 
the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). 
Biodegradation: the ability of certain materials to 
break down naturally without human intervention. 
Biodiversity: a term that encompasses the living 
species that provide the Earth’s life-support system; 
a collection of plants, animals, insects, and fish make 
up the ecosystems that provide us with food, clean 
water, air, and energy.
Bond: a negotiable security representing a debt. 
Therefore, it can be said that when an investor 
purchases a bond, they are lending money to a 
company. The company issuing the bonds assumes 
the obligation to repay the bondholder (once the 
period established in the bond has elapsed) the 
amount of the investment plus a sum of money as 
interest (this is the investor’s return). 
BPO: the outsourcing of business process functions 
to service providers, whether internal or external to 
the company. 
Braille: A reading and writing system composed of 
raised dots used by people with visual impairments 
to understand text through touch with their fingers. 
Bre-B: Colombia’s interoperable instant payment 
system, administered by the Central Bank, which 
enables real-time transfers and payments between 
users and merchants from different financial 
institutions using “keys” (e.g., cell phone number, ID 
number, or email) and/or QR codes. C
C 
Carbon Footprint: an indicator of the environmental 
impact of human activities in terms of the number 
of resources used and generated.
Career Plan: a defined growth path that allows 
employees to plan their careers at Banco de Occidente 
in accordance with their skills and expectations. It 
is integrated with our Corporate University, and we 
are currently developing learning pathways for each 
position. The operational and commercial career 
plans are currently in place. 
Carpooling: an English term meaning “to share a 
vehicle,” where several people travel along defined 
routes to the same destination, with the aim of 
reducing the use of private vehicles with only one 
person on board. 
CDC: In technology, this stands for Change Data 
Capture, software that allows for the integration, 
optimization, and efficient management of databases. 
Coaching: Professional training provided to 
an individual to help them achieve their goals 
through communication, self-confidence, personal 
development, and leadership. 
Collective Investment Funds: a mechanism or 
vehicle for saving or managing sums of money or 
other assets, formed through contributions from a 
number of identifiable individuals once the fund 
begins operations. These resources are managed 
collectively to achieve collective economic results. 
Glossary
Commercial Trust: a legal arrangement whereby a 
person, known as the settlor, transfers one or more 
specified assets to another, known as the trustee, 
who undertakes to manage or dispose of them to 
fulfill a purpose determined by the settlor, for the 
benefit of the settlor or a third party known as the 
beneficiary or trust beneficiary. 
Content Hub: a web space where all of the platform’s 
content converges, regardless of format. 
Contractor: a person hired by the reporting 
organization to perform work that would otherwise be 
performed by an employee, at a workplace controlled 
by the organization. 
Credit Risk: the possibility that one party to a 
financial contract will be unable to meet its financial 
obligations; as a result, the other party suffers a loss.
Credit Scoring: a credit assessment methodology 
that consists of assigning a score to a potential 
borrower. This is intended to measure the customer’s 
ability to pay. 
Critical Talent: high-impact positions that are crucial 
to achieving the organization’s objectives; replacing 
them entails significant costs, so they are carefully 
selected from the workforce.
CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score): This is the 
metric that measures customer satisfaction with 
the channel used to submit a request or complete 
a transaction.

Customers: individuals or companies that purchase, 
for their own use, products and/or services offered 
by Banco de Occidente and its subsidiaries. 
Cybersecurity: the practice of protecting critical 
systems and confidential information from potential 
digital attacks.
D
Dale: a digital wallet from Grupo Aval that allows 
users to send and receive money, make payments, 
withdraw cash from ATMs, and top up their balance 
easily and securely from their cell phone, without 
the need for a traditional bank account. 
Dashboard: A tool or control panel that displays 
performance indicators to track business objectives 
and processes.
Dematerialized Promissory Note: a security backing

than in physical form. 
Digital Ratio: In marketing, this refers to the 
percentage of interested parties who visit a website 
and complete the process of being promoted. 
Disability: Disability is a concept that encompasses 
the sensory, physical, cognitive, intellectual, 
psychosocial, and multiple differences a person 
may have. It is linked to physical, attitudinal, and 
communication barriers that limit their participation 
and access to various work, social, and economic 
settings, among others. 
Discharges: the final disposal of liquids into bodies 
of water, soil, or sewers. 
Emotional benefit: the benefit received by an 
employee, in addition to their financial compensation, 
related to their feelings and emotions that create a 
bond with the company or brand. 
Employee: a person who has a direct employment 
relationship with our Bank through a fixed-term or 
indefinite employment contract, and who fulfills 
certain duties in exchange for compensation that 
includes statutory and non-statutory benefits. 
Employee Journey: A metric that tracks an employee’s 
trajectory and performance within the company from 
their start date to their retirement. 
Employer Brand: processes for recruiting, engaging, 
and retaining talent. 
Energy efficiency: the ability to achieve the same 
or better results using the least possible amount of 
energy resources.
ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance): 
an approach that evaluates how an organization 
manages its environmental impacts, its relationships 
with people (employees, customers, the community), 
and the quality of its corporate governance. 
F
Fiduciary Arrangements: a fiduciary arrangement 
under which one person entrusts one or more specific 
assets to another without transferring ownership, 
for the purpose of having the latter fulfill a specific 
objective, either for the benefit of the settler or a 
third party. 
Discrimination: actions or omissions that exclude, 
harm, or otherwise affect (physically, psychologically, 
structurally, or through other forms of violence) a 
person because of their sexual orientation, gender 
identity, ethnicity, age, disability, place of origin, 
class, or other distinguishing characteristics. 
Diversity: refers to the many ways of being that 
characterize the groups and societies that make up 
humanity; it manifests itself in the plurality of identity, 
social, cultural, ethnic, and religious characteristics, 
among others, which define each person and add 
value to society. 
Donation: a purely voluntary act by which a natural 
or legal person provides resources in cash or in kind 
for the benefit of another, without receiving anything 
in return. 
E
EASPBV: Low-Value Payment System Administrators. 
Electric Vehicle: A car or land vehicle that uses 
electrical energy for mobility and must be connected 
to a power source. 
Electronic Channels: mechanisms or options offered 
by our Bank to conduct transactions online. E
Electronic kiosks: a physical self-service channel 
that allows users to perform transactions such as 
payments, inquiries, and withdrawals, among others, 
using a debit or credit card from Banco de Occidente 
or Grupo Aval entities. 
Finance for Biodiversity: a global initiative that 
seeks to mobilize the financial sector to support the

responsible investments and sustainable strategies. 
Financed Emissions: greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 
resulting from loans. 
FINDEV: Canada’s development finance institution

Franchise: a commercial contract through which 
a license is granted for the use of a brand and 
procedures. 
Fusiondata: a government entity management 
system and technological platform of the Attorney 
General’s Office of Colombia. 
G
Global Compact: a UN initiative that encourages 
companies to adopt principles regarding human 
rights, labor standards, the environment, and anti￾corruption to promote sustainability and corporate 
responsibility. 
GPTW Certification: an award granted by the Great 
Place to Work Institute and Icontec that certifies 
organizations with high standards of quality in the 
workplace and highlights the best places to work 
nationally and internationally.
GRI - Global Reporting Initiative: An international 
standard that guides organizations in the preparation 
of sustainability reports, defining how to transparently 
report their economic, environmental, and social 
impacts.

H
Hybrid: A work arrangement that allows employees 
to work from home a few days a week and in the 
office the rest of the time. 
Hybrid Vehicle: A car or land vehicle that combines 
gasoline or diesel combustion with an electric motor 
for propulsion. 
I
IDB (Inter-American Development Bank): a 
multilateral organization whose objective is to 
provide financial solutions for the economic and 
social development of the region. 
INS (Response Satisfaction Index): An indicator 
that measures customer satisfaction with the quality 
and clarity of the responses they receive to their

L
Licenses: The right to use software or any other 
creation associated with a programming language. 
Liquidity: The ability of a person or company to 
convert their assets into cash to meet their financial 
obligations. 
Liquidity Risk: the probability of incurring losses due 
to a lack of sufficient resources to meet assumed 
obligations. 
Loan Reference Rate (LRP): the benchmark interest 
rate used by commercial banks to set interest rates on 
loans granted to their most creditworthy customers.
M
Market Risk: potential loss in the value of financial 
assets caused by adverse changes in the factors 
that determine their price.
Market Share: in marketing, this refers to the indicator 
of the organization’s market share or market fraction 
within a specific segment. 
Material efficiency: a metric that compares measures 
of cost, efficiency, and the flow of raw materials in 
their consumption, transformation, and disposal to 
optimize processes.
Materiality: In sustainability management, this 
refers to the environmental, social, and governance 
aspects that the organization prioritizes based on 
their positive or negative impact on its stakeholders.
MSCI Colcap: an index created jointly by MSCI and 
the Colombian Stock Exchange (BVC), designed 
to represent the performance of the Colombian 
stock market and aimed at including a minimum 
of 25 securities and 20 issuers based on market

N
Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR): corresponds to 
the ratio between Available Stable Funding (ASF)

NEXA BPO: a trademark of the subsidiary Ventas

O 
Occupational Hazards: a source or situation that 
can cause injury or harm to health.
Occupational Illness: a work-related injury, ailment, 
or illness resulting in any of the following: death, days 
of sick leave, work restrictions or transfer to other 
positions, fainting, or medical treatment beyond 
first aid; or a serious injury or illness diagnosed by a 
physician or other certified healthcare professional, 
even if it does not result in any of the foregoing.
Omnichannel: refers to all touchpoints in the customer 
lifecycle—such as websites, social media, real-time 
chats, emails, and phone calls—working together 
to ensure that the user’s needs are met quickly and 
seamlessly. 
Open Banking: a model that facilitates the exchange 
of information among all types of financial institutions 
through application programming interfaces (APIs). 
In this model, users are the owners of their financial 
information; therefore, they decide whether or not 
to share their data, with the aim of offering new 
products and services tailored to customer needs.N
Operational Risk: the possibility that the entity 
will incur losses due to deficiencies, failures, or 
inadequate functioning of processes, technology, 
infrastructure, or human resources, as well as due to 
the occurrence of external events associated with 
these. It includes legal risk.
Organic Content: refers to advertising (ads, news) 
or content that is distributed through digital media 
at no cost. 
Other Intellectual Property Rights: any other 
right that recognizes ownership of an invention in 
accordance with current regulations. 
P
Parental Leave: leave granted by the company to 
employees who become parents. Our Bank grants 
additional days beyond those required by law.
Patents: an industrial property right that recognizes 
the invention of a product or process, with an inventive 
step and industrial applicability. 
Payment Gateway: a service that allows merchants 
to process customer payments through the electronic 
(online) exchange of data between the seller’s and 
buyer’s banks, enabling the use of various payment 
methods (e.g., PSE, credit card, debit card, cash,

services such as building the merchant’s website, 
integrating payment buttons via Web Services or 
APIs, and providing enriched online information.
Pensioner: a person receiving a pension, primarily 
due to retirement, widowhood, disability, or incapacity.
Pet-Friendly: Offices that allow pets (primarily 
dogs and cats) to enter and remain on the premises 
accompanied by their owners so that the owners 
can carry out their work activities.
Pricing: The process of setting prices for products 
and services.

Senior Citizens: adults aged 60 and older; also

Share of Cash: An indicator that measures the

Share Of Wallet: An indicator that estimates the

Solar Energy: a renewable energy source produced

Solvency Ratio: corresponds to the ratio between

Sponsorship: financial support provided to an entity

Stakeholders: individuals or groups of individuals

Success Factor (SSFF): a cloud-based application

Supplier: an individual or legal entity that offers

Sustainable Mobility: a transportation program

Retention Plan: consists of the various actions or

Self-managed: when an individual independently

Private Equity Funds: closed-end collective

Prospects: A person or company that shows interest

PSE Button: a digital tool that allows our customers

Public Trust: fiduciary arrangements entered into

R
Ransomware: A type of malware that locks or

Recruitment: the process of hiring or selecting

Recycled PVC: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) plastic

Recycling: The reprocessing of products or product

About 
this report
| GRI 2-1; 2-2; 2-3; 2-4; 2-5 |
At Banco de Occidente, we view sustainability as a 
cross-cutting element of our management and the 
way in which we create value for our stakeholders. In 
this context, we present the 2025 Management and 
Sustainability Report, prepared on an annual basis 
and which outlines the main progress, challenges, and 
actions undertaken by the Bank during the period from 
January 1 to December 31, 2025. Unless otherwise 
indicated, the information presented pertains to 
Banco de Occidente S.A. and its main subsidiaries, 
which are specifically mentioned where applicable.
This report has been prepared in accordance with 
the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards 
and is supplemented by other frameworks relevant 
to the financial sector, such as the Sustainability 
Accounting Standards Board (SASB) sectoral 
indicators and the recommendations of the Task 
Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures 
(TCFD), as well as in compliance with Circular 031 
of 2021 issued by the Financial Superintendency of 
Colombia. Additionally, the report details our voluntary 
sustainability management efforts, in alignment with 
international initiatives and frameworks such as the 
ten principles of the United Nations Global Compact,
the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and 
our participation in financial sector assessments and 
benchmarks, including the Dow Jones Sustainability 
Index (DJSI) and the United Nations Environment 
Program Finance Initiative (UNEP FI).
The report’s content is structured based on the 
results of our updated double materiality analysis, 
conducted with the support of Deloitte, which allows 
us to prioritize our most material topics in terms of 
impact on both the Bank and the environment. The 
results of this analysis, as well as the report’s content, 
were reviewed and approved by Senior Management 
and the Board of Directors as part of the Bank’s 
sustainability governance mechanisms.
To enhance the credibility of the reported information, 
the report underwent an independent limited 
assurance process conducted by BDO Audit S.A.S. 
Additionally, regarding financial information, the 
Bank is audited by KPMG S.A.S., whose scope 
and conclusions are detailed in the corresponding 
appendices. 
Throughout the report, the term “Bank” refers to Banco 
de Occidente S.A., and “Organization” includes the 
Bank and its main subsidiaries, which are specifically 
mentioned where applicable. 
For inquiries, comments, or requests related to this 
report or the information presented, please contact 
us at:
Daniel Lopez
Sustainability Manager
dflopezs@bancodeoccidente.com.co

## Pagina 11

Message from the President
having achieved 66 points on the Dow Jones 
Sustainability Index, placing us in the 89th percentile. 
In addition, we successfully completed the audit of 
our Carbon Footprint verified by ICONTEC and 
strengthened our ESG strategy with clear policies 
on human rights, biodiversity, and climate action.
Sustainability is becoming a structural pillar of risk 
management and business strategy.
In digital transformation, we further advanced the 
modernization of our channels and processes,
strengthened our participation in the instant payments 
ecosystem and the use of artificial intelligence with 
more than 87 analytical models and over 10 assistants, 
and expanded digital solutions for individuals and 
businesses. Today, more than 205,000 customers
manage their relationship with the Bank through our 
digital channels. 
We consolidated our reputational standing, climbing 
21 positions in the Merco Empresas ranking to reach 
52nd place nationally and sixth place in the financial 
sector. We positioned our spokespersons as leaders 
in the country’s financial and economic sectors. 
Celebrating 60 years was also a symbolic act: we 
illuminated our headquarters in Cali as a tribute to 
the city where we were founded and as a sign of 
our focus on the future. That light symbolizes our 
aspiration to continue being a solid, accessible, and 
relevant institution for the country’s development.
| GRI 2-22 |
In 2025, we celebrate 60 years of history. Six 
decades supporting people and businesses 
across Colombia from Cali, the city where we were 
founded, evolving with a presence in the country’s 
various regions, its businesses, and its families. This 
anniversary is not just a number; it is the confirmation 
of a journey built on trust, strength, and long-term 
vision. 
We are marking our 60th anniversary at a time of 
consolidation and growth. We closed the year with 
sustained growth, net income of $533.655 billion 
(+7.81%), and assets of $82.16 trillion (+13.1%), 
reflecting a robust and disciplined business model. 
Our loan portfolio reached $51.8 trillion (+4.2%) and 
deposits $53.86 trillion (+11.8%), reaffirming the trust 
of our customers and the market. 
But beyond the financial results, 2025 was a year 
that reaffirmed who we are. 
For the third consecutive year, we were recognized 
as the best place to work in Colombia by Great 
Place to Work. This recognition confirms that an 
organization that cares for its people strengthens 
its ability to better serve its customers and generate 
sustainable value over time.
In sustainability, we made decisive progress. For 
the first time in our history—and in just two years—
we were listed in Standard & Poor’s (S&P) Global 
Sustainability Yearbook in the Members category,
We are part of Grupo Aval, operate in accordance 
with international standards, and have maintained 
a triple-A (AAA) rating for the twenty-eighth 
consecutive year. This consistency reflects the 
discipline, prudence, and responsibility that guide 
our actions. 
Looking ahead, our commitment is clear: to continue 
making the development of individuals and their 
families, business growth, and the sustainable 
transformation of Colombia a reality. With a personal 
touch, rigor, and a vision that combines profitability, 
impact, and purpose. 
Thank you to our employees, customers, 
shareholders, and partners for these 60 years of 
trust. We will continue moving forward, with the 
determination of those who understand that our 
true strength lies in building long-term relationships 
and consistently supporting our customers in every 
decision that drives their growth.
Gerardo Silva Castro. 
President, Banco de Occidente.

## Pagina 12

About Us
We are Banco de Occidente, a financial institution 
with 60 years of experience in Colombia, committed 
to the country’s economic and social development. 
Since 1965, when we began operations in Cali, 
we have supported individuals, businesses, and 
productive sectors in their projects and decisions, 
offering financial solutions that meet their needs and 
contribute to sustainable growth and the creation 
of value for our stakeholders.
Our history is reflected today in a broad presence 
across the country, with more than 168 branches, 13 
Credit Centers, and 269 ATMs in Colombia, as well 
as in our international operations through subsidiaries 
in Panama and Barbados. This network allows us to 
stay close to our customers and respond promptly 
to the dynamics and needs of the different regions 
and markets where we operate.
Our purpose guides the way we operate and make 
decisions: to make the development of people, 
the growth of businesses, and the transformation 
of the country a reality. Based on this purpose, 
we seek to build long-term relationships with our 
customers, drive business development, promote 
financial inclusion, and contribute to the well-being 
of the communities where we operate, always acting 
with responsibility, ethics, and a vision for the future.
As part of the Colombian financial system and 
Grupo Aval, we conduct our business with a strategic 
approach that integrates sustainability into our 
operations. This approach allows us to adapt to a 
constantly evolving environment, manage risks and 
opportunities responsibly, and strengthen the trust 
of our stakeholders. 
To achieve our purpose, we are guided by four 
strategic pillars that define our roadmap and 
strengthen our ability to generate sustainable value 
over the long term.
Values that guide our management
Honesty
We build trust through 
consistency between what we 
think, say, and do.
Respect
We recognize and value 
people for their integrity.
Determination
We believe in our ability and 
talent to make things happen.
Cooperation
We work together to make 
things happen.

## Pagina 16

For 60 years, at Banco de Occidente we have evolved alongside Colombia, supporting the 
development of people and businesses in a changing environment. Our history is marked by 
expansion, innovation, a commitment to sustainability, and the continuous transformation of our 
business, always maintaining closeness and trust as the pillars of our operation.
Our History and Legacy
Foundation and 
Consolidation
We were founded in Cali and took our first steps 
as a financial institution, consolidating our 
regional presence and laying the foundations 
for a banking model.
Growth and 
Diversification
We expanded our coverage nationwide, opened 
our first branches outside Cali, and integrated 
new subsidiaries, strengthening our service 
portfolio and our national and international 
reach, including the consolidation of operations 
in Panama and Barbados.
Modernization and 
Financial Innovation
We pioneered innovative solutions such as 
the launch of the Credencial Credit Card in 
1976, strengthened our business units, and 
advanced the transformation of our brand 
image, processes, and channels to respond 
to new market dynamics.
Sustainability, digital 
transformation, and 
customer experience
We have established sustainability as a strategic 
pillar of our business, from historic initiatives 
such as the National Ecology Award in 1993 to 
the strengthening of our Sustainability Strategy 
in 2021. At the same time, we have accelerated 
the digitization of our services, implemented 
new business models, and modernized our 
branches to enhance customer experience 
and strengthen our reputation.
To learn more about the key milestones in our history, we invite you to visit the 
Our History section on the Bank’s website.

Banco de Occidente de Panamá
Banco de Occidente de Panamá operates under the International Banking License framework and 
holds a Securities License that allows it to offer clients a wide variety of investment portfolios, with 
a business model focused on international lending and portfolio placement and raising foreign 
currency funding, primarily from Colombia, through time and demand deposits. Its operations 
strengthen the Bank’s international presence and enhance its ability to serve clients with cross-border 
financial needs. 
Occidental Bank Barbados
Occidental Bank Barbados is part of the International Banking License regime and plays a key role in 
managing international loan portfolios and attracting foreign currency deposits. From Barbados, 
the subsidiary supports clients engaged in cross-border operations and contributes to the Bank’s 
geographic and financial diversification.

Fiduciaria de Occidente
Fiduciaria de Occidente is a company specializing 
in the fiduciary administration of assets and 
estates, dedicated to entering into commercial 
trust agreements and fiduciary mandates without 
transfer of ownership. It provides investment, 
administration, guarantee, and custody services 
for individuals and companies, adhering to high 
standards of transparency, information security, 
and responsible management.
Since 1991, it has established itself as a key player 
in Colombia’s economic and social development, 
supporting project structuring and execution 
through the management of mutual funds, 
private equity funds, trusts, estate planning 
solutions, and guarantee schemes, thereby 
helping its clients achieve their financial goals.

## Pagina 20

In Panama, we operate an office that allows us to serve corporate clients and facilitate foreign trade operations, investments, and specialized financial services. 
This service enhances our connection to international markets and contributes to the strengthening of cross-border business. Meanwhile, in Barbados, we 
maintain an office whose objective is to support international financial operations, provide services related to corporate management, and facilitate interaction 
with Caribbean jurisdictions. This presence allows us to offer more comprehensive and competitive solutions to clients with regional needs.
Our market 
presence 
National and 
International Presence
Banco de Occidente has a broad national presence 
that allows us to serve our customers and users 
throughout Colombia. Through branches, ATMs, and 
an extensive network of banking correspondents, 
we facilitate access to financial services in urban, 
intermediate, and rural areas. This coverage 
strengthens our connection with communities and 
helps reduce geographical barriers to accessing 
the financial system.
At the end of 2025, the Bank reported a net profit 
of $533.655 billion, representing annual growth of 
7.81%. At year-end, the gross loan portfolio reached 
$51.12 trillion, and deposits totaled $53.86 trillion. 
In terms of assets, the Bank closed the year with a 
balance of $82.16 trillion, reflecting annual growth 
of 13.1%.
In addition to our presence in Colombia, we have 
a strategic international footprint that strengthens 
the Bank’s regional reach.

Business 
Model
Our business model is based on creating value for 
our customers, shareholders, and other stakeholders 
through financial solutions that meet the needs of a

Inclusion, Sustainability, and Customer Experience 
We integrate inclusion, sustainability, and customer experience as central elements in the design of our solutions 
for people. Through initiatives that combine innovation, accessibility, and social impact, we seek to eliminate 
barriers, generate shared value, and strengthen our relationship with our customers and communities.
The development and consolidation of the UNICEF 
Credit Card have enabled us to channel resources 
to support initiatives for access to drinking water, 
sanitation, and hygiene practices in communities 
in La Guajira. In 2025, the Bank had 14.524 active 
cards, all of which were manufactured using 85% 
recycled PVC, and through this product, more 
than $2.134 billion has been allocated over the 
past four years, under the agreement with our 
strategic partner.
Won Gold at the Fintech Americas Financial 
Innovators Awards of the Americas in the 
Customer Experience category for solutions 
that strengthen the inclusion and usability of our 
products.
Key initiatives and progress:
Implementation of Touch Card on our credit 
and debit cards, which allows people with visual 
impairments to easily identify them by touch, 
improving accessibility and user experience.
We developed the “Shopping with a Purpose” 
campaign, through which we will contribute to 
Terrasos the equivalent of 1% of the average daily 
sales from purchases made with credit cards. This 
contribution will be used to acquire biodiversity 
units, helping to conserve more than 490 species 
of flora and fauna at the El Globo Habitat Bank, 
located in Antioquia.

International Context 
In 2025, we saw a global economy undergoing a process of disinflation that progressed 
at different rates across regions and without clear convergence toward central 
banks’ targets. In developed economies, inflation continued to moderate, creating 
room for some normalization of monetary policy. Even so, pressures in the services 
sector and inflationary risks kept authorities on a cautious footing, preventing rapid 
rate cuts. 
In financial markets, the year’s movements were primarily 
influenced by political, geopolitical, and trade factors. 
While there were episodes of correction in equity markets, 
these were temporary and did not imply a significant 
deterioration in economic fundamentals.  
The most notable development was the resurgence of global trade tensions, driven 
by the tightening of U.S. tariff policy under the Donald Trump administration. These 
measures targeted strategic sectors such as manufacturing, technology, automobiles, 
and intermediate goods, reintroducing the risk of fragmentation in international 
trade. Consequently, investors began demanding a higher risk premium linked to 
trade and economic policy.
Source: LSG, own calculations.
In this context, equity markets experienced a first half of the year marked by 
episodes of high volatility, driven by the uncertainty caused by trade tensions. 
However, in the second half of 2025, that volatility subsided as investors came 
to terms with the fact that tariff announcements would be gradual, subject to 
debate, or of limited scope (Figure 1).
At the same time, artificial intelligence established itself as a structural driver 
of growth and valuation in the global market. The rapid adoption of AI-based 
solutions enabled productivity gains, cost reductions, and the development of 
new business models, with a notable impact on sectors such as technology, 
financial services, manufacturing, and logistics. This phenomenon was reflected 
in the performance of leading companies like Nvidia, whose market value 
rose 38% between late 2024 and the end of 2025.
Against this backdrop, risk appetite stabilized, and equities ended the year 
on a positive note, driven by technology companies. As a result, Nasdaq rose 
20,2% in 2025, followed by S&P 500 (+16,4%). dec -24 jan -25 feb -25 mar -25 apr -25 may -25 jun -25 jul -25

## Pagina 38

United States: Labor Market 
and Protectionist Policies   
In 2025, the U.S. labor market showed signs of cooling. Unemployment rate rose, 
closing the year at 4,40%, compared to 4,00% at the end of 2024. In line with 
this, job creation also moderated: 584.000 jobs were created during the year, 
down from the 2 million created in 2024 (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Nonfarm payroll growth and 
unemployment rate (United States)
Chart 3. Annual Inflation and Interest Rate (United 
States)
Source: LSEG, own calculations.
Meanwhile, inflation ended in 2025 at 2,7%, down from the 2,9% recorded at the 
end of 2024. Although it still stood above the FED’s target (2,0%), the result was 
lower than expected, especially considering the potential effects of the tariff 
policies promoted by the Donald Trump administration.
In this context, and with a strong focus on labor market performance, the Federal 
Reserve began a cycle of monetary policy rate cuts in September. Two additional 
cuts were made throughout the year, bringing the rate to 3,75% from 4,50% at 
the end of 2024 (Figure 3).
Source: LSEG, own calculations.
Europe and China: Uncertain 
Growth Outlook  
In 2025, the European economy maintained weak growth, close to 1%, affected by 
low domestic demand, fiscal constraints, and a fragmented political environment 
that particularly impacted the region’s major economies. Eurozone inflation tempered 
from 2,4% in December 2024 to 2,0% in December 2025, reaching the European 
Central Bank’s target. Against this backdrop, the monetary authority cut rates four 
times (by 25 basis points each) during the first half of the year and then kept them 
unchanged at 2,0% in the second half, adopting a cautious stance in light of fiscal 
and political risks in countries such as Germany and France.
China continued to grow below its potential and failed to reach the 5% target. The 
prolonged real estate crisis and the lack of confidence among households and 
businesses limited the effectiveness of stimulus measures, in a scenario further 
marked by the trade war with the United States. In May 2025, the People’s Bank of 
China cut its benchmark rates by 10 basis points, bringing the one-year LPR (China’s 
preferential lending rate) to 3,0% and the five-year LPR to 3,5%. Subsequently, it 
kept rates unchanged, awaiting further cuts that could boost economic activity 
amid global uncertainty.

## Pagina 39

Commodities: Mixed 
Performance  
2025 was a year of mixed results for commodities, 
reflecting a combination of macroeconomic, 
geopolitical, and supply-side factors. Among the 
most notable gains were coffee (53,6%), natural gas 
(50,1%), gold (44,2%), and silver (42,0%). In contrast, 
the worst performers were soybeans (-5,7%), wheat 
(-6,9%), and coal (-10,9%) (Table 1). 
Table 1. Commodity Prices
As for oil, Brent averaged US$68,2 per barrel, a 
14,6% decline compared to 2024 (average: US$79,9 
per barrel). This performance was influenced by 
the imbalance between moderate global demand, 
OPEC+’s bullish production policy, and the absence of 
prolonged supply disruptions, despite a geopolitical 
context that remained complex.  
Local Context 
In 2025, the country presented a mixed picture. The 
disinflation that had begun in 2023 lost momentum, 
and inflation remained above target, with some spikes 
that led the Central Bank to maintain a prudent stance 
and a rate virtually unchanged from 2024. Even so, 
the economy recorded solid growth, supported by 
strong household consumption and firm domestic 
demand.
In 2024, the Colombian economy had shown a 
recovery with growth of 1,6%, higher than the 
0,7% observed in 2023. During the third quarter of 
2025, we observed that Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP) accelerated to 2,8%, driven primarily by the 
strong increase in government spending (6,6%) and 
investment (3,2%). However, the external sector 
dampened growth, as imports grew faster (10,6%) 
than exports (1,4%). Although investment began 
to show signs of recovery, it has not yet reached 
pre-pandemic levels. Overall, growth continued 
to depend largely on domestic consumption and 
public spending.

By sector, public administration, entertainment, and commerce stood out in 2025. In contrast, mining and 
construction remained in contraction, affected by still-high interest rates and relatively low international 
crude oil prices. We project growth of 2,7% for 2025 and 3,2% for 2026.
In terms of prices, between 2024 and 2025, inflation slowed by a mere 10 basis points, closing at 5,10%. This 
persistent inflation was linked to pressures on rents, services such as transportation and restaurants, and food. 
In this context, the Central Bank maintained a cautious stance and made a single cut of 25 basis points to 
its policy rate, which ended in 2025 at 9,25%. This cautiousness was also a response to fiscal deterioration 
and the decoupling of inflation expectations.
Looking ahead to 2026, the 23,7% increase in the minimum wage will be a key factor, as it could lead to higher 
labor costs, price adjustments for goods and services, and greater indexation in sectors such as housing, 
health, and education, in addition to an increase in fiscal spending of around 0,30% of GDP. Given these 
factors, we project that inflation will close at around 6,0%, which we expect will lead the Central Bank to 
raise the interest rate to 11,00% by mid-year. Subsequently, we expect the rate to remain at 11,00% through 
mid-2027.

## Pagina 40

Chart 5. Inflation and Central Bank Interest Rate
In 2025, Colombia’s exchange rate showed a marked 
downward trend. It started the year at $4.409 and 
closed at $3.757, representing an appreciation of 
nearly 14,8% and cementing its status as one of 
the strongest currencies globally. Throughout the 
year, the TRM fluctuated within a range of $4.480 
to $3.685.
This performance was driven by a combination 
of factors: the easing of international financial 
conditions, the peso’s appeal due to high local 
interest rates, and increased appetite for emerging 
markets. Added to this was the weakening of the 
dollar, which depreciated by nearly 10,0%, and the 
government’s debt management operations, which 
generated a significant inflow of dollars into the 
country. Together, these factors created a favorable 
environment for the appreciation of the Colombian 
peso.

At the same time, public debt deteriorated significantly 
in 2025, as reflected in the fixed-rate TES curve, which 
recorded an average decline of 103 basis points, 
with greater pressure on the short- and medium-term 
segments. In particular, the 2028 TES benchmarks 
rose by 203 basis points, while the 2030 TES showed

points.

the Ministry of Finance’s suspension of the fiscal 
rule. However, the debt management strategies 
implemented in the second half of the year by 
Crédito Público succeeded in partially containing 
the depreciation by improving the government’s 
liquidity and facilitating the meeting of its financing 
needs.

## Pagina 44

Bank 
Performance 
and Key 
Changes 
In the Commercial portfolio, there was a 5,7% decrease 
in balances corresponding to categories C, D, and 
E when comparing the variation between 2024 and 
2025. This reduction is explained by payments or loan 
normalization in 78,4% of cases, with the remainder 
attributed to write-offs.
In the Consumer portfolio, there was a 14,5% decrease 
in the balances corresponding to categories C, D, 
and E year-over-year between 2024 and 2025. This 
reduction is mainly explained by the decline in Credit 
Cards (-32,4%), which represents the most significant 
adjustment within the portfolio. Added to this trend are 
the decreases observed in Free Investment (-13,6%) 
and Vehicles (-11,7%), products that also contribute 
significantly to the deterioration in CDE categories.
Finally, in the Housing portfolio, there was a 2,3% 
decrease in the balances corresponding to categories 
C, D, and E when comparing the change between 2024 
and 2025.
In line with portfolio management, total Financial 
Investment Assets and Trading Derivatives reached 
$20,83 billion, representing a 29,3% increase compared 
to the previous year. This performance was driven by 
investments in debt securities, which showed annual 
growth of 42,3%, with a change of $3,51 billion.
In terms of liability, we closed 2025 with a total balance 
of $76,45 billion, recording an additional $9,28 billion 
compared to the previous year-end, equivalent to an 
annual increase of 13,8%.
According to the latest information available from the 
Colombian Financial Superintendency, as of December 
2025, Banco de Occidente held a 7,2% market share 
of total deposits, broken down as follows: 8,8% in 
checking accounts, 8,7% in savings accounts, and 
5,2% in time deposits. 
Within this trend, the performance of total deposits 
stood out, reaching $53,86 billion as of December 
31, 2025, an increase of $5,68 billion compared to 
December 2024, representing annual growth of 11,8%. 
Standalone Financial 
Statements  
In 2025, we recorded 13,1% annual growth in total assets. 
These increased by $9,51B compared to December 
2024 and reached a total balance of $82,16B.
The loan portfolio is the Bank’s primary asset, 
representing 61,3% of total assets as of December 
2025. The total gross portfolio closed December 
2025 at $51,12B, up 4,3% from December 2024, with 
a market share as of Dec-25 of 7,0%. By portfolio 
type: the commercial portfolio closed at $34,34 billion, 
representing a year-over-year growth of 3,6% and 
a market share of 9,0% as of Dec-25. The consumer 
portfolio reached a balance of $12,95 billion, an annual 
increase of 1,0%, and a market share of 6,4% as of 
December 2025. Finally, the housing portfolio recorded 
a balance of $3,83 billion, a 26,4% increase, and a 
market share of 3,1% as of December 2025.
The credit portfolio classified as C, D, and E recorded 
a total balance of $3,02 trillion, representing 5,92% 
of the total gross credit portfolio in local and foreign 
currency and an annual variation of -4,7%. 
This result was primarily driven by the growth in savings 
accounts, which recorded a balance of $30,72 billion, 
an increase of $2,86 billion compared to the previous 
year, equivalent to 10,3%.
In terms of deposit composition, savings accounts, 
checking accounts, and CDs accounted for 57,8%, 
14,0%, and 28,1% of the total, respectively. This growth 
in savings products is primarily due to our funding 
strategy, which is focused on meeting liquidity indicators 
(particularly CFEN) and optimizing the cost of funds.
Regarding other funding sources, it is worth noting 
the growth in Interbank Funds and Overnight Funds, 
where the year-end balance reached $12,28 billion, 
representing a year-over-year increase of 42,2%.

## Pagina 46

Consolidated Financial 
Statements  
On a consolidated basis, total assets reached $88,16 
billion at the end of 2025, an increase of $9,76 billion 
compared to the end of 2024. This increase was 
primarily driven by growth in investments in debt 
securities, associated with strategies implemented 
to support the increase in loans, both at the parent 
company and at the subsidiaries.
As for total liabilities, they stood at $81,90 billion 
at the end of 2025, representing a 13,1% increase 
compared to the end of 2024, in response to the 
funding needs of our commercial operations. 
Meanwhile, total consolidated equity closed at $6,26 
billion, an increase of $272.811 million compared 
to the end of 2024.
Consolidated net income attributable to controlling 
interests was $574.816 billion, representing a 
21,4% increase compared to 2024. This increase 
was primarily driven by growth in net income from 
financial assets or liabilities held for trading, which 
reached $890.049 million, a 36,4% increase 
compared to the previous year, mainly due to net 
gains on marketable investments, which showed 
annual growth of $463.459 million. Added to this 
was the 11,6% change in net interest income after 
impairment, equivalent to $113.072 million, broken 
down primarily into interbank lending activities.
Finally, the “other net expenses” category rose by 
12,9%, amounting to $296.371 million. A breakdown 
of this figure reveals increases in personnel expenses 
(9,3%), general and administrative expenses 
(14,2%), and depreciation and administrative 
expenses (15,7%).
Annual Return on Assets was 0,7% of total assets 
and 9,5% of equity.   
Solvency Performance  
In 2025, we continued to analyze and implement 
actions aimed at strengthening proactive capital 
management, ensuring an adequate level to meet 
both regulatory indicators and our internal risk 
appetite. This work was carried out in a context of 
increased capital requirements, stemming from the 
Bank’s designation as a Systemically Important 
Institution (SII), as declared by the Colombian 
Financial Superintendency (SFC) through Circular 
Letter 074 of 2024 and Resolution 2629 of 2024. 
This designation entailed a 60-basis-point increase 
in the capital requirement during 2025, under a 
transition framework to implement the systemic 
buffer, distributed across four phases:  
Phase 1: 30% of the buffer by Jun 30, 2025.
Phase 2: An additional 30% by Nov. 15, 2025.
Phase 3: An additional 20% by May 31, 2026.
Phase 4: An additional 20% by Nov. 15, 2026.  
At the end of 2025, on an individual basis, we recorded 
a total solvency ratio of 12,50%, representing a 
decrease of 20 basis points compared to the end 
of 2024. This decrease was primarily due to two 
factors:  
i. The reduction in the value of equity instruments 
included in the additional capital, resulting from 
the appreciation of the exchange rate and the 
lower weighting of subordinated bonds issued 
in local currency nearing maturity.
ii.The devaluation of the fixed-income portfolio 
recorded in Other Comprehensive Income 
(OCI), stemming from macroeconomic 
conditions that affected security prices, which 
reduced the value of technical reserves.
  
At the consolidated level, the total solvency ratio 
increased by 5 basis points compared to the 
previous year, standing at 12,90%. This result was 
driven primarily by the year’s profits and by the 
reduction in capital consumption driven by market 
risk.   
As relevant information, it is important 
to note that in November 2025, 
the SFC reaffirmed the Bank as a 
Systemically Important Institution 
(SII) for 2026, via Circular Letter 
068. This reaffirmation implies the 
continued application of additional 
capital requirements, in accordance 
with the current regulatory framework 
and transition plan.

## Pagina 47

Subsidiaries and Principal Affiliates  
In 2025, our subsidiaries maintained a focus on financial soundness and business continuity, with results reflecting portfolio adjustments and strategic investment moves, 
in a context influenced by the behavior of international interest rates.
Banco de Occidente (Panamá) S.A.
Overall, the operations of our subsidiary in Panama achieved the following milestones: 
Portfolio: recorded a significant change, falling from USD 546 million in 2024 to USD 523 million 
in 2025, representing a 4% decrease in balances. 
Investments: There was a 24% increase, rising from USD 281 million to USD 363 million, associated 
with the purchase of securities in response to market conditions.
Liquidity: increased by 93%, rising from USD 173 million to USD 335 million, primarily due to the 
decrease in the loan portfolio and the increase in time deposits.
Time Deposits: Balances increased by 19%, rising from USD 775 million to USD 922 million. Interest 
paid decreased from USD 39 million to USD 38 million, as a result of lower funding costs following 
the Fed’s rate cut.
Provisions: In 2024, loan loss provisions increased by 58%, due to adjustments in risk models.
Net Income: Net income for the year increased by 7%, closing at USD 16,5 million with a return on 
equity of 16,1%. 
Occidental Bank (Barbados) Ltd.
In 2025, our subsidiary’s operations in Barbados reported the following results:
Portfolio: It recorded an increase of USD 29,4 million, equivalent to 18%. 
Investments: the portfolio decreased by 5,2%, equivalent to USD 5,5 million, primarily due to the 
maturity of securities during the year and sales of securities in the second half of the year.
Liquidity: decreased by 16%, equivalent to USD 9,1 million, due mainly to the increase in the loan 
portfolio.
Time Deposits: increased by 3,3%, equivalent to USD 18 million. This performance was reflected in 
a 7,1% increase in expenses, associated with the higher volume of time deposits, although the impact 
was moderate due to the decline in funding costs.
Provisions: There was a 9% decrease, associated, in part, with adjustments to risk models.
Net Income: Net income for the year increased by 0,8%, closing at USD 5,2 million, with a return 
on equity of 10,3%. It should be noted that, during 2025, the tax rate in Barbados rose to 15%, higher 
than the 3% rate in effect in 2024. 
For the year 2025, neither Banco de Occidente Panamá nor Occidental Bank Barbados reported 
any material impacts on liquidity or solvency.   
The subsidiaries have posted solid financial results in recent years based on sound cost-cutting 
strategies, strategic alignments with their parent company, and strong long-term funding structures, 
among other factors, which help support the assumption that the business will continue to operate for 
the next twelve months.

(-4,5%), falling from $102.002 million in 2024 to 
$97.382 million in 2025, and net income decreased 
by $3.059 million (-3,5%), falling from $88.189 
million in 2024 to $85.129 million in 2025.   
In terms of liquidity and solvency, the Trust Company 
did not experience any material changes in its 
financial position, as liquid investments plus cash 
on hand remained at adequate levels: for 2024 and 
2025, they reached $85.023 million and $63.727 
million, respectively. Regarding the solvency margin, 
double-digit indicators were maintained in both 
years, with values of 28,25% in 2024 and 24,05% in 
2025, levels well above the regulatory minimum (9%).
In accordance with the requirements of Article 47 of 
Law 222 of 1995, it is hereby stated that there have 
been no significant external or internal events that 
could affect the normal course of the Trust Company’s 
operations or its results from the balance sheet date 
to the date of this report.
However, we hereby state that through Public Deed 
No. 2.647 of December 19, 2025, issued by Notary 
Public No. 37 of Bogotá, D.C., and registered on 
January 1, 2026, with the Chambers of Commerce 
of Bogotá and Cali, the spin-off was formalized 
between Fiduciaria Bogotá S.A., Fiduciaria de 
Occidente S.A., and Fiduciaria Popular S.A. (the 
splitting companies) and Aval Fiduciaria S.A. (the 
beneficiary company). Pursuant to this transaction, 
the splitting companies, without being dissolved 
or liquidated, spun off en bloc a portion of their 
assets representing the entirety of their fiduciary 
business—including managed fiduciary businesses 
and products, liabilities and assets related to said 
business, as well as the transfer of associated 
contractual positions—to be absorbed by Aval 
Fiduciaria S.A.
The spin-off was approved by the Financial 
Superintendency of Colombia through Resolution 
No. 1777 of September 23, 2025, which became 
effective on October 10, 2025.

Free Circulation of Invoices  
In compliance with the provisions of Law 1231 of 
2008 and its amendment by Law 1676 of 2013, we 
hereby state that we do not retain invoices from our 
suppliers. To this end, we have established internal 
policies designed to ensure the free circulation of 
invoices issued by vendors or suppliers.
Transactions with Related 
Parties 
For transactions with affiliated parties or related 
parties, we have procedures defined in manual 
MAN-COL-431, which stipulates that transactions 
conducted with customers classified as affiliated 
parties or related parties must be approved by the 
Bank’s Board of Directors. To this end, we maintain a 
reference list that allows the responsible departments 
to identify when a customer is included on this list. 
Additionally, we conduct a monthly review to verify 
that new active transactions with affiliated parties 
and related parties have the required approval from 
the Board of Directors.

Risk Rating 
As of the end of 2025, we continue to underpin our 
financial management with ratings that reflect market 
confidence and recognition of the Bank’s strength, 
both locally and internationally.
 Local ratings: for the twenty-eighth consecutive 
year, we have maintained the triple-A rating—the 
highest credit quality for long-term debt—and 
BRC1+, the highest payment certainty for short￾term debt, as assigned by BRC Standard & Poor’s. 
We also hold a national rating from Fitch Ratings 
of AAA (Col) for long-term debt with a Stable 
outlook, and F1+ (Col) for short-term debt.
 International ratings: According to the update by 
Fitch Ratings, we hold a Long-Term BB rating 
with a Stable outlook and a Short-Term B rating,
supported by the quality of our assets, our business 
model, and our ability to sustain modest profitability 
and capital metrics.

## Pagina 52

We continue to strengthen 
our reputation and 
brand strategy: 
On the brand front, in 2025 we strengthened and 
acknowledged our connection with people through 
focus groups held in Barranquilla, Bogotá, Cali, and 
Medellín, where we spoke with customers, sales 
teams, and employees. Thanks to these sessions, we 
confirmed that trust and closeness are the attributes 
that best represent us and reaffirm our commitment 
to building lasting relationships with those who seek 
to make a difference; that is why we developed our 
new brand campaign: “We choose to be on your 
side, on the side of those who make a difference.” 
We also participated in national cultural events 
that promote our identity, including the Manizales 
Fair, the Flower Fair, the Barranquilla Carnival, the 
Minfull Festival, the Cartagena Festivities, and the Cali 
Fair, among others. This strengthened our regional 
presence and our bond with our customers. Also, 
as part of our 60th anniversary, we illuminated the 
Bank’s main headquarters in Cali, giving the city a 
new symbol of regional pride.
Similarly, we promoted Cali’s culture and salsa 
through the documentary *La Salsa Vive*, as well 
as our support for *Ensálsate* and *Delirio*. Finally, 
we promoted sports, health, and family unity by 
supporting major sporting events such as the Giro de 
Rigo in Barranquilla, the Cali Marathon, the Medellín 
Marathon, Yeison Aristizabal’s Maratón de Sueños at 
the national level, and the Juancho Correlón Races in 
Cali, reaffirming our commitment to stand by people 
during the moments that inspire them. 
We launched the 42nd edition of our eco-book 
“Colombia, The Garden of Orchids,” reaffirming our 
commitment to showcasing our country’s natural 
riches and continuing to raise awareness about 
their care and preservation. We also welcomed a 
new collaborator to our team who will serve as 
our sustainability spokesperson: Occigüiro. We 
created new spaces for conversation (ECOS, Banco 
de Occidente’s Sustainability Forum), fostering 
community and networking among individuals 
and companies interested in sustainability. We 
exceeded our goal for visitors and views on our 
Planeta Azul Community, reaching 192.000 views 
and 119.000 visitors.
Finally, on the reputation front, we secured fourth 
place for the second quarter in the Punto Cardinal 
ranking of the banking and financial sector. We 
moved closer to our goal of entering the top 50 of 
Merco Empresas, climbing 21 positions from 73rd to 
52nd and gaining one position in the sector to reach 
6th place. Regarding press release management 
(Freepress) with our partner Llorente y Cuenta (Llyc), 
we published 970 press releases in the media, 
reaching an audience of over 579 million-nearly 
11 times the country’s population.
We continue to support our clients through our 
Distribution Desk and Economic Research team: 
We reached more than 500 companies in the 
country’s major cities through 23 in-person forums on 
economic topics. We hosted two nationwide virtual 
events with over 3.000 attendees, featuring Maria 
Claudia Lacouture and Juan Carlos Echeverry. We 
supported our clients with a regional tour schedule, 
visiting key cities such as Cali (8), Medellín (5), Pereira 
(3), Cartagena (2), and Manizales (2), where we held 
our “A 3 Voces” forums alongside the presidency 
and forums at universities.
We made significant progress in establishing 
ourselves as leaders in the financial sector, 
with 345 media appearances and an estimated 
audience of 122.3 million people. We increased the 
readership of our reports by 22%, reaching over 
5.000 readers who follow our daily analysis of the 
economic landscape, providing information relevant 
to their business and decision-making.
From the Distribution Desk, we closed the year 
with a profit of over $104 billion, achieving 117% 
of the established target. We held a 20% market 
share in TES for clients, with a volume of $68 trillion, 
representing a 12,53% increase compared to the 
previous year. 
We promoted the use of the Occidivisas tool, 
facilitating the trading of foreign currencies 
through our Personal Banking and OcciRed portals, 
resulting in a trading volume of USD 374 million—a 
figure seven times higher than that recorded in 2024.

Key 
Developments   Loans and deposits: We reached loans exceeding $33,9 
billion with annual growth of 3,95% (equivalent to $1,3 
billion), achieving 96,8% of our target and an 8,99% market 
share. In deposits, we recorded growth of 10,14%, with an 
increase of $3,9 billion, a 101,52% target achievement, 
and a market share of 7,13% (as of December 26).
We continue to strengthen our value propositions for strategic segments, with the 
conviction that every company, institution, and public entity needs tailored support. 
That is why, in 2025, we strengthened our Close, Specialized, and Timely (CEO) 
service model, with comprehensive solutions that adapt to each client’s reality and 
the unique challenges of their business.  
Corporate Banking Results 
In 2025, the Corporate Banking Division continued to 
advance our mission of driving growth for businesses and 
contributing to the country’s sustainable transformation, 
while maintaining a recommendation rate that reflects our 
customers’ trust.  
Customer Recommendation (NPS): We closed the year 
at 69%, meaning 7 out of 10 customers recommend our 
service. This result was supported by initiatives aimed at 
strengthening the customer experience, and we remain 
committed to continuing to advance practices that improve 
this key indicator for our value proposition.
Foreign currency and sustainable lines: We rank fourth 
in Colombia in foreign currency with a 10,24% market 
share, consolidating our position as a comprehensive, 
accessible, agile, and passionate financial option. 
Additionally, we managed credit lines with correspondent 
banks totaling USD $110 million with a sustainable focus 
and use (environmental and social), contributing to our “We 
Are Sustainable” strategy and the growth of the foreign 
currency portfolio (USD 50 million Citibank and USD 
60 million CAF – Development Bank of Latin America 
and the Caribbean).

Here is the performance by

$3,8 billion. 
Corporate and Institutional Segment: We 
achieved a 32,1% market share in loans, 38,7% in

to meet our clients’ needs, achieving over 20.000

rate of 71%.
SME Segment: We remained leaders in wallet share, 
with 28,04%. We drove customer engagement 
through advanced analytics models and digital

certificate programs, podcasts, and networking 
events, training more than 108.000 people and

management, with a clear focus: better supporting 
each segment, enhancing our teams’ capabilities, 
and making our service more effective through 
proximity and specialization.

developing a dedicated engagement line, currently 
in the implementation process. Additionally, we 
conducted a strategic update of the SME segment’s 
scope, adjusting service capacity and focusing 
commercial efforts on clients with greater financial 
depth and growth potential.
Prioritization and focus on higher-value 
customers: We strengthened the prioritization 
model by incorporating external potential variables 
and commercial viability criteria. This allowed 
us to classify the customer base and manage it 
more effectively, maximizing portfolio profitability 
and focusing on higher-value customers. In this 
regard, we achieved 105% compliance with the 
Financial Superintendency’s requirements, with 
indicators of 90% for beneficial ownership and

Regional presence and connection to the 
community: We strengthened our presence in the 
regions by promoting our CEO value proposition 
(Close, Specialized, and Timely) and our portfolio 
of financial solutions through partnerships, trade 
shows, and impactful events in target segments, 
such as women leaders.
Marketing and valuable content: We ran 
campaigns that reached over 9 million people.
And through our “Specialists” pillar, we provided 
valuable information via in-person tax forums 
featuring expert Tulio Restrepo, held in the 
country’s major cities, with attendance (both in￾person and virtual) of over 7.500 people. 
Through our agile framework and its scaling, we 
succeeded in turning priorities into concrete progress 
for our clients, strengthening our value proposition 
with solutions that are more digital, timely, and 
aligned with the needs of each sector.

and, in general, our clients’ daily 
cash and investment operations, we 
continue to expand our portfolio 
of solutions and services, with

self-management, and greater 
operational capacity.

Digitally Empowered Executive suite, targeting 
non-PEP SME and Corporate clients, with updated 
information in CRM/Siebel and SARLAFT. This tool 
now accounts for 10% of digital account sales; 
after two months of widespread adoption, we 
closed the year with 117 active accounts across

opening time from 1,5 days to 3,2 hours, generating 
significant operational efficiencies.

In cash management product implementations, we 
achieved 2,3 times more implementations compared 
to the previous year, consolidating the adoption of 
the portfolio among our clients. In corporate credit 
cards, specialists contributed 37% of total revenue, 
achieving 108% of the target. This was reflected in 
the following impacts: third-party payments (12,6 
million transactions totaling $368,7 billion), physical 
collections (11,4 million transactions totaling $13,9 
billion), and PSE collections (29 million transactions 
totaling $43,3 billion).
Commercial and Operational Efficiency in SMEs:

Implementation Desk, separating implementation 
tasks from commercial activities. This led to a 2,07-
fold increase in closed and implemented deals, 
improving operational and commercial efficiency. 
We increased the team’s overall compliance by 11 
percentage points (from 89% to 100%) and reduced 
the number of underperforming specialists by 6%. 
Additionally, we achieved a 20% increase in collections 
from managed accounts, boosting productivity and 
deal closures.

## Pagina 58

Retail Banking Results 
In 2025, at Retail Banking, we remained committed 
to people development, business growth, and the 
country’s progress. It was a year of challenges—
including portfolio acquisitions, inflation that did not 
behave as expected, and market liquidity needs—
but also of solid results and progress that drive us 
to continue improving.   
These were our main 
achievements: 
Portfolio and Growth Dynamics: We reached 
$17,2 billion in portfolio, an increase of $851 million 
compared to the previous year (+5,2%). This growth 
was driven by lower-risk products such as Housing, 
Vehicles, and Payroll Loans. Mortgages grew 
26,4% (an increase of $801 million), Auto Loans 
increased 3,2% ($80 million), and Payroll Loans 
grew 3,8% ($199 million).
Disbursements: We grew disbursements by 10%, 
reaching $11,7 billion, broken down into $1,4 billion 
for Housing and $10,3 billion for Consumer Loans.
Portfolio and quality: We maintained a portfolio 
aligned with our low-risk product strategy: Payroll 
Loans $5,4B, Housing $3,83B, Free Investment 
$3,34B, Vehicles $2,55B, and Credit Cards 
$1,54B. Thanks to this strategy, we achieved a 
Consumer Non-Performing Loan Ratio (NPL) 
of 3,88% as of November 2025, below the sector 
average (4,91%).
Stable deposits: We closed the year with $4,51 
billion and 22% growth, driven by CDs and savings 
accounts, which grew 27% and 22%, respectively. 
This result was driven by new products such as 
Kubo Rentable, accounts for the self-employed, 
campaigns targeting affluent Elite Plus and Elite 
customers, and our position as a market leader 
in CD rates.
Preference in Core Segments: We remain the top 
choice in the banking system for our key customers. 
As of December 2025, we achieved a market share 
of 60% in Elite Plus, 38% in Elite, 35% in Preferente 
Plus, and 20% in Preferente.
Work Environment and Satisfaction: We improved 
our work environment, raising the Great Place to 
Work score from 84,8% to 90%, and increased 
external customer satisfaction to 64% (NPS).
Housing and Vehicles: In Housing, we disbursed 
$1,4B, a 40,4% increase compared to 2024, 
thanks to the strengthening of our strategy 
targeting Colombians abroad, the increase in 
the penetration of subrogated projects from 
18% to 42%, our collaboration with construction 
companies, and improvements in legalization and 
service perception. In Vehicles, we disbursed $1,3B, 
with 4,3% growth, driven by the expansion of 
independent customers, growth in used vehicles, 
the self-managed channel, and our presence at 
dealerships.
Credit Cards: We recorded $4,1 billion in revenue 
in 2025, exceeding the target by 108% and growing 
14,8% compared to 2024.
Value proposition in high-end segments: We 
relaunched the Black Mastercard with 5% 
cashback on entertainment and integrated 
the Priceless premium experiences platform, 
positioning ourselves as the only bank in Colombia 
with this ecosystem of benefits.
Product Innovation and Sustainability: We began 
issuing the Black Mastercard Metal Card, made 
from recycled stainless steel, as a demonstration 
of our commitment to sustainability and a strategic 
focus on high-value segments.
Partnership with Terrasos: We established a 
pioneering partnership that allows Colombians 
to invest in biodiversity through an average 
percentage of their purchases made with the 
Classic Credencial Card (Mastercard or Visa). 
The Bank will allocate 1% of the average daily 
turnover during the campaign period to purchase 
Tebu®, supporting the restoration of 340 hectares 
in the Bosque de Niebla – El Globo Habitat Bank.

## Pagina 60

Fiscal Approach 
Our fiscal management is based on clear governance, 
defined responsibilities, and an ongoing commitment 
to transparency and regulatory compliance. The Vice 
Presidency of Finance and Strategy is the executive 
body that reviews, approves, and adjusts the Bank’s 
strategy and Fiscal Policy whenever necessary, ensuring 
its relevance in light of regulatory changes and business 
developments.
To achieve this goal, we conduct a comprehensive analysis 
of both typical and atypical transactions and economic 
events, taking into account current regulations and their 
tax implications, as part of our strategy for preventing 
and mitigating risks, including tax evasion.
Our approach combines prevention, control, and 
specialized support to ensure regulatory compliance 
through:
SOX internal controls, which strengthen the 
traceability, consistency, and substantiation of 
financial and tax information.
Operational risk management (SARO), aimed at 
identifying and mitigating risks that may affect tax 
processes.
Support from specialized external advisors, who 
assist with technical analysis and the documentation 
of criteria when applicable.
This work is supported by reports and periodic review 
sessions with the Vice President in charge, which allows 
us to make informed decisions, strengthen transparency, 
and ensure responsible tax management aligned with 
our business and sustainability strategy. 
Tax Governance, Control, 
and Risk Management   
Our tax governance is based on a clear principle: 
compliance with the Tax Policy is a commitment of 
the entire organization, from senior management to 
the teams involved in processes with tax implications. 
This allows us to act with consistency, transparency, 
and responsibility in every decision.
We integrate the tax approach into operations 
through policies and controls that strengthen 
traceability and prudent risk management. We have 
SOX, which reinforces information assurance and 
internal controls, and SARO, which supports the 
management of operational risks associated with 
relevant processes.
When an uncertain tax position arises due to 
differences in interpretation or regulatory gaps, we 
document the case with the support of tax advisors 
and escalate it to the Vice President and, when 
applicable, to the President, for evaluation and 
management based on technical analysis and 
evidence.
We assess compliance with this framework through an 
annual external tax audit, which reviews compliance 
and validates the quality of tax processes and 
deliverables. Additionally, we strengthen internal 
capabilities through training in collaboration with 
industry associations and specialized institutions such 
as Asobancaria, ANDI, and ICDT, among others, 
keeping the team up to date on regulations, decrees, 
resolutions, case law, and applicable doctrine to 
minimize risks and promote an optimal tax burden.
To address concerns related to integrity and corporate 
conduct in tax matters, we have mechanisms for 
reporting to regulatory bodies via physical channels 
and email, ensuring traceability and a timely response. 
Finally, the verification of tax-related content relies 
on specialized third parties: the external tax auditor
reviews tax returns and issues its annual audit report, 
and external tax advisors assist in verifying the 
income tax return, retaining supporting evidence 
in all cases. 
Relationship with Business 
Strategy and Sustainable 
Development 
Our tax approach is integrated into the Bank’s 
strategy because we comprehensively 
evaluate every transaction or economic 
event-including atypical cases-considering 
not only legal compliance but also the 
potential tax impact.
In doing so, we seek to anticipate and 
prevent risks, strengthen transparency, 
and ensure responsible management, 
consistent with our vision of sustainability.

and Management of Tax￾Related Concerns 
Our commitment to tax authorities is supported 
by a robust compliance framework: we have 
tax advisors, as well as internal and external 
audits that help ensure regulatory compliance. 
Additionally, the tax audit acts as a key 
mechanism for identifying potential errors and 
validating their correction, in line with legal 
requirements.
Regarding the development and discussion of 
public tax policies, we participate through trade 
groups and associations such as Asobancaria, 
ANDI, and ICDT, among others. These forums 
allow us to contribute technical expertise, share 
best practices, and stay aligned with regulatory 
debates relevant to the sector and the country.
To gather and consider opinions and concerns￾including those of external stakeholders-we 
participate in meetings and forums where 
observations, needs, and opportunities for 
improvement are raised. These meetings result 
in agreements and action plans, documented 
through minutes or emails, ensuring traceability 
and follow-up.

## Pagina 64

Our Risk Management Cycle 
To ensure that this management is consistent and effective, we have structured the SIAR into four stages that 
we apply comprehensively: 
Risk Governance 
Our comprehensive risk management is supported by a risk governance framework that enables decisions 
to be guided by a long-term vision, technical discipline, and accountability. 
The Board of Directors, the Integrated Risk Committee, and the President lead and oversee risk management, 
supported by the Vice President of Risk and Collections, who coordinates a specialized team comprising 
four departments and one division: 
1. Identification
In this stage, we identify current 
and potential risks associated 
with the activities we carry out 
or plan to implement. 
3. Measurement
We assess and quantify our exposure 
to risks and estimate the impact they 
could have if they materialize. This 
measurement can be qualitative or 
quantitative, depending on the type 
of risk. 
2. Control
We define mechanisms to mitigate 
and reduce the probability of 
occurrence, as well as to minimize 
the impact when appropriate. 
4. Monitoring
We continuously monitor risk 
sources, the risk profile, deviations 
from established limits, and the 
effectiveness of the controls 
implemented.

## Pagina 65

Roles and 
Responsibilities 
From the Vice Presidency of Risk and 
Collections, and in coordination with Grupo 
Aval Holding, we work to: 
Define risk indicators, limits, and 
thresholds in accordance with the 
organizational structure, business 
lines, and guidelines of our risk 
appetite statement, based on internal 
methodologies and models.
Ensure that risk appetite, limits, and 
thresholds, as well as the associated 
results, are discussed and approved by 
specialized committees (for example: 
Financial Risk Committee—Corporate 
Banking and Retail Banking—, Treasury 
Financial Risk Committee, ALCO (Asset and 
Liability Committee), SARO Committee, 
and Grupo Aval Risk Committee). These 
elements are subsequently presented to 
the Board of Directors’ Comprehensive 
Risk Committee for consideration and 
approval.  
Commitment to Integrity and 
Prevention 
Management oversight is carried out by the 
departments under the Vice Presidency of Risk 
and Collections, which report results to the various 
committees. In addition, the Board of Directors’ 
Comprehensive Risk Committee (CIR)-chaired by 
an independent member-meets quarterly to oversee 
management, monitor the risk profile, and verify that 
policies and procedures are adequate.
Among its functions, the CIR also advises the Board 
of Directors on operations, events, or activities that 
may affect risk exposure and profile, approves 
adjustments to the SIAR, and promotes continuous 
monitoring of the risk culture. 
The Compliance Officer oversees money 
laundering risk and reports directly to the Chair, 
submitting detailed reports to the Board of 
Directors each quarter.  
Audits and Independent Evaluation
On an annual basis, KPMG conducts an internal 
audit of the management of various types of 
risk. In these audits, the results have generally 
been satisfactory; when opportunities for 
improvement are identified, each risk function 
develops action plans to address gaps, which 
are monitored and reported to the relevant 
committees. Additionally, our Holding Company 
has a Corporate Comptroller’s Office that 
periodically evaluates risk management across 
the various entities.  
2025 Focus on Cybersecurity 
and Business Continuity 
Among the high-impact risks we prioritize, we 
highlight: 
Information security and IT security 
(Cybersecurity)
Focused on preventing losses in the integrity, 
reliability, availability, and security of customer 
information, accounts, and cybersecurity in general. 
Our main mitigation actions include: 
Monitoring and management of IT security 
alerts.
Defining action plans and following up on 
findings from vulnerability and penetration 
testing of systems and technology infrastructure.
Monitoring compliance with the information 
security model of the Bank and its subsidiaries.
Approval, dissemination, and verification of 
compliance with the information security model.
Administration and renewal of the Cyber Policy.
