Risk culture: Building 
Organizational 
Capabilities 
In 2025, we continue to strengthen a robust risk 
culture, recognizing that prevention and effective 
management require both methodologies and 
ownership by individuals.
Among the initiatives we maintain and strengthen 
are: 
Strategic risk training 
for senior management
In 2025, we continue to strengthen informed decision￾making through training and refresher sessions aimed 
at senior management and the Board of Directors. 
We conduct ongoing sessions on fraud prevention 
and training on specific topics—such as interest rate 
risk in the banking book-in addition to promoting 
the dissemination of best practices in the capital 
markets.
In addition, we maintain timely communication 
regarding recent regulations, address specific 
concerns with the support of the AMV, and update 
methodological guidelines for the mark-to-market 
valuation of Treasury products.
This effort is coordinated with periodic feedback 
sessions, where each Risk Management team reviews 
results, identifies opportunities for improvement, and 
supports the implementation of corrective measures 
with the teams responsible. 
Strengthening 
Environmental and Social 
Risk Management
As a complement to our comprehensive management 
approach, and recognizing that environmental and 
social risks can affect both our clients and society at 
large, we continue to strengthen the implementation 
of SARAS (initiated in 2023 and fully implemented 
in July 2024), which covers the segments and 
commercial divisions of Corporate Banking and 
reinforces our ability to manage risks associated 
with environmental and social impacts that may 
also affect our clients’ ability to make payments . 
For more information, please refer to the Subchapter 
(Environmental and Social Risk Systems—SARAS).

Training for third parties in Operational

Business Continuity Plan (BCP) crisis

Training for process owners and

SDG 9.3; 13.2 
Risks in new products: 
prevention from 
the design stage 
In line with the regulations of the Colombian 
Financial Superintendency, we identify 
risks prior to the launch of new products, 
services, or technologies, as well as when 
entering new markets.
In this process, the risks of money laundering, 
terrorist financing, and the proliferation 
of weapons of mass destruction are 
integrated from the initial analysis, along 
with the establishment of specific controls. 
The Balance Sheet and Treasury Risk 
Management team actively participates in 
the development of new products, validating 
valuation methodologies and assessing the 
impact on risk metrics.
In this way, we seek to ensure that every 
new development remains aligned with 
our principles of prudence, control, and 
regulatory compliance, and with our 
commitment to offering responsible solutions 
to our clients. 
Emerging 
Risks 
At Banco de Occidente, we monitor emerging risks 
using the PESTAL methodology, which helps us 
analyze the environment across six dimensions:
Political, Economic, Social, Technological, 
Environmental, and Legal. Based on this analysis, 
we have identified that factors such as Climate 
change and Artificial Intelligence, along with new 
technologies that can be used in criminal activities, 
could have significant impacts—both in Colombia 
and globally—on the local economy and on our 
clients over a 3- to 5-year horizon. 
In this regard, we perform the following, 
among other tasks:
Verification of the operation of the 
alternate data center.
Testing the continuity plan for critical 
processes and testing defined 
contingency plans.
Monitoring compliance with the BCP 
management of critical third parties.
Reporting and monitoring of relevant 
BCP events to the SARO Committee.
Reporting relevant Operational Risk and 
critical third-party service disruptions 
to the Comprehensive Risk Committee 
– Board of Directors.

## Pagina 68

Emerging Risk Category Potential Impact Mitigation Actions Related governance
Geopolitical tensions
The rise in global and regional geopolitical 
tensions has created an environment of high 
economic and financial uncertainty, characterized 
by more volatile international relations, economic 
sanctions, and trade restrictions. This context may 
affect macroeconomic stability and the payment 
capacity of the Bank’s clients.
Geopolitical  Potential impacts on the business
Market risk: increased volatility in interest rates, 
exchange rates, and asset prices.
Liquidity risk: potential restrictions on international 
capital flows and increased regulatory pressure.
Credit risk: deterioration in repayment capacity 
and an increase in delinquency rates.
Operational risk: disruptions in international 
payment channels and increased exposure to 
cyber incidents.
Reputational risk: increased regulatory scrutiny 
and exposure to sanctions.
As a bank, we continuously develop policies, limits, and indicators to 
measure exposure to various risks. These parameters are continually 
adjusted in line with market conditions to anticipate and prevent 
situations arising from geopolitical tensions that could impact the 
bank’s results.
Additionally, we constantly monitor and track portfolio performance, 
identifying the economic sectors, types of companies, and customer 
profiles most affected. This information is used to propose adjustments 
to lending policies and strengthen portfolio normalization strategies 
for customers already experiencing adverse effects.
This monitoring is complemented by periodic reviews in various 
senior management committees, where the bank’s current situation 
is analyzed and timely decisions are made to mitigate the potential 
effects of this risk. 
Financial Risk Committee –

Artificial Intelligence and New Technologies for 
Criminal Purposes
The misuse of artificial intelligence and emerging 
technologies can increase the Bank’s exposure to 
digital fraud, identity theft, information theft, and 
sophisticated cyberattacks, affecting information 
security and business continuity.
Technological Currently, this risk has a significant impact on 
our sector, exposing us to critical impacts such 
as information theft through applications, loss 
of resources due to identity theft, extraction of 
confidential data using emerging technologies 
installed on frequently used devices, as well 
as information hijacking and extortion for its 
recovery. These situations can result in fraud, loss 
of customer data, and sensitive bank information, 
which increases the likelihood of reputational 
risk due to the impact on service continuity and 
quality.
The Bank is moving forward with the implementation of communication 
strategies for customers and employees, aimed at reinforcing 
preventive measures and authenticity verification against potential 
requests generated by artificial intelligence. Additionally, we are 
strengthening authentication protocols across the Bank’s channels 
and services.
To mitigate the risks associated with the use of new technologies 
for criminal purposes, we have incorporated malware protection 
solutions for business clients and developed digital risk awareness 
initiatives aimed at clients and employees. We have also strengthened 
our cybersecurity tools to prevent unauthorized access and potential 
impersonation attempts.
Additionally, the Artificial 
Intelligence Committee was 
created, tasked with monitoring 
emerging risks and promoting 
timely actions for their mitigation.

## Pagina 69

Credit Risk 
Nature of the risk
As of December 31, 2025, our total loan portfolio 
stood at $51,12 billion, representing annual growth 
of 4,34%. This portfolio was broken down as follows: 
67,17% commercial loans, 25,33% consumer and 
retail loans, and 7,50% housing loans. Compared 
to December 2024, the commercial portfolio grew 
by 3,62%, the consumer portfolio by 0,99%, and the 
housing portfolio by 26,36%. 
In the commercial portfolio, the breakdown by 
product was: 71,21% ordinary loans, 19,14% leasing, 
6,69% treasury, 2,67% factoring, and 0,29% credit 
cards. In the consumer portfolio, payroll loans 
accounted for the largest share (42,15%), followed 
by unsecured loans (25,74%), auto loans (19,88%), 
credit cards (11,97%), and revolving credit (0,26%). 
We serve commercial clients across various economic 
activities, grouped into 18 sectors. The most significant 
sectors were: manufacturing with 15,38% ($5.282.664 
million), financial and insurance activities with 
13,34% ($4.580.681 million), wholesale trade with 
9,89% ($3.395.962 million) and retail trade with 
7,76% ($2.664.831 million). The remaining 53,63% 
was concentrated in other activities. During 2025, the 
growth of the commercial portfolio was driven, in part, 
by increased exposures to clients such as the Bogotá 
Mayor’s Office, the APP GICA Autonomous Fund, 
the Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia, 
and the Special District of Science, Technology, 
and Innovation, among others.
Portfolio Quality and Market 
Position
In the commercial portfolio, we ranked fifth in the 
system, with a market share of 9,01% as of November 
2025. The Non-Performing Loan Ratio (NPL Ratio) 
stood at 3,14% as of November 2025, unchanged 
from the level in November 2024. Compared to 
the major banks, we maintain the second-best 
commercial NPL Ratio, 20 basis points below the 
banking system’s NPL Ratio (3,34%).
In the consumer loan portfolio, we ranked sixth 
in terms of outstanding balance, with a 6,45% 
share of the total system. The non-performing 
loan portfolio increased by 0,40%; however, most 
product categories saw declines, with credit cards 
(-34,73%) and unsecured loans (-24,76%) posting 
the largest decreases. The consumer ICV maintained 
a downward trend throughout 2025 and closed at 
3,97%, a decrease of 0,02% compared to the end 
of 2024 (3,99%).
In the housing portfolio, the non-performing portfolio 
increased by 24,19% compared to 2024. However, 
the ICV decreased by 0,08% and closed at 4,83%. 
During 2025, inflation and unemployment continued 
to fall and GDP grew, which strengthened repayment 
capacity. 
Overseas Subsidiaries: 
Portfolio Performance 
Among our international subsidiaries, as of December 
2025, Banco de Occidente Panamá reported a loan 
portfolio of US$523.318.550. 99,97% of which was 
in the commercial portfolio. Its non-performing loan 
ratio stood at 0,43%, the at-risk loan ratio at 1,94%, 
and the loan loss coverage ratio at 1,05%, indicating 
stable portfolio indicators at the end of 2025.
Meanwhile, Occidental Bank Barbados closed 
December 2025 with a portfolio of US$198.800.333, 
100% of which was in the commercial portfolio. The 
non-performing portfolio stood at 1,41%, the portfolio 
at risk at 2,00%, and the provision coverage ratio at 
0,96%. Overall, we observed strong performance in 
portfolio quality indicators across our subsidiaries.
Assessment and Measurement
To extend credit responsibly, we use various internal 
risk measurement models that help us make 
consistent decisions, classify our customers, and 
monitor portfolio performance in a timely manner.
In the consumer loan portfolio, we use scoring 
models that, starting with the initial assessment, 
assign a score to the customer based on credit 
bureau variables and industry-specific behavior. 
We use this score to verify whether the applicant 
meets the Bank’s policies, including the minimum 
required score. In addition, we have monitoring 
models that rely primarily on payment behavior 
variables and product usage, which allow us to rate 
customers and estimate the probability of default 
over the next 12 months.

## Pagina 70

Management, Monitoring, and 
Mitigation
To ensure that our models remain useful and 
reliable over time, the credit risk models applied 
to the commercial and consumer portfolios are 
monitored semi-annually (June and December). In 
this exercise, we evaluate their ability to distinguish 
between customers with good and poor payment 
behavior through backtesting, using the Accuracy–
Ratio (AR) as a measure of fit. If the AR is equal to or 
greater than 50%, the model remains in production; 
when the AR is less than 50%, a new model is 
estimated.
In addition to technical monitoring, we complement 
our management with specific analyses that allow us 
to anticipate changes in the environment and adjust 
policies when necessary. During 2025, for example, 
we assessed the impact of foreign exchange risk 
on clients in the commercial portfolio and concluded 
that clients with a focus on imports continue to 
perform well. Along the same lines, the foreign 
currency portfolio maintained healthy levels of 
past-due and at-risk balances, even though the 
total balance of this portfolio showed a downward 
trend over the year.
We also analyzed the potential impact of the tariff 
increases imposed by the United States, as well 
as the impact on sectors exposed to developments 
such as government reforms and fluctuations in 
input prices. These analyses allowed us to identify 
exposure by sector, the number of clients involved, 
and possible effects on portfolio dynamics. Based on 
the results, we concluded that exposure to clients and 
sectors with potential impacts is low and/or under 
In the commercial portfolio, we use rating 
models built primarily on financial indicators
derived from clients’ financial statements. These 
variables generate the input models, and for the 
monitoring models, we also incorporate payment 
behavior variables. This approach applies to the 
industry, commerce, services, construction, local 
government, and financial institutions segments, 
with input and monitoring models designed for each.
These models serve as a cross-functional tool within 
our management framework. We use them, among 
other purposes, for: credit approval, customer 
classification, determining recommended 
loan amounts, structuring commercial lending 
programs, follow-up, portfolio rating, estimating 
loan loss reserves, and monitoring the portfolio’s 
composition by risk level.
In terms of control and monitoring, we conduct 
periodic reviews that allow us to keep management 
under control:
In the commercial portfolio, we monitor exposure 
limits by economic sector on a monthly basis; and 
as of the December 2025 cutoff, 100% of the sectors 
were within the established risk appetite.
In consumer and housing portfolios, we conduct 
monthly monitoring such as Through The Door 
(monitoring of scoring policies by product), analysis 
of disbursements by different variables, and payroll 
deduction diagnostics, where we review the evolution 
of collections and, when necessary, make policy 
adjustments to improve portfolio performance.
control. Nevertheless, as a preventive measure, we 
implemented a policy of short maturities for the 
debt levels assigned to corporate clients in sectors 
considered vulnerable (no longer than 6 months), 
to monitor financial statements and anticipate 
any deterioration that could affect the fulfillment 
of obligations.
In the consumer loan portfolio, we monitored lending 
policies based on credit scores, borrower profiles, 
and risk factors for each product throughout the 
year. These policies yielded satisfactory results 
for the 2023 and 2024 loan cycles, reflecting a 
decrease in the non-performing loan portfolio 
and the non-performing loan ratio compared to 
the previous year, and an even greater decrease 
compared to 2023.
Regarding policy adjustments, for payroll loans we 
implemented more restrictive guidelines by payroll 
provider to strengthen risk control. In contrast, for 
credit cards, we moved toward more flexible policies, 
with adjustments to the product with a guarantee 
fund and to cutoff points, among other changes. 
Additionally, on the campaign front, we launched 
initiatives that strengthened the consumer portfolio 
and contributed to a 28% growth in disbursements, 
relying on segmented, high-impact campaigns that 
increased commercial effectiveness.
Together, these actions enabled us to manage 
lending policies more timely and efficiently, 
manage origination campaigns more effectively, 
and adequately monitor portfolio performance.

## Pagina 71

Country Risk Management
During 2025, we continued to apply the impairment 
adjustment model to our foreign equity investments. 
At the Bank, we define these investments as the equity 
value reported in the financial statements of Banco 
de Occidente (Panamá) S.A. and Occidental Bank 
Barbados Ltd. In turn, this equity is supported by loans 
granted by the subsidiaries in various countries—
primarily in Central and South America—and by their 
portfolio of short- and long-term investments.
To assess this risk, we conduct an annual country risk 
study that incorporates economic, social, political, 
and market variables, and uses them to assign a rating 
to Panama and Barbados. As part of this exercise, 
we take into account that a significant portion of the 
exposure associated with these investments is located 
outside those two countries; therefore, we adjust the 
final rating using the weighted average of the countries 
where the exposure is actually located.
As a result of the analysis, Panama was classified in 
Category B within the SIAR country risk framework. 
In this case, the rating remains at its original level, 
and no further analysis was necessary; therefore, 
no impairment adjustment is required. In the case 
of Barbados, the weighted average of the countries 
where the exposure is concentrated allowed its rating 
to improve to B, reaching its highest classification.
During 2025, we strengthened the implementation 
of the TCFD through a structured approach focused 
on governance, internal capabilities, and climate 
risk management. Multiple training sessions were 
conducted for key areas, aimed at strengthening the 
technical understanding of climate risk and its financial 
impact, which allowed for better adoption of the TCFD 
framework and its integration into risk management 
and decision-making processes.
Additionally, with Deloitte’s support, the Bank developed 
and received a specialized tool for climate risk analysis, 
which will serve as the basis for the systematic 
assessment of physical and transition risks. This tool 
will enable progress toward more consistent and 
comparable analyses, facilitating the identification 
of potential financial impacts and consolidating the 
climate risk measurement and management process 
in 2026.
In 2025, the environmental and social risk management 
process was consolidated, improvements were made 
to the categorization form, and the visibility of relevant 
aspects—such as the final categorization result—was 
enhanced. Additionally, the process was successfully 
integrated into the credit workflow, which improved 
the timeliness and quality of information for reporting 
and monitoring operations.

## Pagina 72

Operational Risk
In accordance with the provisions of Chapter XXXI 
of the Basic Accounting and Financial Circular 
(Parts II and III, on Operational Risk Management), the 
Bank manages operational and business continuity 
risk through a continuous cycle of identification, 
measurement, control, and monitoring.
In practice, this involves continuously updating risks 
and controls within processes, tracking the risk 
profile, and monitoring the event log to identify 
corrective actions that help prevent events from 
occurring and reduce our exposure. This approach 
is particularly important because operational risk is 
a key component in the calculation of the solvency 
ratio.
As of December 31, 2025, the Operational Risk 
Management System consolidated the following 
indicators:
Concepto Total 
Processes 139 
Risks 711 
Failures 1.075 
Controls 2.252 
Operational Risk Profile
As of December 2025, our residual risk profile 
remains at a low level: 75% of the 711 risks fall into 
the low-exposure quadrant.
For this assessment, we considered, among other 
factors, the following elements:
Inherent and residual risk ratings.
Effectiveness of controls.
Changes in personnel associated with Risk 
Managers.
Updates to applications and procedures.
Adjustments to processes documented by 
Process Management.
Operational risk losses
In 2025, net losses associated with operational risk 
events totaled $7.562 billion, resulting from:
Gross losses: $17.046 MM. 
Recoveriess: $9.484 MM. 
According to the Basel II classification, losses were 
concentrated primarily in:
Process execution and administration: 80% 
($6.016 billion).
Internal fraud: 27% ($2.085 billion).
Other categories: 5% ($374 million).
Additionally, recoveries from external fraud totaled 
$9.182 billion, resulting in a net loss of -$913 million 
(equivalent to -12%), reflecting the effectiveness of 
recovery mechanisms, primarily through the insurer. 
Reports to Senior Management
On a monthly and quarterly basis, we present 
information to the SARO Committee and the Board 
of Directors’ Comprehensive Risk Committee, 
including:
Follow-up on corrective actions for high and 
extreme risks
Trends in operational risk losses
Analysis of materialized events
Updates to the risk profile
Changes in processes, risks, and controls
In addition, we continuously monitor the submission 
of regulatory reports by each area of the Bank to 
ensure regulatory compliance.

## Pagina 74

Conduct Risk
In 2025, we advanced in consolidating our Conduct 
Risk Management System, in line with the External 
Guide for the Supervision of Conduct Risk issued 
by the Financial Superintendency of Colombia 
on September 24, 2024. For us, this work is key 
because it helps us protect the rights of financial 
consumers and strengthen, day by day, confidence 
in the financial system.
We understand conduct risk as the potential for 
negative impacts on consumers or the market arising 
from practices carried out by supervised entities. For 
this reason, we have been developing a management 
framework that integrates guidelines, protocols, and 
tools to promote actions that are ethical, transparent, 
and consistent with our customers’ expectations, 
with the aim of offering responsible products and 
services.
Since 2024, we have been driving the implementation 
of this system and keeping the Board of Directors 
informed of its progress, challenges, and results. To 
identify conduct risks, we conducted an analysis 
based on our operational risk matrix and a detailed 
review of the processes that make up the product 
and service lifecycle. In addition, we incorporated 
the pillars of the Customer Service System (SAC) 
defined in Law 1328 of 2009, the nature of complaints 
received during the past year , and the categorization 
of risk factors established in the Superintendency’s 
guidelines.
As a result, we adjusted the institutional risk inventory, 
which now consists of 17 behavioral risks and 238 
associated controls. In turn, during 2025, we began 
a refinement and prioritization exercise to make 
management more effective and focus specifically 
on the risks with the greatest relevance or potential 
impact on our customers.
Complementarily, we continue to promote a 
customer-centric organizational culture, supported 
by ongoing training programs for all employees. 
Through these initiatives, we aim to strengthen 
prevention, promote appropriate conduct, and 
continue to build relationships based on trust.
Liquidity Risk
Liquidity risk refers to the possibility that Group 
entities may not, at any given time, have the necessary 
resources to meet their obligations to clients and 
financial market counterparties in a timely manner, 
in any currency and location. Therefore, each entity 
reviews its resource availability daily to ensure the 
continuity and stability of operations.
At the Bank, we manage this risk under the standard 
model defined in Chapter XXXI (Appendices 9 
and 12) of the Basic Accounting and Financial 
Circular issued by the Financial Superintendency 
of Colombia, and in accordance with the principles 
of the Comprehensive Risk Management System 
(SIAR). This framework establishes the minimum 
prudential parameters that guide liquidity risk 
management and allows us to maintain consistent 
and disciplined management.
To measure liquidity risk, we calculate the Liquidity 
Risk Indicator (IRL) weekly for 7-, 15-, 30-, and 
90-day horizons, in accordance with the Financial 
Superintendency’s methodology. Additionally, we 
evaluate this indicator quarterly for the subsidiaries 
to monitor the conglomerate’s liquidity risk.
Complementarily, we measure the stability of funding 
relative to the asset composition and off-balance￾sheet positions on a monthly basis, with a one-year 
horizon, using the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), 
also under the Superintendency’s standard model.
Our daily monitoring is not limited to compliance with 
reserve requirements: we seek to anticipate changes 
in the liquidity risk profile and make timely decisions. 
To this end, we rely on early warning indicators that 
allow us to identify our current scenario and define 
the strategies to follow. These indicators include,

In these forums, senior management analyzes and 
defines aspects such as: the levels of high-quality 
liquid assets to be maintained, the minimum liquidity 
tolerance, funding and deposit-taking strategies, 
policies for managing excess liquidity, adjustments 
to existing and new products and new developments, 
the diversification of funding sources to avoid 
concentrations, hedging strategies, and changes 
in the balance sheet structure.
During 2025, the Bank maintained a sufficient

risk appetite threshold (minimum 120,0%) and well

management, ongoing monitoring of early warning

remained stable and within established limits.

## Pagina 77

The most significant exposure within market risk management was concentrated in the Parent Company’s 
fixed-income portfolio, which averaged $14,48 billion in 2025, with an average duration of 45 months 
and a 35% concentration in the medium term (more than 2 and less than 5 years). This level was higher than 
that observed in 2024, primarily due to the dynamics of the market maker scheme. It is important to note 
that this portfolio remained hedged through securities derivatives (sales) and short sales, which allowed 
for the mitigation and control of risk.
Additionally, as of March 31, 2025, the entire ALM Available-for-Sale investment portfolio (Banking Book) 
was excluded from market risk exposure under Regulatory Value at Risk (VaR), pursuant to a corporate 
decision approved by ALCO and the Treasury Financial Risk Committee.
As a result of the above, the SFC regulatory VaR showed lower exposure: the annual average was $208.939 
million, and as of December 31, 2025, it stood at $109.891 million. In any case, the Value at Risk results 
remained within the risk appetite limits defined in relation to technical reserves (annual average: 3,52% 
versus a maximum allowed of 5,50%).
As part of our management, we perform sensitivity analyses of the investment portfolios to changes in 
interest rates (measured in basis points) in order to anticipate potential impacts and adjust the strategy when 
appropriate.

Qualitative Analysis 
of Market Risk
We participate in the money, foreign exchange, and 
capital markets to meet our needs and those of our 
clients, always in accordance with internal policies 
and defined risk levels. Within this framework, we 
manage various financial asset portfolios within 
permitted limits and exposure levels.
Market risk arises from our open positions in 
investment portfolios of debt securities and derivative 
instruments, due to adverse movements in factors 
such as interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, and 
their volatility, as well as changes in the liquidity of 
the markets in which we operate.
When trading financial instruments, we pursue several 
objectives, including:
Offering products tailored to our clients’ needs, 
including solutions that serve as hedges against 
their financial risks.
Structuring portfolios to take advantage of 
arbitrage opportunities across yield curves, 
assets, and markets, seeking returns with an 
appropriate level of capital consumption.
Conducting derivative transactions for the 
purpose of intermediation with clients or to 
capitalize on arbitrage opportunities, both in 
exchange rates and interest rates, in local and 
foreign markets.

## Pagina 79

In conducting these transactions, we assume risks 
within defined limits and, when appropriate, mitigate 
them through the use of other derivative financial 
instruments.
Senior management and the Board of Directors 
actively participate in risk management and control 
through a reporting protocol and the leadership of 
various committees that conduct comprehensive 
monitoring—both technical and fundamental—of 
the variables influencing markets internally and 
externally, to support strategic decision-making.
Complementarily, the ongoing analysis and 
monitoring of risks associated with our operations 
is key to making timely decisions and evaluating 
results. Along the same lines , continuous monitoring 
of the macroeconomic environment helps us seek 
an appropriate balance between risk, return, and 
liquidity.
The risks assumed are managed through a limit 
structure for positions in different instruments, defined 
by considering each portfolio’s specific strategy, the 
depth of the markets in which we operate, the impact 
on risk-weighted assets and the level of solvency, as 
well as the balance sheet structure. These limits are 
monitored on an ongoing basis and reported daily
to senior management, biweekly to the Finance 
Committee, monthly to the Risk Committee, and 
quarterly to the Board of Directors.
To quantify market risk, we use value-at-risk models 
(internal and standard). The Boards of Directors 
approve a limit structure based on the value-at￾risk associated with the annual profit budget and 
establish additional limits by risk type.
We use the standard model to measure, control, 
and manage market risk related to interest rates and 
exchange rates, both in the treasury book and the 
banking book. These measurements are performed 
daily for the parent company and monthly for each 
of its subsidiaries, to measure and monitor risk at 
the conglomerate level.
Currently, we map the asset and liability positions of 
the treasury book into zones and bands based on 
portfolio duration, investments in collective portfolios, 
and the net foreign currency position (assets minus 
liabilities) for both the banking book and the treasury 
book, in line with the standard model recommended 
by the Basel Committee.
Additionally, we have internal parametric management 
models based on the Value at Risk (VaR) methodology, 
which complement our management by identifying 
and analyzing variations in risk factors (interest rates, 
exchange rates, and price indices) on the value of 
the instruments comprising the portfolios. These 
models correspond to JP Morgan’s RiskMetrics 
methodology.
VaR measurement methodologies are periodically 
evaluated and subjected to performance tests to 
verify their effectiveness. Furthermore, we have 
tools to conduct stress and/or sensitivity tests on 
the portfolios, based on the simulation of extreme 
scenarios.

## Pagina 80

Interest Rate Risk 2025 
– Banking Book 
Banking book interest rate risk is defined as the “current 
or prospective risk to the entity’s capital and earnings 
arising from adverse movements in interest rates that 
affect banking book positions.” In turn, Banking Book 
Credit Spread Risk (RSCLB) corresponds to “any type 
of credit spread and liquidity spread risk not accounted 
for by RTILB or by credit risk.” In line with our policies, 
we define this risk as applying only to banking book 
positions that do not consume capital due to market 
risk, and it includes asset, liability, and off-balance￾sheet items that present this exposure.
In this context, we are exposed to fluctuations in interest 
rates that may impact future cash flows. This risk may 
arise from mismatches in the repricing timing between 
assets, liabilities, and off-balance-sheet positions; 
from the use of different rate reference points ( , DTF, 
SOFR, fixed rates, among others); and from optional 
features that may alter cash flows in both asset and 
liability positions (for example, prepayments). As a result 
of changes in rates, interest margins may increase or 
decrease, which in turn may impact the institution’s 
results. To manage this exposure, we employ mechanisms 
such as hedging using derivative instruments, aimed 
at mitigating interest rate risks in the banking book.
We manage Banking Book Interest Rate Risk (RTILB) 
in accordance with the standard model established in 
Chapter XXXI (Annex 15) of the Basic Accounting and 
Financial Circular of the Financial Superintendency 
of Colombia, which defines the minimum prudential 
parameters that institutions must monitor to efficiently 
manage this risk.
To measure RTILB, we calculate two indicators:
∆VEP (sensitivity of the economic value of 
equity): estimated under six shock scenarios 
(parallel shift up, parallel shift down, flattening, 
steepening, short-term rise, and short-term fall).
∆MNI (sensitivity of the net interest margin): 
calculated under two shock scenarios (parallel 
shift up and parallel shift down), according to the 
SFC’s standard model.
∆MNI takes a short-term approach, as it measures 
the impact of the shock over a one-year horizon and 
under the assumption of a constant balance sheet, 
i.e., without growth or decline in positions. This metric 
captures the effect on the net interest margin in the 
face of a parallel shock of +/- 400 bps. Additionally, 
we calculate the sensitivity for a parallel shock of +/- 
100 bps.
For its part, ∆VEP has a long-term focus and is 
estimated under the assumption of a balance sheet 
in liquidation; that is, the entire horizon is evaluated up 
to the final maturity of the balance sheet positions. This 
metric reflects, under different scenarios, the change 
in the present value of interest-rate-sensitive assets 
and liabilities and, therefore, their final effect on the 
economic value of equity.
In accordance with the regulatory framework, the SFC 
requires that the maximum value of ∆VEP across the 
six scenarios remain below 15% of the sum of Common 
Equity Tier 1 (CET1) and Additional Tier 1 (AT1) capital. 
Accordingly, we monitor compliance with this indicator 
and maintain a risk appetite statement, which we review 
on a monthly basis.
Below, we present the results of the sensitivity analysis for VEP and MNI as of December 31, 2025, which show 
that we are within the risk appetite limit defined by the Bank (<13,00% according to internal thresholds) and have 
a margin relative to the regulatory limit (15,00%).

The management of the RTILB, incorporating credit

Stress 
tests 
Funding Ratio (NSFR), and do not constitute an 
expectation for the medium or long term.
The exercise was conducted using balance sheet 
figures as of December 2024 and projected for 
the years 2025, 2026, and 2027. Additionally, 
we incorporated 25 macroeconomic variables
for each scenario, which serve as inputs for the 
exercise and are presented in subsequent sections.
Capital Adequacy Results
In the Base scenario, the Bank meets the minimum 
requirements for Basic Solvency, Additional 
Basic Solvency, and Total Solvency under Basel 
III throughout the entire horizon. In the Adverse 
scenarios, the simulated shocks strain the indicators 
and push total solvency below the internal risk 
appetite limits, as provided for in Circular Letter 018 
of 2025. However, even under severe assumptions, 
Basic Solvency and Total Solvency remain above 
regulatory minimums, reflecting the Bank’s capital 
strength. The application of mitigants in the Adverse 
and Adverse with uncertainty in commercial 
relationships scenarios allows the indicator levels 
to be restored above internal risk appetite limits.
Liquidity Results (CFEN)
In the Base scenario, CFEN maintains a stable 
trajectory thanks to growth in available stable 
funding, offset by higher funding requirements, 
preserving regulatory compliance throughout the 
projection. In the Adverse scenario, a downward 
| SASB FN-CB-550a.2 | 
For the 2025 stress tests, conducted in accordance 
with Circular Letter 018 of 2025, we defined five 
scenarios: a Base scenario, two Adverse scenarios 
(one general and one involving uncertainty in 
trade relations), and two Adverse scenarios with 
Mitigants.
The Base scenario represents a context without 
unexpected shocks to the economy and the 
banking system.
The Adverse scenario incorporates severe 
shocks with an impact on economic activity, 
the banking system, and solvency and liquidity 
indicators, and includes a cybersecurity event 
that increases the institution’s operational risk.
The Adverse scenario with uncertainty in trade 
relations considers geopolitical tensions and 
reduced access to global markets.
The Adverse Scenarios with Mitigants maintain 
the assumptions of the adverse scenarios but 
incorporate actions by the Bank aimed at 
strengthening solvency and liquidity beyond 
the limits of internal risk appetite, as appropriate.
It is important to note that the adverse scenarios 
are hypothetical: they are constructed to model 
impacts on solvency indicators and the Net Stable 
trend is observed, explained by reduced dynamism 
in funding sources and maturities that reduce the 
availability of stable resources, without breaching 
regulatory limits. The application of mitigants, 
primarily the shift toward more stable funding and 
the anticipation of subordinated issuances, partially 
reverses the decline and restores adequate liquidity 
levels.
Meanwhile, the Adverse scenario involving uncertainty 
in trade relations shows a more favorable performance 
than the general adverse scenario, due to lower 
pressure on required funding and stress conditions 
concentrated in macroeconomic variables. In this 
scenario, the CFEN remains above the appetite limit 
and exhibits a stable trajectory, which is strengthened 
by the implementation of additional mitigants.
In line with the supervisor’s guidelines, we incorporated 
a cybersecurity event into the Adverse scenario by 
simulating a significant technological incident with 
the potential to affect operational continuity and the 
provision of critical services. The analysis considered 
operational, reputational, and financial impacts, 
as well as the activation of response and recovery 
measures, with the aim of evaluating institutional 
resilience and strengthening management capabilities 
in the face of such events.
Finally, the Stress Test exercise is a key tool for planning 
and monitoring the Bank’s financial situation, as it 
facilitates the anticipation of risks, the coordination 
of efforts, and the definition of actions to preserve 
our soundness and sustainability, offering society a 
reliable Bank to accompany its financial evolution.

## Pagina 83

SARLAFT 
The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter￾Terrorist Financing Risk Management System 
(SARLAFT) enables us to comply with national 
and international regulations for the prevention 
of financial crimes, protect our reputation, and 
reduce the risk of becoming involved in illicit 
activities. 
Within this framework, we primarily carry out 
the following actions:
 Customer due diligence: It is essential for 
us to know our customers by collecting 
and verifying information such as identity, 
source of funds, and economic activity, 
among other aspects. Based on this, we 
conduct a risk assessment that considers 
the customer’s profile, transactional behavior, 
and geographic location.
 Transaction Monitoring: We continuously 
monitor transactions to identify unusual 
patterns or red flags that may indicate 
money laundering or terrorist financing, such 
as large-sum transactions, international 
transfers, or behavior that does not match 
the customer’s profile.
 Reporting of Suspicious Transactions: 
When we identify a suspicious or attempted 
transaction, we report it to the Financial 
Information and Analysis Unit (UIAF), as 
the competent authority in this matter.
 Ongoing training: We regularly train 
our employees to strengthen their ability 
to identify red flags and understand the 
importance of SARLAFT compliance in daily 
operations.
 Audit and evaluation: We conduct internal 
audits to assess the effectiveness of the 
system, verifying that procedures are 
functioning properly and that applicable 
requirements are met.
 Comprehensive risk management: We 
identify and assess the risks inherent in 
our operations and implement mitigation 
measures against money laundering, 
terrorist financing, and the financing of the 
proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. 
This includes, among other things, the 
segmentation of higher-risk customers, 
controls over specific financial products, 
and additional security measures when 
appropriate.

In accordance with Circular Letter 068 of 2025 
from the Financial Superintendency of Colombia 
(SFC) and in compliance with paragraph 2.1.1.4.3 of 
Decree 2555 of 2010, the SFC published the list of 
Systemically Important Institutions (SIIs) for fiscal 
year 2026, based on the methodology defined for 
their identification. For this calculation, information 
as of June 30, 2025, submitted to the Financial 
System Coordination and Monitoring Committee, 
was used.
With these results, we ranked third, with a score 
of 9,58%, above the threshold of 6,45%, meaning 
that once again, and for the second consecutive 
time, we were considered a systemically important 
bank. It is important to note that this classification 
does not represent a risk assessment or rating of 
the institutions.
In this context, the Bank must continue to build 
the additional buffer for systemically important 
institutions, equivalent to 1% of assets weighted for 
credit, market, and operational risk, in accordance 
with the instructions and deadlines issued by the 
SFC in Resolution No. 2629 of December 27, 2024, 
as follows:
Regarding the leverage components under Basel III:
Tier 1 Capital (Basel III): It increased by $108.951 billion, driven primarily by sustained capital growth 
resulting from the accumulation of profits during the year, which rose 7,8% compared to 2024. This 
performance, combined with responsible decisions regarding profit retention, reflects our commitment—
together with our shareholders—to maintain an adequate level of capital to meet regulatory requirements, 
support risk appetite, and preserve a solid capital structure that leverages future growth in line with the 
strategic and business plan.
Total Exposure (Basel III): This corresponds to the aggregate value of all the Bank’s credit exposures, both 
on and off balance sheet. The observed increase was primarily driven by the growth of the loan portfolio 
and the investment portfolio, consolidating our position as an active and increasingly relevant competitor 
within the Colombian banking system.

## Pagina 85

Environmental 
and Social Risk 
Management 
System (ESRM)
in Spanish SARAS
Beyond compliance, SARAS pursues a specific objective: 
to reduce our exposure to regulatory, credit, operational, 
and reputational risks, and to ensure that the financing 
we provide is delivered according to responsible criteria, 
with traceability and consistency.
Scope and ESG Approach 
in Credit Analysis
Our SARAS applies to Corporate Banking operations, 
including the Small Business 1 and 2, Corporate, and 
Government segments, as well as operations managed 
by the Structured Finance Unit (UFE). This scope cuts 
across all industries and sectors and is incorporated as 
part of the analysis we conduct for every transaction we 
evaluate.
We integrate environmental, social, and governance 
(ESG) criteria into our credit analysis to better understand 
the nature of risk and anticipate potential impacts. In this 
assessment, we consider, among other aspects, elements 
such as the client’s relationship with protected areas or 
the SINAP, potential impacts on water resources and 
soil, respect for human rights, and practices related to 
gender equality and equity. This approach allows us 
to strengthen our comprehensive risk assessment and 
define, where applicable, recommendations or conditions 
associated with the transaction.
This approach results in an environmental and social risk 
classification that guides subsequent management and 
decision-making, maintaining a principle of consistency; 
100% of SARAS assessments are applied to our Corporate 
Banking clients, and the assessment is triggered in 
accordance with the guidelines and criteria defined in 
the system.
In 2025, we continued to consolidate the Environmental 
and Social Risk Management System (SARAS) as a key 
component of our risk management and our commitment 
to increasingly sustainable finance. This system allows 
us to identify environmental and social risks associated 
with our clients’ activities at an early stage, manage them 
proactively throughout the credit process, and make 
more informed decisions.
The development of SARAS began in 2023, based 
on an assessment and guidance from the consulting 
firm NINT, with whom we defined clear parameters for
classifying environmental and social risks among 
Corporate Banking clients. Building on this foundation, 
we have advanced in the evaluation, monitoring, and 
tracking of risks that may arise during the credit cycle, 
strengthening our ability to prevent adverse impacts and 
protect business stability.

## Pagina 86

SARAS Methodology
To ensure that the environmental and social assessment does not remain merely an intention, we have turned 
it into a clear and repeatable process. SARAS is designed to accompany the credit cycle with consistent 
criteria, from the initial screening to monitoring, and to ensure that risks are identified in a timely manner 
and managed with defined responsibilities.
How SARAS works: three stages that structure the management
Frequency of assessment and 
monitoring
Since SARAS applies to Corporate Banking 
operations, its assessment is ongoing: we analyze 
operations as they enter the process and monitor 
them using the tools defined to identify, report, and 
monitor environmental and social risks.
Governance
In 2025, we maintained a working model where 
different areas contribute their perspectives, and 
where environmental and social assessment is not 
an isolated step, but part of the comprehensive 
discussion regarding the risk and viability of each 
transaction. A collaborative effort with clear 
responsibilities.
SARAS management is built on the contributions of 
several complementary areas:
Corporate Banking Sales Force: supports the 
client and gathers the information needed for 
the analysis, ensuring that inputs are complete 
and timely.
Sustainability: conducts the environmental and 
social analysis in a technical and independent 
manner, in accordance with SARAS guidelines.
Credit and Credit Risk: conducts the financial 
and credit analysis and comprehensively 
reviews the transaction based on the Bank’s 
risk criteria.
3. Environmental and Social 
(A&S) Risk Assessment 
When an operation is classified as Risk A or B, we 
conduct a more in-depth assessment to identify 
potential impacts and define recommendations, 
commitments, and, if applicable, mitigation measures. 
This stage applies to clients categorized as Risk A 
or B.
We work with three categories, defined in our SARAS 
manual and based on specific criteria:
Risk A (high): operations associated with the 
UFE that correspond to projects in the pre￾construction or construction phases and 
exceed USD 10 million.
Risk B (medium): transactions whose activities 
may require an environmental license under 
applicable regulations and/or exceed USD 10 
million.
Risk C (low): operations with lower environmental 
and social exposure, which follow the normal 
credit cycle.
1. Exclusion List
We begin by defining what we do not finance and 
what could only be considered under very specific 
conditions. This list allows us to identify activities that 
are ineligible for financing due to their environmental 
and social impacts, and it also includes some 
exceptions, always ensuring that such activities 
do not exceed 5% of the Bank’s total portfolio
2. Risk categorization 
Based on information about the client and the 
transaction, we determine the environmental 
and social risk category. This stage applies to all 
Corporate Banking clients and allows us to focus 
our efforts where they are truly needed.

## Pagina 87

This parallel and independent 
work strengthens the quality of 
the evaluation, as it allows for the 
comparison of perspectives and 
ensures that the final decision is 
supported by comprehensive analyses.
When the nature or level of risk 
of the operation requires it, the 
approving bodies receive a technical 
environmental and social report 
that compiles considerations, 
conclusions, recommendations, and, 
where applicable, specific clauses or 
conditions associated with the loan.
This report is prepared by the Senior 
Environmental Analyst, who leads 
the comprehensive assessment of 
environmental and social risks based 
on SARAS guidelines. Its purpose is to 
provide technical input that enables the 
approval bodies to identify, assess, 
and manage potential risks, and to 
define the commitments required of 
the client as part of the approval.
Approval Levels and 
Final Decision 
All credit operations, regardless of their environmental 
and social risk category, go through the same levels 
of analysis and approval defined by the Bank. The 
difference lies in the depth of the assessment and 
the technical requirements that are triggered based 
on the identified risk level.
In general, the process unfolds as follows:
The sales team gathers information on the 
client and the transaction.
Credit and Sustainability analyze the financial/
credit and environmental/social components 
in parallel.
The findings are consolidated and presented to 
the credit approval bodies, which make the final 
decision with a comprehensive view of the risk, 
considering the analyses and recommendations 
of the involved departments.
  
Environmental and 
Social Due Diligence   
There are transactions that, due to their nature, 
complexity, or level of exposure, require a more in￾depth review. In such cases, environmental and social 
due diligence helps us make more informed decisions 
and define specific commitments that protect both 
the Bank and our clients.
When SARAS identifies a transaction with a high 
risk level, we activate a specific procedure that 
requires specialized analysis. The client must hire 
an independent external expert to conduct the 
environmental and social due diligence and prepare 
the corresponding report. This document becomes 
a key input, as it allows for a deeper examination of 
potential impacts, gaps, management measures, and 
recommendations.
Before the transaction proceeds to the decision￾making stages, the report is reviewed by the Senior 
Environmental Analyst, who validates its scope and 
conclusions and grants approval as a prerequisite 
for its submission to the credit approval body.
Through this process, we ensure that, if necessary, 
approval includes clear conditions, requirements, or 
commitments for the client, aligned with preventive 
risk management.
Integration of SARAS 
into Credit Analysis 
In 2025, we took a key step to strengthen the 
consistency of SARAS by incorporating it into the 
automated credit workflow on the Bizagi platform. 
This integration allowed approximately 90% of credit 
operations to be managed through that workflow, 
with a more organized process and clearer controls 
from the outset.
Beyond technological advancements, the 
implementation of Bizagi has had a very practical 
impact on management: we have improved the 
traceability of each assessment, as well as the 
monitoring and quality of information related to 
environmental and social risks. At the same time, 
Bizagi continues to undergo a process of constant 
improvement to achieve 100% implementation of 
our operations in the tool and consolidate a robust 
database, enabling us to conduct increasingly precise 
monitoring and tracking. This approach helps us 
work with greater rigor, identify opportunities for 
improvement, and ensure that decisions are made 
with complete, comparable information available 
at the right time.
87

Risk B: 102 transactions (0,76%), where we initiated more targeted reviews and management and monitoring

Financing Large￾Scale Projects
In large-scale projects, risk management requires 
looking beyond the financial picture. That is why, at 
the Structured Finance Unit (UFE), we incorporate 
ESG criteria across the board as part of our analysis 
of transactions, especially in construction projects, 
where exposure and potential impacts can be greater.
This approach results in a comprehensive review 
that combines technical, financial, and ESG 
considerations. In our analysis, we verify aspects 
such as the existence and validity of permits, 
licenses, and authorizations required for the project’s 
development, and we maintain open dialogue with 
the client to understand their context, management 
capacity, and the need to conduct environmental and 
social due diligence, depending on the complexity 
and level of risk.
To present a transaction to the Credit Committee, 
we first prepare term sheets, which are reviewed 
and validated by the team involved in the analysis. 
Additionally, we involve a Project Engineer, who 
assists in validating the technical information and 
supporting documentation provided by the client, 
thereby strengthening the consistency of the 
evaluation.
We adhere to a clear principle in this process: we 
do not make disbursements when the client has 
not provided the required information or does not 
meet the defined conditions. That is why we establish 
conditions precedent for disbursements, including 
the mandatory requirement that the client hold 
the permits and licenses required by applicable 
regulations and necessary for the project’s execution. 
In doing so, we seek to mitigate environmental, 
social, regulatory, and reputational risks, and ensure 
that financing is carried out in accordance with 
responsible standards.
In terms of amounts, this classification also helps us understand where exposure 
is concentrated and in which cases we should strengthen monitoring or establish 
additional commitments with the client.
These results, together with the traceability of the process, allow us to track the 
consistency of the assessment and how SARAS is integrated into decision-making.
In 2025, we recorded:
• 1 transaction rejected due to environmental or social risks.
• 0 transactions approved with mitigation conditions reported in the indicator.

## Pagina 90

Equator 
Principles 
Currently, the Bank is not a signatory to the Equator 
Principles. However, we have our Environmental and 
Social Risk Management System (SARAS), applied 
to Corporate Banking operations with a special 
emphasis on projects structured and financed by 
the Structured Finance Unit (UFE).
This emphasis has a practical reason. Due to their size, 
complexity, and nature, the projects handled by the 
UFE are those most likely to fall into medium or high 
environmental and social risk categories. Therefore, 
within the categorization process, we incorporate 
differentiated information for these cases, such as 
the transaction amount and the project phase 
(pre-construction or construction), elements that 
directly influence the final risk classification.
Specifically, when a project is in the pre-construction 
or construction phase, its environmental and social 
risk classification is defined as high, given the greater 
exposure and potential impacts inherent in this type 
of activity. From there, the SARAS team conducts 
the assessment using the tools and guidelines 
established in the policy and manual, and works 
closely with the sales force and the client to ensure 
proper management of the information and identified 
risks.
Lessons Learned 2025
Monitoring higher-exposure operations (risks 
A and B): we made progress in strengthening 
monitoring processes throughout the credit 
cycle, with a partially completed result.
Full integration of the process into Bizagi: 
we worked to incorporate SARAS into the 
credit workflow. This goal was also partially 
completed, with a key milestone: the system 
operated in Bizagi for nearly 90% of the 
evaluated transactions.
Training to minimize errors and improve 
quality: this goal was completed, leaving 
established capabilities within the commercial 
and credit teams.
Our 2025 Achievements
We implemented SARAS within the Bizagi credit 
workflow, which is the path a transaction follows 
from the moment it enters the system until its 
assessment is completed. Its objective is to 
standardize, automate, and ensure traceability 
throughout the entire SARAS process, thereby 
strengthening traceability and the quality of 
information.
We strengthened technical capabilities in 
commercial areas and within credit teams, 
improving understanding of environmental and 
social risk.
Thanks to the training, we identified cases that 
initially appeared to be low-risk but required 
further review. This led us to conduct a double 
check, and to apply more targeted assessments 
when appropriate.
We adjusted and refined the process to improve 
the quality of the data and analysis.
Goals, Challenges, Opportunities, 
and Lessons Learned
In 2025, we continue to strengthen SARAS, learning from daily operations, adjusting tools, and building 
capacity so that environmental and social assessments become increasingly consistent, traceable, and 
useful for decision-making. This progress was reflected both in the integration of the system into the 
credit workflow and in our work with the teams involved in the assessment.

Social Taxonomy 
In 2025, we continue to consolidate our Social 
Taxonomy as a tool that directs financing 
toward initiatives that generate well-being 
and expand opportunities for people and 
communities. This framework allows us to identify 
and support projects with social impact, such 
as strengthening SMEs and microenterprises, 
employability and entrepreneurship among 
vulnerable populations, affordable basic 
infrastructure, and access to essential services 
like housing, education, health care, drinking 
water, and sanitation. In this way, we foster a 
banking system that promotes inclusion, equity, 
and territorial development, linking financing 
to tangible social outcomes.

Growth of the sustainable portfolio 
Our commitment to sustainable finance is reflected in concrete results. At the end of 2025, the sustainable 
portfolio reached $4.5 billion, demonstrating the Bank’s progress in mobilizing resources toward 
initiatives with positive environmental and social impact. This performance reaffirms our role as a 
strategic partner in promoting sustainable businesses and supporting the country’s transformation. 
Composition of the sustainable portfolio 
Of the total sustainable portfolio as of the end of 2025: 
91% corresponds to the Bank’s own portfolio and 9% to the development portfolio.
$4,3 billion comes from the commercial portfolio (Corporate, Business and SME, and Government), 
representing 95% of the total.
Retail Banking (consumer and housing) contributed $0,2B, equivalent to 5%.
Balance between social 
and environmental impact 
Our sustainable portfolio demonstrates a solid 
balance between financing aimed at social welfare 
and projects that contribute to climate change 
mitigation and adaptation: 
Social portfolio: $2,6B, with a primary focus on 
women-owned SMEs.
Environmental portfolio: $1,9B, focused on 
environmental and transition initiatives. 
These results cement sustainability as a cross-cutting pillar of our banking approach:
We promote access to financing for socially impactful projects.
 We support environmental initiatives that promote efficiency, energy transition, and climate resilience.
 We strengthened the Bank’s capacity to identify and classify opportunities using an ESG approach, ensuring 
consistent portfolio growth.
With these advances, we remain motivated to strengthen capabilities, 
partnerships, and value propositions by 2026, expanding the positive 
impact of our sustainable portfolio and accelerating the transition toward 
a more resilient and competitive economy.

Sustainable financing for women-led SMEs 
In 2025, we strengthened our commitment to economic inclusion and closing gaps in access to financing by 
promoting credit solutions aimed at women-led SMEs. For us, this approach not only contributes to business 
development but also enhances well-being in local communities by supporting businesses that generate 
employment, stability, and social impact.
We provide financing to women-led SMEs that meet at least one of the following criteria:
Ownership: more than 50% of the shares are owned by women.
Management: more than 20% of the shares are owned by women, or there is at least one woman on the 
management team (legal representative), or at least 30% of the board of directors is composed of women.

Development Portfolio 
To continue expanding access to impact financing, 
we have consolidated a development portfolio 
that strategically leverages the rediscount lines 
of Bancóldex, FINDETER, and FINAGRO. These 
funding sources allow us to offer our clients favorable

ecosystem.

development portfolio of $392,117 million, focusing 
primarily on renewable energy, energy efficiency, 
clean transportation, and women-owned SMEs. 
More than just numbers, this portfolio represents 
a concrete tool for reducing gaps in access to 
financing, supporting SMEs and productive sectors 
in their adaptation, and accelerating investments 
that generate environmental and social value.

Integration of digital tools with the Bank’s legacy 
systems (retail banking).
We connected the digital tools for assisted 
customer workflows with the Bank’s legacy systems 
for Housing and Free Investment. This freed the 
sales team from the operational burden associated 
with double data entry and generated savings by 
eliminating duplicate queries in the processes. 
By early 2026, the digital tool for Vehicles will be 
connected to the legacy system, completing this 
initiative.
Digital Transformation
Aligned with the Bank’s corporate strategy, since 
2024 we have focused our teams on building an 
end-to-end (E2E) digital experience for individuals 
and businesses. Our goal has been clear: to enable 
customers to digitally obtain approval, open accounts, 
or receive disbursements for key products—including 
credit cards, personal loans, savings accounts, and 
CDs—with greater autonomy.
In 2025, we moved forward with a practical vision: to 
connect digital capabilities with the Bank’s systems, 
simplify steps, and reduce processing times without 
sacrificing security or support when needed. This 
combination of self-service and assisted workflows 
allowed us to improve customer experience, free 
up operational capacity within the sales force, and 
accelerate processes that were previously longer 
and manual.

## Pagina 103

Digital CDT
In early 2025, we rolled out the digital CD on the 
Banking Portal, and in October we supplemented it 
with a flow in Mobile Banking. Both are self-service: 
customers can simulate and view the product’s returns 
and open an account through a more intuitive, easy, 
and fast experience.
In just two screens and in approximately two minutes, 
without having to visit a branch, the customer can 
open the account.
Fewer steps, faster 
processing
We focused on reducing the steps required for product 
applications by implementing short, assisted, and 
self-service workflows. This enabled faster and more 
effective account openings, reducing the number of 
screens and the total time to activate a product, with 
workflows taking as little as 2 minutes.
In total, we developed 7 short workflows distributed 
across the Banking Portal, Mobile Banking, and the 
Website.
Digital international 
transfers (individuals)
We enabled international transfers for individuals 
through the Banking Portal (November) and Mobile 
Banking (December) for transfers in dollars and euros 
for amounts under USD $10.000.
This was a milestone: we digitized the customer￾facing process, reducing the time from one hour to 
10 minutes, with a more intuitive workflow.
Self-managed credit card
We achieved a key milestone by enabling self￾managed credit card workflows, creating a fully digital 
experience for the customer and freeing up the sales 
force.
Savings Ecosystem
We designed an addition to our savings ecosystem: 
in March, we launched Kubo Rentable, a high-yield 
savings account with one of the most competitive 
rates on the market, offering an 8,25% effective annual 
rate of return (rate as of December 2025).
By year-end, we had opened 7.516 Kubo accounts. 
Electronic Signature
Thanks to the electronic signature, in addition to 
improving customer experience, we processed nearly 
50.000 transactions, which represents approximately 
38 trees saved.
SME and Corporate MVP
In line with our digital strategy, the MVP aimed at 
SME and Corporate clients enables the opening of 
digital accounts (savings and checking) through an 
assisted process, reducing opening times from 1,5 
days to 3,2 hours.
This MVP is designed for companies seeking greater transactional incentives and fewer operational and 
documentation hurdles, with 24/7 access to the portal.
Digital Payroll MVP 
We established a comprehensive workflow for the creation, activation, and delivery of accounts to employees, 
combining automated processes, self-service, and in-person support.
This enabled 75% of employees at companies with a legal agreement to set up their accounts through self￾service.

The results show a clear focus on Digital Campaigns,

effective channel for driving high sales volumes 
thanks to the reach and segmentation capabilities of 
digital strategies. In second place, the Banking Portal 
accounts for $146.727.600.325 (15,48%), remaining a 
solid alternative for customers who prefer to manage 
their transactions via the web platform. Meanwhile, 
WhatsApp recorded $56.104.000.000 (5,92%),
standing out as a more direct and personalized 
interaction channel, useful for inquiries and simple 
transactions. Finally, Mobile Banking reached 
$11.028.097.247 (1,16%), highlighting an opportunity 
to further strengthen the adoption and usage of 
the mobile channel, improving the experience, and 
promoting its use at key moments in the customer 
journey.

into concrete results: we sold 11.809 units through 
our digital platforms, confirming that more customers 
are choosing to meet their needs in an agile, simple, 
and frictionless way. This performance reflects not 
only the adoption of these channels but also the 
effort to design clearer and more effective customer 
journeys for each product.

in each channel and where we can further 
promote self-service.

Cybersecurity  
In 2025, we continue to view cybersecurity as 
something very simple in essence, though demanding 
in practice: safeguarding trust. Every transaction, 
every piece of data, and every digital interaction 
requires us to be vigilant, to anticipate risks, and 
to respond rigorously when a risk arises. That is 
why, rather than talking about technology, we talk 
about a way of working: prevent, monitor, learn, 
and strengthen.
Our management is supported by an information 
security framework that brings together guidelines, 
practices, and controls to protect our clients’ and the 
Bank’s information. To stay aligned with recognized 
best practices, we use international standards such 
as ISO 27001:2022, NIST 800-53 (v2.0), and local 
regulations such as the regulatory circulars issued by 
the Colombian Financial Superintendency regarding 
compliance with security and cybersecurity controls. 
We periodically review our approach to adapt it to 
changes in the environment and the evolution of our 
digital services.
| SASB FN-CB.230a1 |  
SDG 16.10  
We also test our capabilities. We complement our 
internal audit and corporate compliance functions 
with assessment exercises that help us identify 
opportunities for improvement and prioritize actions. 
In recent processes, we shared the results of an 
external assessment conducted in 2024 with the 
consulting firm Ernest & Young (EY), and during 2025 
we made progress on a new assessment with Deloitte, 
which was ongoing at the end of the period.
And because security is proven when it is needed 
most, we have processes and tools to manage cyber 
risk and an incident response framework designed to 
mitigate impacts on the availability, confidentiality, 
and integrity of our services. Thus, we continue 
to strengthen a reliable, responsive, and prepared 
digital operation, serving our customers and the 
commitments we have made to our stakeholders.

## Pagina 108

Information Security and 
Cybersecurity Strategy 
To ensure that cybersecurity is consistent and 
sustainable, we manage it with a comprehensive 
approach: people, processes, and technology, under 
clear supervision and with defined responsibilities. In 
2025, we maintained a governance framework that 
allows us to make timely decisions, monitor risks, 
and ensure that security priorities align with the 
evolution of the business and our digital channels.
Our information security and cybersecurity strategy 
is led and overseen by senior management, with 
support from the Vice Presidency of Operations 
and Technology and the participation of the Vice 
President of Risk in oversight activities. This approach 
strengthens coordination between technical and 
risk management teams and helps us maintain a 
balanced focus on prevention, business continuity, 
and customer experience.
Cyber Risk Assessment 
and Mitigation
Prevention is strengthened when risk is managed 
in a structured manner. That is why we have a risk 
assessment model (ANX-APY-1186) that identifies 
threats, probability, and impact on the Bank’s assets 
and services. Based on residual risk, we prioritize 
mitigation actions, assign responsibilities, and 
track progress using documented matrices. This 
approach is complemented by our cybersecurity 
tools, which generate alerts and early warnings to 
adjust parameters and strengthen controls when 
the environment demands it.
Our Management 
We have an Information Security Committee that 
guides, prioritizes, and monitors management in 
accordance with the NTC-ISO 27001 standard 
and CE 007 of 2018.
We conduct periodic incident monitoring, with 
monthly internal reviews to assess trends, corrective 
actions, and opportunities for reinforcement. 
However, when an event exceeds defined thresholds, 
it is escalated to the appropriate authorities.
We promote management based on continuous 
improvement; we not only address events but also 
analyze lessons learned and strengthen controls 
to reduce recurrences.
We define escalation mechanisms to ensure that 
relevant incidents or risks are addressed in a timely 
manner by decision-makers.
Priorities and improvement plans are guided by 
criticality and risk level, seeking a balance between 
security, continuity, and customer experience.
With this governance, we aim to ensure that security 
is not an isolated effort, but a cross-functional 
capability that informs our decisions and protects 
what matters most: our customers’ trust and the 
stability of our services.
To ensure close and effective oversight, cybersecurity 
has clearly defined responsibilities starting at the 
executive level. 
In 2025, we maintained a governance framework that allows us to make timely decisions, monitor risks, and 
ensure that security priorities keep pace with the evolution of the business and our digital channels.

## Pagina 109

In our model, leadership comes from the Vice 
President of Operations and Technology and is 
articulated through specialized roles such as the 
Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) / Chief 
Security Officer (CSO) and the Chief Technology 
Officer (CTO) / Chief Information Officer (CIO), 
who guide strategy, prioritize actions, and coordinate 
capabilities to protect information and maintain 
service continuity. This structure allows us to make 
timely decisions and maintain cross-functional 
collaboration across departments, with a focus on 
prevention, response, and continuous improvement.
Culture of Information 
Security and Cybersecurity
In 2025, we strengthened our prevention efforts with 
a simple principle: “the earlier we identify a risk, 
the smaller its impact.” That is why we combine 
controls, monitoring, and continuous improvements 
to protect information and maintain the stability of 
our services. This approach allows us to act before 
a threat becomes an incident and to support the 
growth of our digital channels with confidence.
Our prevention capabilities are based on three 
complementary pillars:
1. Information Controls and 
Protection
We aim to ensure that information is protected 
throughout its entire lifecycle, from daily use to 
storage and circulation. To this end, we have 
strengthened access controls and data leakage 
prevention measures, with criteria tailored to the 
sensitivity of the information and the needs of 
each department.
Data Loss Prevention (DLP): We use a DLP 
tool (NetSkope) with general policies and area￾specific rules.
Access Control: We manage access based 
on the principle of least privilege, leveraging 
identity and access management (IAM) and 
privilege access management (PAM) capabilities, 
as well as role matrices and profiles to ensure 
authorization with the least privilege for 
applications. We also have a comprehensive 
security infrastructure that protects everything 
from the perimeter to the endpoints.
Information classification: We organize 
information into four categories, allowing us 
to apply measures commensurate with the level 
of sensitivity.
Scope of sensitive data protection: Our 
classification and least-privilege approach is not 
limited to customer information. It also applies to 
information regarding employees, contractors, 
and third parties, according to their level of 
confidentiality. We classify information into four 
categories (public, internal use, confidential, and 
restricted confidential) and apply appropriate 
controls to protect its confidentiality, integrity, and 
availability.
2. Vulnerability management: 
identify, prioritize, and 
remediate
More than just “detecting,” our goal is to close gaps: 
identifying vulnerabilities, prioritizing them based 
on criticality, and ensuring their resolution through 
accountability and follow-up.
We conduct continuous vulnerability scanning
and generate reports through our specialized 
team (CSIRT).
We have a vulnerability committee that supports 
prioritization, the assignment of responsible parties, 
and follow-up on remediation.
We have an incident response procedure—
CSIRP—that includes a communication and 
response model for any type of security incident.
3. Intelligence and Monitoring: 
Staying Ahead of the Curve 
We supplement internal controls with environmental 
monitoring to identify early warning signs and 
reduce exposure to fraud, impersonation, or 
unauthorized posts through the analysis of attack 
vectors.
We work with a threat intelligence provider 
that monitors mentions of the Bank, potential 
fraudulent sites, references on the dark web, 
and indicators that help us anticipate risks and 
activate preventive measures when necessary.

Operational continuity 
and preparedness  
We know that trust is also built through continuity. 
That is why, in addition to preventing and responding 
to incidents, we work to maintain service availability 
and the ability to recover from events that could 
affect operations. We have contingency and response 
plans and procedures in place, and we conduct 
testing exercises on the applications prioritized in 
the Business Impact Analysis (BIA), following the 
schedule defined for the period.
Culture and Training - 
Security We Live Every Day
When it comes to cybersecurity, we recognize that 
while technology is essential, organizational culture 
is the differentiating factor. Throughout 2025, we 
strengthened our conviction that security is built 
through our daily actions, especially when managing 
emails, protecting credentials, sharing information, 
and responding swiftly to any warning signs.
Rather than “training just for the sake of it,” we aim 
for every person at the Bank to understand their role 
and have practical tools to prevent risks, especially 
against common threats such as phishing attempts 
or digital scams.
Here’s how we promoted a 
culture of security in 2025:
We developed awareness-raising initiatives that 
garnered 5.306 participants in discussion sessions.
We complemented this work with structured 
training, reaching 6.607 participants in the virtual 
information security course.
We maintain an annual awareness plan, which 
allows us to reinforce messages, reinforce habits, 
and update content according to environmental 
risks.
3 phishing exercises.
1 Red Team exercise.
1 cloud-based cyber-incident exercise conducted. 
12 tips sent.
21 messages to customers
With this approach, we aim to ensure that cybersecurity 
does not depend solely on controls, but also on an 
organization that is vigilant, prepared, and committed 
to safeguarding our clients’ information and trust.
Actions in Response to Non￾Compliance and Operational 
Discipline 
Although information security and cybersecurity 
are not part of employee performance evaluations, 
we do have internal guidelines and procedures that 
establish how to respond to non-compliance. These 
mechanisms, aligned with our security policies and 
incident management procedures (DLP Incident 
Response Management Manual), allow us to 
correct issues, reinforce responsibilities, and prevent 
recurrences, maintaining a consistent standard of 
protection.
Key Cybersecurity Indicators 
2025
Our indicators help us understand risk behavior, 
prioritize enhancements, and maintain the reliability 
of our channels. In 2025, we tracked prevention 
efforts, incident response, and the effectiveness 
of our controls.

Information security breaches
This indicator tracks the trend in the number of

Indicator 2025  2024 
Information security
