We significantly reduced the number of incidents 
classified as information security breaches: from 
1.292 in 2024 to 273 in 2025, a reduction of 
approximately 79%. This suggests a significant 
improvement in prevention, control, and/or 
operational discipline regarding these incidents.
The number of people affected remained at very 
low levels, though with a slight increase: from 3 in 
2024 to 4 in 2025. In other words, although there 
were fewer incidents, we still had isolated cases 
with an impact on people, which reinforces the 
need to maintain a focus on controls and daily 
habits to bring the impact down to zero.
In 2025, we faced a significant security incident 
involving a third party. A Bank supplier was the victim 
of a double-extortion ransomware attack, which led 
to the publication of exfiltrated information. Although 
the incident originated outside our infrastructure, we 
activated our management protocols to protect our 
customers, contain risks, and strengthen controls 
with a forward-looking, preventive approach.  
According to the analysis conducted, 
the compromised information 
pertained to customers linked via 
credit cards: 26,533 cardholders, 
equivalent to approximately 3% 
of active individual customers. 
The exposed information included 
identification and contact details, 
such as names, identification 
numbers, addresses, cities, and 
departments.
We acted with a priority-based 
approach to immediately stop 
the breach, regain control, and 
strengthen measures to prevent 
recurrence.

Immediate Measures
We disconnected direct communication with 
the provider and kept it suspended until we could 
proceed with the validation and certification of 
security conditions.
We activated a crisis management team to 
coordinate actions, monitoring, and decisions.
Technical and recovery actions
We performed a complete disconnection of the 
affected environments, along with debugging 
and formatting processes.
We implemented enhanced 24/7 monitoring 
with EDR and hardening measures on critical 
components such as Active Directory.
We performed security reviews and adjustments 
in cloud environments (GCP and AWS), including 
a review of access and privileged users.
We have specialized support for forensic analysis 
and containment, relying on Lazarus, and deploy 
tools such as Thor and SentinelOne to strengthen 
detection and response.
Impact Management and 
Assurance
We activated the relevant policy and monitored the 
management fronts associated with the incident.
This event reinforced a priority we uphold as a 
principle: security is also managed within the 
Bank’s extended ecosystem. Therefore, in addition 
to responding, we used this learning to strengthen 
practices with third parties, raise verification 
standards, and consolidate an increasingly resilient 
digital operation.
Compliance, assessments, and 
continuous improvement 
In 2025, we maintained a cybersecurity approach 
that combines compliance, monitoring, and learning. 
For us, protecting information is not just about having 
controls in place, but about reviewing, testing, 
and continuously improving them, in line with our 
responsibilities and the trust our customers place 
in us.
Communication with clients 
regarding privacy and data 
protection 
For us, transparency is also part of protection. That 
is why we inform our customers in a timely and clear 
manner about our Personal Data Processing Policy, 
available for review on the institutional website. 
Furthermore, when a security incident occurs that 
could compromise personal data, we activate 
the necessary mechanisms to inform potentially 
affected customers, in compliance with Law 1581 
of 2012 and with a focus on care and timeliness.
Compliance and Regulatory 
Reference
Regarding personal data, we conduct our 
operations in accordance with the provisions of 
Law 1581 of 2012, strengthening practices for the 
responsible processing of information.
To guide our model and ensure consistency, we use 
recognized frameworks such as ISO 27001:2022 
and NIST (v2.0) as references, which serve as a 
guide for evaluating and evolving our capabilities, 
without relying solely on formal certification.
External assessments and 
monitoring
We complement our self-management with 
evaluation exercises: in 2024, we shared the results 
of an external evaluation conducted by EY.
In 2025, we made progress on an assessment with 
Deloitte—which was still ongoing at the end of 
the period—as part of our effort to understand our 
level of maturity, prioritize gaps, and strengthen 
action plans.

## Pagina 114

In 2025, we recorded the same number of identified 
data breaches as in 2024 (1 case in each year). 
However, the impact was significantly greater: the 
number of unique affected individuals rose from 
29 (2024) to 26.533 (2025), indicating that while 
the frequency did not increase, the magnitude of the 
event was higher.
In both years, 100% of the breaches involved personally 
identifiable information (PII), so the focus was on 
strengthening controls and response capabilities for 
this type of exposure. Additionally, in 2025 there was 
an increase in complaints received from regulatory 
bodies, rising from 4 (2024) to 9 (2025), suggesting a 
higher level of oversight and associated requirements 
during that period.
Privacy Risk Management 
Strategies
In 2025, we continued to strengthen these capabilities 
to protect our clients’ and the Bank’s data, anticipate 
potential exposures, and ensure consistent handling 
according to the level of confidentiality.
To reduce the risk of data breaches, we use a Data Loss 
Prevention (DLP) tool—NetSkope—which operates 
through both general and area-specific policies and 
rules. This is complemented by ongoing efforts from 
the security team, including a continuous awareness 
program that incorporates information protection 
based on confidentiality levels, reinforcing best 
practices in day-to-day operations.
We complement these measures with access controls designed to ensure that each person has only the permissions 
necessary for their role. Our applications are based on role and profile matrices, following the principle of least 
privilege, to strengthen authorization and reduce the risk associated with unauthorized or unnecessary access.
When situations related to privacy or data security arise, we act according to defined protocols. We have an 
incident response procedure (CSIRP) that establishes a communication and response model to address any 
type of security incident in an orderly and timely manner, including those that may involve personal information. 
Approach to identifying and addressing data security risks. 
Approach Description
Vulnerability Identification
We have a tool that continuously scans devices and provides real-time 
information regarding vulnerabilities. We receive reports from the financial 
CSIRT and the corporate CSIRT regarding emerging infrastructure 
vulnerabilities associated with the entities. 
Addressing risks and 
vulnerabilities
There is a vulnerability committee where the information gathered in 
the previous point is shared and provided to the infrastructure team for 
remediation 
Threat Analysis
Analysis of new or emerging threats: We have a provider that continuously monitors the Bank’s name 
online to detect potential fraudulent sites, customer information exposed on dark web forums, and indicators 
of compromise associated with recent vulnerabilities and new threats. Criteria analyzed: NFC payment 
systems, mobile banking, and web-based banking.
Attack vector analysis: We have perimeter-level and device-level tools that control incoming requests 
and help minimize the risk of attacks such as DoS, phishing, ransomware, and malware. Criteria analyzed: 
ransomware, loan accumulation phases, money fine scams, and remote access attacks.

Environmental and Social 
Assessment of Suppliers 
In 2025, we strengthened our environmental and 
social assessment of suppliers as a practical way 
to understand their level of maturity and, above all, 
to identify opportunities for joint improvement. To 
do so, we started with our universe of suppliers to 
whom payments were made during the year and 
conducted a diagnostic survey, which allowed us to 
establish a baseline comparable to previous years.
During the period, we had 800 suppliers with 
payments, of which 784 were domestic and 16 were 
foreign. As part of the assessment, we conducted 
a structured outreach to corporate suppliers and 
received 454 responses, representing a 56.75% 
participation rate in the exercise. This result provided 
us with insight into environmental practices (such 
as management, carbon footprint, mitigation, and 
efficiency initiatives) and social/labor practices 
(well-being, community contribution, and human 
rights), and allows us to more effectively guide 
training and support initiatives.

## Pagina 120

ESG Strategy 
and Its Impact
SDG 8.5; 9.3; 13.2
| GRI 2-23 |
At Banco de Occidente, sustainability is an essential 
part of our operation and the way we do business. 
Through the Sustainability Department, we coordinate 
efforts with all areas of the organization to ensure 
that the Bank’s activities generate positive change 
in the environment and among our stakeholders. 
Our environmental, social, and governance (ESG) 
vision goes beyond regulatory compliance; we 
seek to strengthen institutional resilience through a 
conscious balance between financial performance 
and social and environmental impact. To ensure 
the integrity of this approach, we have a robust 
governance structure: the Board of Directors exercises 
active and regular oversight of the ESG strategy, 
ensuring its alignment with the Bank’s integrated risk 
management and long-term objectives through its 
specialized committees. 
Our sustainability 
strategy 
Our vision is embodied in a corporate strategy 
that positions sustainability as a cross-cutting 
pillar across all our business lines. By integrating 
ESG criteria, we strengthen our ability to interpret 
the environment, identify responsible business 
opportunities, and consolidate a management model 
aligned with regulatory frameworks and international 
best practices. 
In 2025, we evolved this approach through a dual 
materiality analysis, designed to strengthen the link 
between sustainability and the Bank’s strategic and 
financial planning. This exercise not only allowed us 
to prioritize initiatives and adjust objectives but also 
optimized the allocation of resources toward the 
issues with the greatest impact on the organization 
and its stakeholders. 
Thanks to this evolution, materiality results have become a strategic input for comprehensive 
management. Their technical application in project evaluation, the development of financial 
solutions, and risk management enhances long-term financial performance and strengthens our 
ability to generate sustainable value.

Goals (SDGs)

This alignment allows us to integrate economic, social,

and Sustainability Report, we maintain our focus 
on the prioritized SDGs where, given the nature

decisions, risk management, internal operations, and

through initiatives related to ethics and governance, 
talent management, diversity and inclusion, customer

Materiality 
Analysis 
| GRI 2-29; 3-1; 3-2; 3-3 |
At Banco de Occidente, materiality analysis is a 
key tool for guiding our sustainability strategy and 
ensuring that our decisions consistently address the 
impacts we generate and the risks and opportunities 
that may affect business performance. This exercise 
allows us to prioritize the most relevant ESG issues, 
focus our efforts and resources, and strengthen 
value creation in the short, medium, and long term. 
A strategic approach 
based on double 
materiality 
In 2025, we updated our materiality analysis by 
incorporating a more in-depth approach to double 
materiality, in line with the frequency established 
by the Bank for this exercise, which is conducted 
every two years. This update built on the analysis 
conducted in 2023 and enabled us to conduct a 
structured review of the most relevant ESG issues 
within the current business and environmental context. 
This analysis allows us to align the sustainability 
strategy with the Bank’s organizational purpose 
by providing a comprehensive view of the issues 
requiring priority attention. Through the analysis of 
impacts, risks, and opportunities, we identified those 
issues that, due to their relevance to the environment 
and their potential financial impact, can significantly 
influence business continuity and long-term value 
creation. 
The double materiality update was developed with 
the support and verification of a specialized external 
entity, and the results were reviewed and approved 
by the Bank’s senior management and the Board of 
Directors as the highest governing body. Based on 
this approach, double materiality is established as a 
key tool for guiding decision-making and prioritizing 
actions. 
Double Materiality 
Analysis Process 
The determination of double materiality at Banco de 
Occidente was carried out through a structured and 
progressive process, which allowed us to identify 
and prioritize the most relevant ESG issues from the 
perspectives of impact and finance. This process 
integrates historical analysis, external information, 
internal insights, and strategic criteria, ensuring 
consistency with business management and 
stakeholder expectations. 
To carry out this exercise, we aligned our analysis with 
the main regulatory frameworks and international 
standards regarding sustainability and corporate 
disclosure. Specifically, we took into account the 
guidelines of the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) 
Standards, especially GRI 2 and GRI 3; International 
Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) S1 and S2 of 
the International Sustainability Standards Board 
(ISSB); the recommendations of the Task Force on 
Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD); and 
the sector-specific criteria of the Sustainability 
Accounting Standards Board (SASB). We also consider 
international regulatory developments related to 
the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive 
(CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting 
Standards (ESRS), as well as the applicable national 
regulatory guidelines issued by the Colombian 
Financial Superintendency (SFC). 
This analysis allows us to 
connect the sustainability 
strategy with the Bank's 
organizational purpose, by 
offering a comprehensive 
view of the issues that require 
priority attention.

## Pagina 124

Impact materiality Financial Materiality 
Impact materiality identifies both the positive and 
negative effects that the Bank’s activities have on the 
environment and society. This “inside-out” analysis 
assesses how our operations, products, and decisions 
influence people and the environment, serving as 
the foundation for our strategies for prevention, 
mitigation, and the creation of sustainable value. 
For this exercise, we conducted a structured 
assessment that included a review of Impacts, Risks, 
and Opportunities (IRO) across our value chain 
(suppliers, operations, and portfolio). The analysis 
incorporated information from 147 companies in key 
sectors, applying technical criteria of magnitude, 
scope, and remediability. 
As a result, 125 IROs were prioritized with the following 
distribution: 
Environmental Dimension (29 IROs): Focused on 
emissions management, climate change, eco￾efficiency, and biodiversity. 
Social Dimension (48 IROs): Focused on customer 
experience, talent management, diversity, human 
rights, and community. 
Governance Dimension (48 IROs): Related to 
ethics, cybersecurity, supply chain management, 
and sustainable finance. 
Stakeholders 
Our stakeholders are a central component of 
sustainability and identifying issues requiring 
priority attention. Through ongoing and structured 
engagement cycles, we seek to understand their 
expectations, identify relevant risks and opportunities, 
and strengthen decision-making aligned with the 
context in which the Bank operates. 
As part of the update to our double materiality 
analysis, we incorporated the internal perspectives of 
key vice presidents at the Bank, which allowed us to 
enhance the identification and prioritization of ESG 
issues from a strategic and business perspective. 
Complementarily, financial materiality assesses how 
ESG factors in the environment influence the Bank’s 
value and financial performance. This “outside-in” 
analysis identifies the risks and opportunities that 
may affect our profitability, solvency, competitive 
position, and resilience in the short, medium, and 
long term. 
Under this approach, we analyze ESG issues based 
on their impact on critical variables such as credit, 
operational, reputational, and regulatory risk. This 
process integrated global trends and regulatory 
frameworks with the strategic vision of internal 
departments to identify areas of vulnerability or 
business potential. 
The results of this perspective enable the Bank to 
anticipate emerging risks and guide the design 
of financial solutions aligned with the creation of 
economic value. Thus, financial materiality ensures 
that sustainability is fully integrated into financial 
planning and strategic decision-making. 
Prioritized Stakeholder Groups 
In the materiality assessment and in our ongoing 
management, we consider the following 
prioritized stakeholders: 
Shareholders 
Customers 
Senior management 
Board of Directors
Employees 
Communities 
Strategic Partners
Suppliers
Associations 
These groups represent the stakeholders with 
the greatest level of influence and/or impact 
regarding the Bank’s activities and the impacts 
resulting from its operations and strategic 
decisions.

## Pagina 126

Material issues for creating corporate value 
Material issues for creating corporate value reflect the issues that have a direct impact on the Bank’s financial sustainability, 
competitiveness, and resilience. These issues integrate the ESG perspective into the business strategy and guide the 
management of risks and opportunities across different time horizons. 
Material issue Emissions Management and Climate Change Talent management Information security, cybersecurity, and system availability
Risk or 
opportunity
Emissions management and climate change are critical issues that may impact the Bank’s long￾term performance, given evolving regulations and physical changes in environmental conditions. 
In this context, resilience and the transition to a low-carbon economy entail risks, such as the 
portfolio’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets in the face of stricter regulations and potential 
losses resulting from physical climate events. At the same time, they represent opportunities
associated with attracting new capital flows by financing transition projects and sustainable 
assets through existing products.
Talent management is a critical factor in maintaining the Bank’s competitiveness, 
innovation capacity, and service quality. In this context, attracting, developing, 
and retaining employees with the right skills represents a strategic opportunity, 
as it enables the building of a specialized, innovative workforce aligned with 
the long-term strategy. Conversely, high turnover, skills gaps, or low employee 
engagement can generate operational, reputational, and performance 
risks, reflected in the loss of intellectual capital and higher operating costs 
associated with talent management.
In an environment of increasing digitalization within the financial sector, exposure 
to cyber threats, operational failures, and risks associated with system availability 
is rising, all of which can impact business continuity, reputation, and regulatory 
compliance. Given this context, robust management of these aspects represents 
a strategic opportunity to strengthen operational resilience, build customer trust, 
and differentiate the Bank through solid digital capabilities. However, inadequate 
management can lead to risks such as operational disruptions, regulatory penalties, 
and reputational damage associated with security incidents or system failures.
Business Case Resilience in the face of vulnerability to natural hazards and the transition to a low-carbon 
economy present significant opportunities, such as financing sustainable projects and assets and 
supporting clients interested in green products. At the same time, it presents risks associated with 
increasingly stringent regulations, shifts in market preferences, and the potential obsolescence of 
assets not aligned with environmental criteria. Properly managing these risks and opportunities 
allows us to reduce costs associated with regulatory non-compliance, strengthen business 
resilience, and position ourselves as a responsible entity committed to climate-compatible 
development.
Human talent is a fundamental driver of our operational efficiency and the 
experience we offer our customers. Investing in the training, development, and 
well-being of our employees strengthens their capabilities, reduces turnover, 
and improves productivity . Furthermore, having well-prepared and committed 
teams facilitates adaptation to changes in the environment, innovation in 
products and services, and the effective execution of the Bank’s strategy.
Information protection and service continuity are essential to ensuring efficient 
and reliable operations. Having secure and available systems allows us to offer 
financial products and services that are accessible, efficient, and aligned with 
customers’ expectations. Furthermore, proper cybersecurity management helps 
reduce operational and legal risks, protect information assets, and ensure compliance 
with regulatory requirements applicable to the financial sector.
Business 
Impact
Integrating emissions management and climate change into the business strategy helps mitigate 
financial and operational risks, strengthening the business’s resilience in the face of regulatory 
changes and environmental conditions. This approach reinforces the Bank’s reputation as a 
responsible institution and supports value creation through more efficient portfolio and risk 
management, as well as strong relationships with stakeholders, contributing to the Bank’s 
long-term stability and sustainability.
Effective talent management translates into better organizational performance, 
greater operational stability, and more consistent service for our customers. 
Strengthening internal capabilities promotes business continuity, improves 
process efficiency, and reinforces a positive reputation as a responsible employer.
Effective management of information security and cybersecurity strengthens business 
continuity, operational stability, and customer confidence in our services. This 
approach reduces exposure to operational disruptions and regulatory penalties, 
protects the Bank’s reputation, and reinforces its ability to operate efficiently in 
increasingly demanding digital environments, generating sustainable value over 
the long term.
Business 
Strategies
We are implementing a comprehensive strategy to manage emissions and climate change
in our operations and financing, which includes incorporation of environmental criteria into 
credit decisions and alignment with international frameworks and standards. As part of this 
effort, in 2025 we launched a project with a specialized consultant to deepen the analysis of our 
financed emissions, expand the scope of their measurement, and lay the groundwork for setting 
targets starting in 2026. Complementarily, we are making progress in integrating climate risks 
into our risk management system, supporting regulatory compliance and aligning the Bank’s 
decisions with sustainability goals.
We have developed initiatives aimed at strengthening talent management, 
including training and development programs, well-being, leadership, and 
capacity-building, as well as actions to promote diversity, inclusion, and a 
positive work environment. These strategies are aligned with the Bank’s vision 
and seek to ensure that our employees have the necessary tools to contribute to 
the achievement of strategic objectives and the creation of sustainable value.
Our strategy is focused on strengthening information security, cybersecurity, 
and system availability through the implementation of controls, processes, and 
technologies that protect data and ensure operational continuity. These actions 
include strengthening technology risk management, continuously updating security 
capabilities, and adopting best practices that allow us to anticipate threats, respond 
promptly to incidents, and ensure the availability of our services..

Materiality metrics for creating business value 
Materiality metrics allow us to track how material issues are integrated into the Bank’s strategy and into the risk and opportunity management, 
contributing to alignment between performance, decision-making, and business sustainability.
Material issue Emissions management and climate change Talent management Information security, cybersecurity, and system availability
Objective / 
Metric
Our objective is to advance the reduction of carbon emissions from the loan 
portfolio by 2030, as well as to strengthen financing for projects/assets that 
drive the transition to a low-carbon economy and climate resilience. In this 
regard, the Bank has set a goal to finance COP 8 trillion in sustainable projects/
assets between 2024 and 2030, aligned with environmental and climate criteria.
Our objective is to strengthen talent management to improve 
organizational performance, operational efficiency, and customer 
experience. In this regard, the Bank has set goals to achieve a 93% 
employee satisfaction rate by 2025, based on the results of workplace 
climate surveys, as well as to increase employee participation in training 
programs, with the aim of reaching 83% training coverage by 2025.
Our objective is to strengthen information security, cybersecurity, 
and system availability to ensure business continuity, protect the 
information of customers and other stakeholders, and maintain 
trust in the Bank’s services. In this regard, we seek to advance 
the digitization of operational processes by 2030, as well as 
to consolidate robust management of the technological and 
cybersecurity risks associated with operations. 
Target year The target date for achieving these objectives is 2030, considering both the 
reduction of emissions associated with the portfolio and the growth of the 
sustainable financing portfolio. 
The target date for achieving these objectives is 2025, both for employee 
satisfaction levels and for participation in training and development 
programs. 
The target date for achieving these objectives is 2030, taking 
into account process modernization, system availability, and 
the strengthening of information security controls. 
Progress In 2025, we made progress in measuring carbon emissions, initiating technical 
work with a specialized consultant to review financed emissions and adjust 
the methodology and scope in line with the standards of the Partnership for 
Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF). This process forms the basis for future 
emissions tracking; therefore, the results obtained in this exercise are not 
comparable to previous measurements. 
Regarding the financing of sustainable projects/assets, the Bank has reached 
a cumulative total of COP 4,5 trillion, compared to the overall target of COP 
8 trillion set for 2030.
These metrics are monitored periodically based on the results of 
internal surveys and training indicators. In 2025, the results show 
a 95% employee satisfaction rate, enabling the achievement of the 
workplace environment goal. 
Regarding training, approximately 80% of employees have completed 
the training programs planned for 2025, reflecting the achievement 
of the current goal.
To date, the Bank has successfully digitized a significant portion 
of its operational processes, gradually advancing toward 
the objective set for 2030. These advances reflect increased 
adoption of technological channels and platforms, as well as 
the strengthening of operational efficiency and digital capabilities 
that support business continuity and the customer experience. 
Executive 
Compensation
Compensation for Senior Management at Banco de Occidente incorporates criteria linked to strategic performance and the management of risks relevant to the business, including environmental, social, and 
governance (ESG) aspects. This approach aligns the decision-making of the Bank’s leaders with strategic objectives, business sustainability, and long-term value creation. 
In 2025, incentive schemes incorporated criteria linked to prioritized material issues, consistent with the ESG strategy and the results of the double materiality analysis. Specifically, elements related to talent 
management and development, emissions management and climate change, and information security, cybersecurity, and system availability were integrated into the evaluation of senior management’s 
performance. 
These criteria were applied through indicators related to leadership and capacity building, the management of climate risks and opportunities, and operational continuity and information protection. The design 
and implementation of the compensation scheme were reviewed by internal governance bodies, in line with the Bank’s control and oversight framework.

## Pagina 128

Material Issues for External Stakeholders 
Material issues for external stakeholders reflect the issues that are most relevant to the groups with which the Bank interacts 
outside its organizational structure. These issues capture the expectations of the broader community and help guide the Bank’s 
management, communication, and actions in a manner consistent with its role in the country’s economic, social, and environmental 
development. 
Material issue Emissions management and climate change (Environmental impact) Financial inclusion and access to financial services for women-led 
SMEs (Social impact)
Cause of the 
impact
The Bank’s financing activities can generate both positive and negative 
impacts on greenhouse gas emissions, depending on the type of projects 
and sectors financed. On the one hand, financing carbon-intensive activities, 
particularly in sectors such as energy, infrastructure, and construction, 
can contribute to increased emissions and, if not properly managed, 
exacerbate the effects of climate change, generating adverse impacts on 
people, society, and the environment. 
On the other hand, financing projects and assets related to renewable 
energy, energy efficiency, and transition solutions contributes positively to 
decarbonization and energy security, supporting climate change mitigation 
and progress toward a low-carbon economy. This dual effect makes 
climate change management a central aspect of materiality analysis from 
an environmental perspective.
The Bank’s activities in providing financial products and services can 
have both positive and negative impacts on financial inclusion and the 
development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), particularly 
those led by women, who often face greater barriers to access. On the one 
hand, the lack of a credit history, biases in risk assessment, and limited 
access to financial information can restrict these businesses’ access to 
financial services, exacerbating social and economic inequality and limiting 
their growth and formalization. 
On the other hand, strengthening financial inclusion through tailored 
solutions, support for women entrepreneurs, and more equitable access to 
financial products contributes positively to reducing access gaps, promoting 
social mobility, and supporting the economic and social development of 
traditionally underserved communities.
External 
stakeholders / 
assessed impact 
areas
Customers, local communities, authorities and governments, society at 
large, as well as the environment.
Customers, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) 
Relevance of the 
issue to external 
stakeholders
The impact of carbon emissions and climate change is highly relevant to 
external stakeholders due to its effects on the natural environment, health, 
biodiversity, and community development. At the same time, there is a 
growing expectation among clients, regulators, and other stakeholders 
that financial institutions play an active role in mitigating climate change 
through responsible financing and the development of sustainable products 
and services. 
The way the Bank manages this impact directly affects its reputation, 
stakeholder trust, and its contribution to long-term sustainable development.
The financial inclusion of women-led SMEs is highly relevant to external 
stakeholders, as it directly impacts income generation, employment, and 
local economic development. 
Lack of access to adequate financial services can limit the growth of these 
businesses and widen economic and social gaps. 
At the same time, there is a growing expectation among customers, 
communities, and other stakeholders that financial institutions promote 
more equitable conditions for access to financing. Managing this impact 
helps strengthen trust, the Bank’s reputation, and its contribution to financial 
inclusion and sustainable development.

Impact 
Assessment

with CO₂e emissions. To this end, we measure

This exercise allows us to evaluate the extent to

## Pagina 134

Board of Directors
| GRI 2-9|
The Board of Directors is the Bank’s highest governing 
body and is responsible for managing the entity in 
all matters not exclusively decided by the General 
Shareholders’ Meeting. From there, it sets the Bank’s 
course and closely oversees management. To do so 
effectively, it meets twice a month, generally every 
two weeks, with clear rules regarding participation, 
quorum, and decision-making, and relies on 
specialized committees that delve into key issues. 
During the reporting period, its agenda included the 
approval of policies and guidelines related to the 
social, economic, and environmental impact of our 
operations on stakeholders.
In this vein, the Board of Directors delegates managing 
these impacts through a governance model that 
combines strategic guidelines, ongoing oversight, 
and technical work carried out by committees. The 
Board defines policies and guidelines for matters 
such as risk, sustainability, regulatory compliance, 
and corporate governance, ensuring they are 
integrated into the institutional strategy. For its part, 
management implements these decisions through 
the vice-presidencies and responsible departments, 
which manage the impacts within their respective 
areas and submit periodic reports to the Board. In 
addition, the Board presents to the General Meeting—
together with Senior Management—the reports and 
financial statements for each fiscal year and the 
proposed profit distribution plans, accompanied by 
the report on the progress of business and the Bank’s 
overall situation, which includes the sustainability 
section containing the information reported here.
Currently, the Board of Directors is composed of 
nine members without alternates, seven of whom 
are independent.
The participation of independent members on 
the committees is essential to ensuring effective 
governance and impartial decisions. By having no 
direct ties to the organization, they provide an objective 
perspective that allows for a more balanced and 
transparent evaluation of issues. This independence 
helps prevent undue influence and properly manage 
potential conflicts of interest, strengthening internal 
controls and boosting the confidence of shareholders 
and investors. Furthermore, it facilitates the adoption 
of best practices and compliance with governance 
standards and regulations. Collectively, their 
contributions support the Bank’s smooth operation, 
protect its long-term interests, and promote ethical 
and responsible management.
At the Bank, the process for appointing members of 
the Board of Directors is carried out in accordance 
with the Bylaws and the Appointment and 
Compensation Policy, ensuring a transparent 
procedure based on suitability criteria. The evaluation 
of candidates considers, among other aspects, their 
professional background, skills and knowledge, 
track record, and relevant experience (especially 
in the financial sector), as well as factors such as 
reputation, leadership, and the ability to contribute 
to the Bank’s strategic oversight. This process is 
supported by internal corporate governance bodies 
and culminates in the presentation and election by 
the competent body, ensuring the traceability of 
decisions and promoting a balanced composition 
that strengthens independence of judgment and the 
quality of deliberation.
In 2025, at the General Shareholders’ Meeting held on 
March 26 of that year, considering the slate presented 
by Grupo Aval Acciones y Valores S.A., the following 
Board of Directors was elected for the term from 
April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026, with 96,78% of the 
voting capital in favor:

Subsequently, the legal procedures for taking

The criteria followed by the Bank are those of legal

“...Any person who under no circumstances is: 
1. An employee or executive of the issuer or any of 
its affiliates, subsidiaries, or parent companies, 
including those who held such a position during 
the year immediately preceding the appointment, 
unless the appointment involves the reelection of 
an independent person. 
2. Shareholders who, directly or by virtue of an 
agreement, direct, guide, or control the majority 
of the entity’s voting rights or who determine 
the majority composition of its administrative, 
management, or supervisory bodies. 
3.A partner or employee of associations or 
companies that provide advisory or consulting 
services to the issuer or to companies belonging 
to the same economic group as the issuer, when 
the income from such services represents twenty 
percent (20%) or more of their operating income. 
4.An employee or executive of an NGO, association, 
or company that receives significant donations 
from the issuer. 
5.Significant donations are those that represent 
more than twenty percent (20%) of the total 
donations received by the respective institution. 
6.An administrator of an entity on whose board 
of directors a legal representative of the issuer 
serves. 
7. A person who receives from the issuer any 
remuneration other than fees as a member of 
the board of directors, the audit committee, or any 
other committee created by the board of directors.”

## Pagina 140

Operations Operations
Audit 
Committee
This committee is responsible for generating reports based on transparency and identifying 
opportunities for improvement that contribute to the optimization of processes; these reports are 
issued quarterly. 
Comprehensive 
Risk Committee
It is responsible for monitoring the results of the risk profile and appetite, advising the Board 
of Directors on operations, events, or activities—including new ventures—that may affect 
the entity’s risk exposure and profile, approving adjustments and changes to SIAR policies, 
monitoring the state of the risk culture within the entity, and evaluating the analysis of the results 
of monthly risk management reports, among other tasks. It is also responsible for promoting 
the adaptation of the company’s risk management to an advanced model that allows for the 
configuration of a risk profile consistent with strategic objectives, validating reviews of the 
positive and negative impacts generated by social and environmental issues, supervising 
compliance with comprehensive climate change risk management, and participating in the 
accountability process of the Environmental and Social Risk Management System (SARAS). It 
meets quarterly
Nominations, 
Compensation, 
and Corporate 
Governance 
Committee
This committee oversees and manages various key areas related to the management of senior 
staff, compensation policies, and the entity’s governance structure. Its functions include: 
Proposing or reviewing the appointments of executives and key members of senior management, 
as well as other strategic positions within the Bank. Ensuring that compensation is aligned 
with the entity’s strategic objectives, incentivizing appropriate performance and responsible 
management. Evaluating and proposing improvements to the governance structure, including 
the composition of the board of directors and internal committees. The inclusion of independent 
members on committees is essential to ensure effective governance and impartiality in decision￾making; these members, having no direct ties to the organization, provide an objective and 
unbiased perspective, which allows for a more equitable and transparent assessment of 
situations. Their independence ensures that decisions are made without external influences 
or conflicts of interest, which strengthens internal control, fosters shareholder and investor 
confidence, and facilitates compliance with best practices and governance regulations. Thus, 
they contribute to the Bank’s smooth operation by protecting its long-term interests and 
promoting ethical and responsible management
Credit 
Committee
The Credit Committee’s primary function is to review credit applications submitted by the Bank’s 
management, in accordance with the Bank’s policies, and to issue recommendations regarding 
the credit risk associated with projects presented to the Bank. It is composed of directors 
with experience in financial analysis and risk management, which enables rigorous, objective 
evaluations aligned with the Bank’s strategic objectives. During 2025, the Credit Committee held 
a total of seventeen (17) meetings, during which it evaluated and approved transactions based on 
criteria of accountability, technical soundness, and prudent risk management.
Effective June 27, 2025, the 
composition of the committees 
supporting the Board of Directors 
consisted of three (3) principal 
members, appointed from among the 
members of the Board of Directors 
itself. 
Subsequently, at a Board of 
Directors meeting held on August 
22, 2025, the creation of the Credit 
Committee was approved, and it 
was incorporated into the structure 
of support committees to strengthen 
supervision and management in 
credit matters.

Collective expertise of the highest governing body
| GRI 2 – 17|
During the reporting period, the governing body participated in various training sessions aimed at strengthening 
its collective knowledge on matters relevant to business oversight. The training sessions addressed topics such

as regulations and corporate governance practices. These activities helped strengthen the understanding of 
the financial, regulatory, and operational impacts necessary for informed decision-making.

Board of Directors 
Evaluation
| GRI 2-18 |
As part of the implementation of best practices 
and guidelines regarding corporate governance, 
Banco de Occidente conducted the Board of 
Directors evaluation process for the 2025 period. 
The purpose of the evaluation is to identify and 
establish agreements within the Board of Directors 
and with Senior Management regarding actions 
to strengthen the various factors that affect the 
Board’s performance and its relationship with the 
group’s governing bodies.
In accordance with best practices in corporate 
governance, evaluations alternate between internal 
and external assessments. Therefore, in 2025, the 
Board of Directors, as a collegiate body, and its 
committees conducted the performance evaluation 
with the support of Governance Consultants (www.
governanceconsultants.com), an independent 
firm with over 15 years of experience in evaluating 
the Boards of Directors of leading companies in 
Latin America.
The evaluation for the 2025 period was based 
on an analysis of corporate documents and 
the completion of questionnaires by the 9 
Board members and 8 members of the Senior 
Management team. In addition to an analysis of 
the Board of Directors’ structure, composition, 
and attendance, the evaluation addressed the 
following dimensions: i) Contribution and fulfillment 
of responsibilities; ii) Board focus; iii) Dynamics 
and operations; iv) Roles of the Board of Directors 
(Chair and Secretary); and v) Support committees.
The evaluation demonstrates progress in the 
evolution of the Board’s structure and functioning, 
as well as in the strengthening of support 
mechanisms that have allowed for a greater 
focus of the agenda on strategic matters. It 
also contributes to deepening reflection on the 
Board’s role in the face of an evolving financial 
environment, including risk management and the 
consolidation of corporate governance practices 
aligned with a long-term vision.
Board of Directors 
Compensation Policy
| GRI 2-19 |
Since the General Shareholders’ Meeting of March 
26, 2020, Banco de Occidente, to strengthen best 
corporate governance practices, adopted and 
adjusted the Board of Directors’ Appointment and 
Compensation Policy, which was designed by 
Grupo Aval Acciones y Valores S.A.
What does this policy cover? It is organized into 
three main components:
Composition of the Board of Directors: defines 
the criteria to ensure a board with the appropriate 
profile, considering professional background, 
skills, knowledge, and/or experience related to 
the financial sector, as well as factors such as 
recognition, reputation, and leadership, among 
others.
Nomination and Evaluation: establishes the 
procedure for the submission and evaluation of 
proposals and candidates.
Compensation: sets forth the guidelines regarding 
the compensation of the Board of Directors.

Senior Management
| GRI 2-13 |
Senior Management is responsible for the administration of the Bank and leads the execution of the corporate strategy, integrating sustainability 
practices into daily management that strengthen value creation for the organization and our stakeholders. It is headed by the President and 
comprises the Vice Presidents, who periodically report to the Board of Directors on progress and results, and, together with the Board, reports 
to the General Shareholders’ Meeting on performance and achievements, in accordance with the provisions of Chapter Three of the Code 
of Good Corporate Governance, regarding the mechanisms for evaluating and controlling the activities of administrators, senior executives, 
and directors. The Office of the Ombudsman, as well as the Audit, Treasury, and Compliance departments, also support the President in his 
management duties.
At the Board of Directors meeting on January 10, 2025, the resignation of Iván Mauricio Ricardo Arias was accepted, and the appointment of 
Carlos Andrés Echeverri as Vice President of Companies was approved. On that same day, the Board accepted the resignation of Pedro Luis 
Villegas, and on March 6, 2025, Mario Botina Tovar was appointed Vice President of Operations and Technology. Subsequently, on September 
12, the resignation of Mr. Eduardo Alfonso Correo was accepted, and the appointment of Ángela María Ceballos as Vice President of Human 
Resources and Administration was approved. Finally, at the meeting on September 26, 2025, the resignation of Douglas Berrío Zapata was 
accepted, and the appointment of Juana Beltrán Echeverri as Vice President of Legal Affairs was approved.
A significant milestone in 2025 regarding diversity and inclusion was the appointment of two women 
to vice-presidential positions, strengthening female representation in senior management and 
broadening the diversity of perspectives in decision-making. In this context, the Board of Directors 
approved the appointment of Ángela María Ceballos as Vice President of Human Resources and 
Administration and of Juana Beltrán Echeverri as Vice President of Legal Affairs, marking concrete 
progress toward a more diverse, balanced, and representative leadership.

Senior Management Evaluation
Senior management members are evaluated using 
the Balanced Scorecard (BSC), with monthly 
monitoring and quarterly reporting of results. This 
framework allows for continuous monitoring of 
progress against strategic objectives and timely 
decision-making.
BSC measurement is led internally by the Financial 
Planning and Budgeting Department, based on a 
dashboard of indicators updated according to the 
Bank’s goals. It includes institutional metrics and 
indicators specific to each area—adopted based on 
an external consulting engagement—and is rolled out 
to the various leadership levels through a cascading 
framework, ensuring that management remains 
aligned across the entire organization. These results 
form part of the annual performance evaluation 
of leaders.
Regarding compensation, Senior Management 
receives a base salary and an annual bonus tied 
to the Bank’s results from the immediately preceding 
year, the allocation of which is approved by the 
Chairman of Grupo Aval. In addition, managers who 
support senior management receive a comprehensive 
salary, and in the case of the Treasury Department, 
quarterly variable compensation is also provided, 
contingent upon meeting performance targets for 
each period.
Conflict of Interest
| GRI 2-15|
During the period covered by this report, no 
conflicts of interest arose that required referral 
to the Board of Directors; the cases identified 
were handled through the internal mechanisms 
established for their analysis and resolution.
The bank has a Conflict of Interest Committee 
(CCI), which is empowered to determine, during 
the management phase of a situation that 
could give rise to a potential conflict of interest, 
whether the transaction to be carried out is of 
a recurring nature, part of the ordinary course 
of business, and/or within market conditions, 
or whether, on the contrary, the transaction 
does not fall within the aforementioned criteria 
and must decide whether to approve or reject the 
transaction. 
If, as a result of the situation brought to its attention, 
the CCI determines that the proposed transaction 
represents a conflict of interest and the decision 
regarding it exceeds its scope of authority, the CCI 
must bring this to the attention of the Board of 
Directors of its respective entity. 
 Our Board of Directors evaluates the elements 
constituting the conflict of interest and shall issue 
a reasoned decision, in accordance with its legal 
and statutory powers, indicating: 
i) its approval of the transaction, ii) whether the 
entities must refrain from carrying it out, iii) whether 
it may be carried out subject to the modification of 
certain conditions, or iv) whether the execution of 
the transaction must be submitted for consideration 
by their respective general shareholders meetings. 
The criteria regarding which transactions may be 
decided by the Board and which by the shareholders’ 
meeting shall include, among other matters deemed 
relevant by each entity, certain materiality criteria. 
The policy for the identification, disclosure, and 
management of conflicts of interest was approved by 
the Board of Directors through Minutes No. 1525 dated 
June 28, 2019. In December 2019, we implemented this 
policy at Banco de Occidente through the publication 
of Annex (ANX-COL-711), titled “Annex 1 – Conflict 
of Interest Policy of the Aval-Banco de Occidente 
Conglomerate; and we established the Conflict 
of Interest Committee, composed of the following 
principal members: Chief Financial Officer, Chief 
Risk Officer, and General Counsel; and alternate 
members: Accounting Manager, Credit Risk Manager, 
and Retail Banking Legal Manager.”

## Pagina 150

Information for investors
Internal Control System (ICS)
The Internal Control System (ICS) of the Bank and its 
Subsidiaries is a continuous and dynamic process 
that seeks to strengthen the efficiency and continuous 
improvement of its components—control environment, 
risk management, and monitoring—with the active 
participation of all employees, from operational teams 
to the Board of Directors. Within this framework, Internal 
Audit, acting with independence and objectivity, oversees 
compliance with governance and control processes in 
accordance with the current regulatory framework. To 
this end, it conducts risk-based audits and submits the 
results and recommendations derived from its work to the 
Board of Directors’ Audit Committee on a quarterly basis. 
Additionally, it promotes a culture of risk management 
through an annual training plan, helping to ensure that 
prevention, control, and continuous improvement are part 
of the organization’s daily operations.
Assessment of the Performance of 
the Internal Control System (ICS)
In compliance with the provisions of the Basic Legal Circular 
issued by the Financial Superintendency of Colombia, 
the Internal Control System (ICS) of the Bank and its 
subsidiaries was properly managed during 2025, achieving 
reasonable risk mitigation. This assessment was based on 
a comprehensive analysis of the ICS components, which 
include the Control Environment, Risk Management, Control 
Activities, Information and Communication, Monitoring, 
and Independent Assessments.
Código País Survey (2025, 
report submitted in January 
2026)
The Código País survey is a key input for 
continuing to strengthen our corporate 
governance practices. It allows us to review, 
with a critical and systematic eye, how 
well we align with the highest standards of
transparency, ethics, and accountability; 
identify opportunities for improvement; 
strengthen internal controls; and optimize 
management. In practice, this translates 
into greater investor confidence, a stronger 
reputation, and a better ability to anticipate 
and manage risks.
In 2026, we presented the Bank’s report on the 
implementation of best corporate governance 
practices, based on this survey, which covers 
33 key measures and a total of up to 148 
recommendations. The Código País survey for 
the year 2025 was distributed in January 2026. 
In this exercise, the Bank reported the adoption 
of 132 measures; 2 measures do not apply 
to Banco de Occidente, and the remaining 
ones are under analysis to determine their 
feasibility for implementation. The published 
responses can be viewed on our website, in 
the Shareholder and Investor Information
section.

## Pagina 151

Processes to address 
negative impacts
| GRI 2-25|
Banco de Occidente has made clear and measurable 
commitments in the management of its After-Sales 
Support Model, aimed at addressing negative 
impacts and reducing their likelihood of occurrence. 
In 2025, we continued to strengthen this model with 
concrete actions that combine preventive monitoring, 
timely response, organizational learning, and active 
customer participation to sustainably improve service 
quality.
We have online monitoring mechanisms that enable 
the early identification of technical and operational 
incidents that could affect service continuity and 
quality, triggering timely remedial actions in the event 
of any deviation. In this vein, we have implemented 
the Digital Operations Center (COD), designed 
to monitor critical systems and processes in real 
time. This center enables early alerts, structured 
incident management, and the resolution of failures 
within a maximum of three (3) hours, contributing to 
more efficient operations and service sustainability. 
In addition to identifying and promptly resolving 
incidents that impact customers, we maintain an 
ongoing commitment to prevention and reducing 
recurrence through the implementation of corrective 
and preventive actions.
Our management is based on a root cause analysis 
approach, which strengthens continuous improvement 
and service quality. As a result, in 2025 we achieved 
an 11,5% reduction in the number of Mechanisms 
for Requests, Complaints, Claims, and Suggestions 
– PQRS compared to 2024 and an improvement 
of six (6) positions in the “Number of Complaints 
per Institution” ranking published by the Financial 
Superintendency, demonstrating more efficient and 
customer-oriented management. In addition, we use 
technological and automation solutions to minimize 
impacts associated with manual errors and optimize 
response times. In particular, the implementation 
of process automation tools reduced service 
times by 39%, ensuring faster, clearer, and more 
timely responses, and strengthening the customer 
experience and the sustainability of operations.
Approach to Identifying and 
Addressing Complaints and 
Established Mechanisms
The Bank continuously strengthens a root￾cause analysis model to identify, analyze, 
and address complaints in a timely manner, 
promoting both immediate corrective actions 
and structural improvements that strengthen 
the value proposition and the long-term 
relationship with customers. Additionally, we are 
making progress in simplifying and improving 
the accessibility of complaint mechanisms, 
facilitating customer interaction through 
multiple channels. As a result, as of November 
2025, 18% of Contact Center interactions took 
place through digital channels, diversifying 
the means of contact that were previously 
concentrated mainly on phone calls and 
improving customer experience.
Stakeholder participation 
in the design, review, 
operation, and improvement 
of mechanisms
We facilitate stakeholder engagement, 
particularly that of financial consumers—in 
the design, review, operation, and continuous 
improvement of complaint and grievance 
mechanisms through surveys, satisfaction 
surveys, and direct feedback channels. By 
the end of 2025, we had collected 4.162 valid 
surveys—nearly double the number from 
2024—strengthening the representativeness 
of the customer’s voice in decision-making.
The information obtained, comments, 
perceptions, complaints, and behaviors, is 
systematically integrated into the continuous 
improvement cycle as follows:
Design: We analyze textual comments, 
recurring causes, access barriers, and 
segmented results of experience indicators 
(INS) to redesign documentation, workflows, 
and procedures for complaint mechanisms.
Review: Users evaluate channels, response 
times, and service quality; their observations 
lead to operational, technical, and product 
adjustments across the board.

CSAT for submission channels: we measure

Analysis of causes of dissatisfaction: We

Textual user feedback: We conduct qualitative 
monitoring of direct comments that highlight 
operational failures and aspects of perceived

effectiveness of the mechanisms.
Quality assessment of responses using Artificial 
Intelligence (ARI): We implement an automated 
validator that reviews the relevance, attachments, 
tone, form, and clarity of communications sent 
to financial consumers, enabling continuous, 
preventive, and comprehensive monitoring of the 
quality and effectiveness of the response process.
Together, this framework closes the feedback loop 
with stakeholders, ensuring that their perceptions and 
experiences translate into sustainable improvements 
in complaint, claim, and remediation mechanisms.
Operation and metrics: Perceptions regarding 
channels, mechanisms, and service quality 
are converted into indicators such as INS 
and CSAT, the monitoring of which drives 
decisions regarding automation, process 
simplification, regulatory adjustments, and 
the restructuring of operational workflows.
This approach allows us to close the feedback 
loop with users, ensuring that their participation 
is reflected in concrete and sustainable 
improvements.

and evidence of results

in average response times, dropping from 9,5 days

the greater effectiveness of the implemented 
mechanisms.

Regulatory and Legal 
Compliance
SDG 16.5; 16.6; 17.5
| GRI 2-27 |
Regulatory and legal compliance is a cornerstone of financial security that underpins trust and credibility 
with our customers, shareholders, authorities, and other stakeholders. At Banco de Occidente, we work 
to anticipate regulatory changes, ensure the timely application of current legal requirements, and 
maintain controls that support transparent, ethical, and responsible management. We emphasize that 
the Bank is supported by a robust governance and control structure, which has not been implicated 
in insider trading, antitrust violations, unfair competition practices, market manipulation, malpractice, 
or other regulatory breaches within the financial industry.
Therefore, during the reporting period, there were no instances of significant non-compliance with 
applicable laws or regulations. Consequently, the total number of significant non-compliance cases 
reported in 2025 was 0, with the following breakdown: 
Cases resulting in fines 0
Cases resulting in non-monetary sanctions 0
Cases involving insider trading, antitrust violations, unfair competition 
practices, market manipulation, malpractice, or other regulatory violations 
within the financial industry
0
Regarding the description of cases, to date no significant non-compliance has been identified for 
the 2025 reporting period; therefore, there are no events to describe in this section. To determine what 
constitutes a “significant non-compliance,” the Bank relies on its risk management methodology, 
particularly in the management of operational risk, which includes legal risk. This approach allows for 
the assessment of the materiality and potential severity of events, as well as their impact on the Bank 
and its stakeholders, ensuring consistency in the analysis and traceability of the report.

that their potential impact is reflected appropriately 
and transparently in our financial statements. To 
this end, proceedings against the Bank that could 
have a material impact are reviewed and updated 
annually, in accordance with applicable accounting 
and financial standards. This process includes 
the analysis of contingencies and the application 
of accounting principles to determine, where 
appropriate, the required provision amount.
During the reporting period, the total amount of 
monetary losses associated with legal proceedings 
related to fraud amounted to COP 1.362.366.725, 
associated with 50 lawsuits in 2025, rulings involving 
social engineering fraud, malware, fake websites, 
SIM portability/swapping, and product and card 
impersonation.
At Banco de Occidente, the Legal Vice Presidency 
leads legal and regulatory management, working 
closely with the various departments to ensure 
compliance and proper management of legal risk. 
Four divisions report to this Vice Presidency, working 
in coordination to support operations and strengthen 
our corporate governance:
Legal Department for Retail Banking, Staff, and 
Subsidiaries: supports legal risk management 
within the operational risk framework and oversees 
internal regulatory development, as well as the 
corporate governance structure.
Corporate Banking Legal Department: Provides 
effective and timely legal advice to the Corporate 
Banking segments (Institutional and Corporate, 
Business, and Government) for proper business 
structuring, contract drafting, and clarification 
of legal concerns, thereby minimizing the Bank’s 
legal risk.
Litigation Management: Responsible for managing 
litigation against the Bank and provides specialized 
advice on labor and tax matters.
Asset Normalization Department: Leads the 
recovery of specialized and past-due loan 
portfolios, contributing to the Bank’s results 
through efficient collection management and the 
achievement of demanding budgetary targets.
In addition, we promote the use of conciliation as 
an alternative to resolve disputes more quickly and 
In addition, we have legal risk
management mechanisms in place 
to monitor and prevent situations 
that could lead to litigation. 
When we are notified of a legal 
proceeding, a report is triggered to 
the Operational Risk department, 
which is responsible for managing 
and mitigating the risk. Finally, 
during the reporting period, none 
of our subsidiaries recorded any 
significant legal proceedings 
requiring disclosure.

Ethics and

At the same time, we have specific mechanisms for 
legal risk management that allow us to monitor and 
anticipate situations that could lead to litigation. When 
we receive notification of a legal proceeding, a report 
is triggered to the Operational Risk department for 
analysis, follow-up, and the definition of mitigation 
measures. Additionally, during the reporting period, 
none of our subsidiaries recorded any significant

Looking ahead, our commitment is to continue 
strengthening good corporate practices so that 
the Bank remains a benchmark in the sector: not 
only for its financial strength, but also for the way 
it conducts itself—always with ethics, compliance, 
and responsibility.
At Banco de Occidente, we operate under solid ethical 
principles, because we understand that integrity is not 
merely a compliance requirement: it is the foundation of 
trust and the way we conduct business. This commitment 
helps build a more equitable society and a more 
transparent economic system, promoting responsible 
practices that reinforce our values throughout our 
operations. This approach is supported by our Internal 
and External Fraud Management Process Policy and 
is part of the ABAC program.
Our Fraud Management Process Policy and associated 
compliance initiatives aim to prevent and mitigate 
legal and financial risks, while strengthening 
market confidence and our relationships with our 
stakeholders. To this end:
We implement rigorous internal controls;
We conduct regular training on corporate values 
and business ethics for our employees;
We develop awareness-raising initiatives 
for suppliers, promoting a culture of integrity 
throughout the value chain; and
We have confidential reporting channels that 
facilitate the timely detection and management 
of any irregularities.
In this way, we foster a transparent business 
environment, aligned with our ESG strategy and 
continuously improving to address the challenges 
of a demanding and constantly evolving regulatory 
landscape.
| GRI 2-27; 206-1; 205-1; 205-2; 205-3 |
Throughout 2025, we continued to safeguard one of the 
Bank’s most important assets: trust. We reaffirmed our 
commitment to transparency, financial security, and 
the protection of our customers against risks associated 
with fraud and other practices that could compromise 
the integrity of the system. To this end, we maintained 
and strengthened strategies for prevention, detection, 
and incident management, aligned with regulatory 
standards and industry best practices.
Our approach combines preventive measures and 
timely responses, not only to protect customers but also 
to contribute to the stability of the financial system, a 
key pillar of our sustainable management. By promoting 
a safe and reliable environment, we strengthen market 
confidence and facilitate financial inclusion, ensuring 
that more people and businesses can access financial 
services safely.
To maintain these results, we work with internal controls 
and compliance policies that strengthen the prevention 
of misconduct and risk mitigation. This management 
is based on principles of integrity, transparency, and 
accountability, and seeks to ensure that employees, 
customers, and strategic partners operate within a 
reliable financial environment that is fully aligned with 
current regulations.

## Pagina 159

Our Board of Directors assumes responsibility for identifying and understanding the risks associated with 
corruption. Within this framework, it approves the Internal and External Fraud Management Policy and 
monitors its implementation. Periodically, it receives clear, comprehensive, and timely information on the 
assessment of these risks, based on defined criteria that promote continuous improvement.
To manage these risks, we operate under a three-lines-of-defense model, designed so that each team has 
clarity regarding its role and knows how to contribute to safeguarding the Bank’s integrity:
Line of Defense Actions
First line of 
defense: 
management 
from operations
The first line is closest to the day-to-day business. It is responsible for identifying, 
assessing, and managing the risks associated with the products, activities, processes, 
and systems under its responsibility. It consists primarily of the areas that interact 
directly with stakeholders and support operations, including commercial, administrative, 
procurement and contracting, and financial departments, among others, as well as 
those related to accounting. Its role is key because it allows risks to be prevented at 
the source and strengthens controls in day-to-day management.
Second line 
of defense: 
specialized 
oversight and 
support
The second line, comprising the Risk and Compliance departments, continuously 
monitors compliance with obligations and controls related to corruption risk. It works 
in coordination with the first line, supporting it in identifying risks, assessing controls, 
and evaluating their effectiveness to identify gaps, determine the level of residual risk, 
and facilitate the implementation of corrective and preventive action plans.
These tasks are led by the Vice Presidency of Risk and Collections and, specifically 
regarding corruption, by the Banking Security Department, which coordinates 
investigations into potential policy violations and oversees the implementation of 
corrective and disciplinary actions.
Third line 
of defense: 
independent 
assurance
The third line conducts independent assessments of corruption risk management and 
related processes and systems, submitting periodic reports to the Audit Committee. 
This assurance helps strengthen the confidence of investors and other stakeholders by 
providing an objective view of the effectiveness of controls, the transparency of processes, 
and alignment with international standards. The findings and recommendations resulting 
from these reviews allow us to continue strengthening our governance practices, 
improve risk management, and reinforce our commitment to ethics and sustainability.
For this model to work, we promote an ethical culture 
in which we all play a role. That is why we provide 
training for employees (and for certain suppliers who 
act as intermediaries with public entities and officials) 
to reinforce our commitment to transparency. In 
2025, 100% of employees completed the annual 
online course on the Anti-Corruption and Bribery 
Corporate Policy (ABAC), and the ABAC culture 
survey administered to key personnel achieved a 
100% completion rate. thereby strengthening our 
due diligence processes to ensure that business 
relationships and sensitive transactions are managed 
with transparency and with controls commensurate 
with the level of risk. Within this framework, the 
Risk department reviewed both special operations 
and Third-Party Intermediaries (TPIs) linked to the 
operation, issuing a favorable opinion in all cases. 
This exercise strengthens accountability and the 
trust of our stakeholders by verifiably supporting 
our risk prevention and mitigation practices.

Culture of 
Integrity
Ethics Hotline - 
Whistleblowing 
Mechanism
The Ethics Hotline is our confidential and anonymous 
channel for reporting situations that may compromise 
the institution’s standards. It is available to employees, 
customers, users, suppliers, contractors, and 
anyone who wishes to report incidents related to 
fraud, corruption, bribery, money laundering, or 
other irregular conduct, including potential conflicts 
of interest. Its purpose is to facilitate the prevention, 
detection, and mitigation of risks, while protecting 
the confidentiality of the information and the identity 
of the whistleblower.
Through this channel, the following incidents, among 
others, can be reported:
Inappropriate use or misappropriation of the Bank’s 
assets;
Conduct contrary to the values and principles 
established in the Codes of Ethics, Conduct, and 
Good Governance;
Violation of internal rules or policies;
Improper disclosure of confidential information.
The Ethics Hotline is managed by the Internal Audit 
Department, which guarantees the confidentiality 
of reports and the proper administration of the 
channel. The Ethics Hotline is available on the Bank’s 
website, making it accessible to the general public. 
Its existence and operation are communicated every 
six months via email to customers, suppliers, and 
employees, and are also published on the website.
| GRI 2-26; SASB FN-CB-510a.2. |
At the Bank, we manage ethics and compliance as 
part of our daily operations, with clear rules and 
mechanisms that facilitate timely action. To this end, 
we have the Code of Ethics and Conduct and the 
Internal Work Regulations. Upon joining the Bank, 
and each time these documents are updated, all 
employees sign a commitment to conduct and 
compliance, reaffirming the standards that guide 
the way we work.
When a situation is identified that may constitute a 
breach of these standards, employees are required 
to report it through the appropriate channels, as 
applicable: their immediate supervisor, the Vice 
Presidency of Human Resources, the Internal 
Audit Department, the Compliance Department, 
or the Bank Security Department. This framework 
strengthens our culture of control and risk mitigation 
and supports the trust of customers, shareholders, 
and other stakeholders.
Furthermore, we believe in equality as a right and in 
equity as a guiding principle of our organizational 
identity. In our labor relations, we promote an 
environment free of discrimination, and during the 
period, we did not record any cases of this nature.
Once a report is received, the Internal Audit 
Department conducts an initial analysis and refers 
the case to the responsible departments, setting a 
reasonable deadline for follow-up and reporting of 
results. In complex situations, external specialists—
such as forensic auditors—may be consulted to 
conduct a more in-depth analysis. If irregularities 
are confirmed, the relevant departments, such as 
the Labor Relations Department, handle the case 
and apply the appropriate measures and sanctions 
in accordance with the Bank’s policies.
All complaints received are investigated, and once the 
analysis is complete, they are presented to the Audit 
Committee. Additionally, a report is prepared twice a 
year detailing the number of complaints received and 
how they were handled. Beyond investigating, Internal 
Audit also monitors and analyzes root causes to 
strengthen the ethical culture and continue improving 
internal processes.

In 2025, we continued to strengthen the Ethics Hotline 
as an accessible and trustworthy channel for listening, 
responding, and learning. Overall, the total volume 
of reports remained stable, with 187 complaints 
compared to 195 in 2024 (a decrease of 8 cases, 
equivalent to -4,1%). Looking at the breakdown, a 
significant change is observed: complaints received 
through the Bank + subsidiaries channel fell from 183 
to 154 (-15,8%), while those recorded through the 
Grupo Aval channel increased from 12 to 33 (175%). 
This trend suggests greater use of the corporate 
channel and reinforces the importance of maintaining 
integrated and consistent case management, 
regardless of the point of entry.
Upon examining the types of requests in greater 
detail, the main finding for 2025 is that reports in 
which the information provided was insufficient or 
lacked supporting evidence increased from 67 to 
79 (17,9%). This category became the most prevalent 
of the year, and sets a clear priority for us: to better 
support those who submit reports by providing 
simpler guidelines on what information to include, 
practical examples, and adjustments to the forms 
to facilitate a complete and verifiable account from 
the outset. At the same time, customer complaints 
and requests decreased from 72 to 52 (-27,7%), and 
reports regarding the work environment fell from 42 
to 37 (-11,9%), reflecting a reduction in these areas 
compared to the previous year. On the other hand, 
alerts regarding poor business practices increased 
from 12 to 19 (58,3%), an issue we continue to address 
with special attention due to its direct relationship 
with service, controls, and the customer experience. 
Finally, in 2025, no potential conflicts of interest 
were recorded (in 2024, 2 were reported).
Based on these results, our focus moving forward is 
twofold: on the one hand, to improve the quality and 
completeness of reports (to act more quickly and 
effectively) and, on the other, to deepen the root￾cause analysis of categories that have grown or 
remained steady, such as unfair commercial practices.
This involves strengthening 
communication within the channel, 
simplifying reporting guidelines 
and fields, and using each case as 
input for continuous improvement, 
so that the Ethics Hotline is not only 
a reporting mechanism but also 
a concrete tool for strengthening 
integrity, prevention, and trust.

## Pagina 167

Emissions 
Management 
and Climate 
Change
As a financial institution, we understand that 
our climate impact extends beyond our direct 
operations and is largely realized through the sectors, 
projects, and activities we finance. In this regard, 
the management of financed emissions is a key 
component of our climate strategy, as it allows us to 
understand, manage, and support the transition of 
our portfolio toward more sustainable and climate￾resilient production models.
To advance this objective, we have been progressively 
strengthening our technical and analytical 
capabilities, integrating climate criteria into 
portfolio management, and aligning with recognized 
international standards.
Climate change represents one of the main long￾term environmental and financial challenges. At 
Banco de Occidente, we address this challenge in 
a structured manner, integrating climate strategy 
and decarbonization as cross-cutting pillars of our 
environmental and risk management. Our approach 
combines the progressive reduction of greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions, the efficient use of resources, 
and the integration of climate-related criteria into 
decision-making, with the aim of strengthening 
organizational resilience, supporting our clients in 
their transition, and contributing to the sustainable 
development of the regions where we operate.
Within this framework, we are making consistent 
progress in defining goals, metrics, and action plans 
aligned with international benchmarks, prioritizing 
data-driven management, continuous improvement, 
and transparency toward our stakeholders.
SDG 7.3; 13.2; 15.1
For more detailed information on 
the Bank’s approach to the risks 
and opportunities associated 
with climate change, as well as 
the methodology, scenarios, and 
results of the climate analysis, 
please refer to Annex 3 – TCFD 
Report, which provides additional 
information on our climate strategy, 
risk management, and climate 
performance measurement.
