## Pagina 169

Carbon 
Footprint
| GRI 305-1; 305-2; 305-3; 305-4; 305-5 |
Methodological Approach
Measuring our carbon footprint is a fundamental 
step toward responsibly managing our climate 
impact and guiding decisions that drive the Bank’s 
decarbonization. Therefore, we have developed 
a quantification process that is consistent and 
comparable over time, allowing us to understand 
where our emissions are generated and how we can 
progressively reduce them.
The calculation of our greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions is carried out in accordance with the 
GHG Protocol, the most widely used international 
standard, applying an operational control approach, 
meaning we include those operations over which 
the Bank has the authority to implement policies 
and management measures. Based on the identified 
emission sources, this calculation incorporates the 
main greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide 
(CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), and 
refrigerant gases such as SF₆, HFCs, and HCFCs, 
allowing us to reflect our climate impact more 
comprehensively and accurately.
Our carbon footprint includes Scope 1, 2, and 3 
emissions, providing a comprehensive view of our 
climate impact:
Scope 1: direct emissions primarily 
associated with fuel consumption from 
mobile sources (the Entity’s own vehicles) 
and stationary sources (power plants), as 
well as fugitive emissions from refrigerants 
in air conditioning systems and gases 
contained in fire extinguishers. 
Scope 2: indirect emissions resulting from 
the consumption of electricity purchased for 
our offices and administrative headquarters.
Scope 3: Indirect emissions relevant 
throughout the upstream and downstream 
value chain, including categories such 
as purchased goods and services, paper 
consumption, business travel (ground and 
air), employee commuting, waste generated 
in operations, fossil fuel consumption in 
courier services, and cash-in-transit and 
logistics.
GHG emissions measurement covers 100% of the data for Scopes 1, 2, and 3. For fiscal year 2025, the Bank 
set emission targets of 1.102,77 tCO₂e (Scope 1), 2.344,27 tCO₂e (Scope 2), and 3.485,54 tCO₂e (Scope 3) 
as the basis for monitoring and evaluating its climate performance.

For Scope 2, we report emissions associated with electricity consumption using both location-based 
method and market-based method, in accordance with GHG Protocol guidelines. This dual method allows 
us to transparently reflect both the intensity of the national electricity grid and the impact of our operational 
decisions.
To calculate emissions, we use nationally and 
internationally recognized emission factors, 
prioritizing those specific to Colombia when available, 
and updating them periodically to reflect changes in 
the energy mix and system conditions.
We have defined 2022 as the base year, as we have 
consistent and traceable information that allows us 
to make robust comparisons and track our reduction 
targets. We continuously work to improve data 
coverage and quality, strengthening the systems for 
collecting, validating, and consolidating environmental 
information.

The trend in GHG emission intensity indicators, 
calculated as the ratio of total emissions to 
the total number of employees, demonstrates 
a ustained improvement in the Bank’s climate 
performance, showing a gradual reduction in 
emissions relative to our operational metrics.
Between 2021 and 2025, total emissions 
intensity decreased from 2.48 to 0.71, 
confirming that the reduction in emissions is 
not only due to lower absolute values but also 
to greater operational efficiency. This trend 
reflects the integration of climate management 
criteria into decision-making and process 
optimization.
The reduction is mainly explained by the 
decrease in Scope 3 emissions intensity, 
which has historically represented the largest 
component of the indicator, as well as by 
consistent improvements in Scopes 1 and 2. 
In particular, a trend toward stabilization and 
reduction in intensity has been observed in 
recent years, aligned with energy efficiency 
initiatives, optimization of fuel consumption, 
and strengthened value chain management.
Reduction in GHG 
Emissions
*Figures in percentage (%) of GHG emissions reduction in 
metric tons of CO₂equivalent (tCO₂e).
In 2025, we made significant progress in reducing 
greenhouse gas emissions, reflecting the impact of 
actions implemented consistently across the different 
scopes and strengthening our emissions management 
strategy.
Under Scope 1, the reduction in emissions is primarily 
due to lower fuel consumption from mobile sources, 
as well as more efficient management of refrigerants 
used in air conditioning systems. Additionally, ongoing 
preventive maintenance helped prevent leaks and 
reduce fugitive emissions, directly contributing to 
improved performance under this scope.
In Scope 2, the reduction observed in 2025 is due 
to lower electricity consumption, combined with 
a change in the emission factor of the National 
Interconnected System, published by XM, which 
showed a 55,76% reduction compared to 2024. This 
combination of factors resulted in a 58% decrease in 
Scope 2 emissions, positively impacting the overall 
result of our carbon footprint.
Meanwhile, a significant reduction in emissions was 
achieved for Scope 3, primarily due to the decrease 
in paper consumption, the reduction in waste 
generation, and more efficient management of 
outsourced transportation. Regarding employee 
transportation to and from the Bank, there was a slight 
increase, associated with both the hybrid work model 
and the strengthening of our Sustainable Mobility 
Program, which continues to focus on optimizing 
these commutes in the medium term.
Overall, our total emissions were reduced by 28,9% 
compared to 2024, and by approximately 44% 
compared to the 2022 baseline. These results reflect 
the impact of the initiatives and actions implemented 
during 2024 and 2025, and put us on a positive path 
toward meeting the reduction targets established 
under the 2030 Agenda, our Emissions Management 
Plan, and the Operational Eco-efficiency Plan.

Financed Absolute Emissions – Scope 3
At Banco de Occidente, we understand that managing financed emissions is a key component of our 
sustainability strategy and our commitment to the transition toward a low-carbon economy. These emissions, 
classified as Scope 3, correspond to the climate impacts associated with financing provided through our 
products and services, and represent one of the financial sector’s main challenges and opportunities in the 
face of climate change.
Senior Management and the Sustainability Committee play a central role in overseeing this process, ensuring 
that the measurement and management of financed emissions are aligned with the Bank’s Sustainability 
Strategy, comprehensive risk management, and our long-term decarbonization goals. This strategic oversight 
allows us to progressively integrate climate criteria into decision-making and strengthen our portfolio’s 
resilience to transition risks.
We recognize that measuring financed emissions is an evolving process that requires continuous improvements 
in methodologies, data quality, and internal capabilities. In this regard, we adopt the Partnership for Carbon 
Accounting Financials (PCAF) standard and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol guidelines as our reference, 
taking into account emissions associated with loans and investments over which we have no operational or 
financial control.
As part of our commitment to decarbonizing our 
portfolio, we have conducted an initial assessment 
of financed emissions for the 2023 portfolio, 
which includes loans, investments, and insurance 
policies. This assessment initially focuses on sectors 
prioritized due to their higher exposure to climate 
risk. Subsequently, with the aim of obtaining a 
more robust, consistent, and technically sound 
estimate, we decided to expand the scope of the 
exercise to 100% of the commercial and consumer 
portfolio, strengthening data quality, traceability, 
and consistency processes.
In 2025, with the support of a specialized consultant, 
we measured the financed emissions of the 2024 
portfolio under this expanded scope, in accordance 
with the PCAF standard and the GHG Protocol 
guidelines. This exercise allowed us to identify 
information gaps, opportunities for improvement, 
and needs for technical strengthening—fundamental 
elements for advancing in a structured and progressive 
manner in the portfolio’s climate management.
As a result, we continue to strengthen our internal 
capabilities to ensure increasingly reliable and 
comparable information, which will allow us, in the 
medium and long term, to define clear, measurable, 
and achievable portfolio decarbonization targets, 
as well as expand opportunities for sustainable 
financing and actively contribute to a more resilient 
economy aligned with global commitments on climate 
change.

Intensity of financed 
emissions
As part of our efforts to strengthen our 
climate management, we have incorporated 
an analysis of the emissions intensity of the 
investments we finance, using the Weighted 
Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) metric. This 
indicator allows us to understand our portfolio’s 
level of exposure to carbon-intensive activities 
from a financial perspective.
WACI is calculated based on the weight of 
each company or asset within the portfolio 
and its respective emissions intensity relative 
to its revenue. While this metric does not 
represent a direct link to actual emissions in 
the physical world, it does provide a relevant 
signal regarding the portfolio’s climate 
risk profile, which is particularly useful for 
strategic decision-making and transition risk 
management.
During the period analyzed, we observed a 
significant evolution in portfolio coverage, 
rising from 6,36% in 2023 to 98,38% in 
2024, reflecting substantial progress in the 
availability and quality of the information used 
for this exercise. In 2024, the total intensity of 
Scope 3 financed emissions stood at 0,07269 
tons of CO₂e per million COP (MCOP), 
establishing this indicator as a key baseline 
for future monitoring.

Goals, challenges, and opportunities in financed emissions
The management of financed emissions is a strategic pillar in the evolution of our ESG strategy and in the transition process toward a 
portfolio aligned with a low-carbon economy. In this context, during 2025 we made progress in strengthening technical and information 
capabilities, laying the groundwork for defining future decarbonization goals. 
Goals
Challenges
Opportunities
2025 Goal (short term): Measure financed emissions 
corresponding to the 2024 portfolio, expanding the 
scope and coverage of the exercise. Result: Goal 
achieved. The measurement was carried out with 
the support of a specialized consultant, achieving 
98.38% coverage of the portfolio and incorporating 
assets from Corporate Banking and Retail Banking 
under the PCAF methodology.
2026 Goal (short–medium term): 
Deepen the calculation of financed 
emissions with a higher level of 
granularity, especially in material areas 
and relevant sectors, strengthening the 
quality, consistency, and traceability of 
the information.
Consolidate a solid and validated baseline that allows for the 
definition of realistic, measurable, and comparable commitments 
over time, within a context of high methodological complexity 
and variable availability of information.
Progressively integrate the management of financed emissions 
into business decision-making, ensuring consistency with the 
Bank’s business strategy, risk appetite, and climate management.
Transform climate impact analysis into a competitive 
advantage, strengthening risk management, transparency, 
and the Bank’s positioning in the financial market.
Support clients in their transition by offering more 
sustainable financing alternatives and promoting practices 
that reduce their environmental impact and strengthen 
their resilience to climate change.
2026–2027 Goal (medium term): 
Define and establish portfolio 
decarbonization goals and targets 
based on a robust and reliable baseline, 
aligned with the Bank’s strategy, risk 
management, and international best 
practices in sustainable finance.

Sustainable 
Mobility Program 
Key Program Results
Thanks to the active participation of our employees, we 
closed 2025 with significant results:
More than 2.000 registered users on the Try My Ride 
app.
More than 1.200 active participating employees, 
59% of whom are women.
Promotion of multiple sustainable mobility alternatives 
for commuting between home and work.
36,3 tons of CO₂e avoided in 2025, equivalent to 
the CO₂ absorption of 1,212 trees.
Cumulatively since 2022, more than 120 tons of CO₂e 
avoided, equivalent to approximately 3.000 trees.
Generation of savings exceeding $84 million pesos 
in public transportation fares during 2025.
Contribution to reducing harassment of women on 
public transportation, promoting safer and more 
supportive journeys.
2026 Projection
Looking ahead to 2026, we will continue to strengthen 
the Sustainable Mobility Program by expanding the 
number of users and published routes, with the goal of 
increasing emissions avoided and continuing to contribute 
to environmental sustainability and the overall well-being 
of our employees.
SDG 9.3; 11; 13.2
| BdO-7 |
Our commitment to sustainable mobility was strengthened in 2025 through 
the optimization of the Try My Ride platform, which facilitates environmentally 
friendly transportation alternatives. Throughout 2025, this initiative established 
itself as a cornerstone of our decarbonization strategy, enabling us to 
mitigate indirect emissions while ensuring safer and more equitable commutes 
for our employees.
To encourage participation, we launched digital campaigns through our 
internal platform, the Try My Ride app, and company emails. These efforts 
were complemented by in-person outreach events at our administrative 
offices in Bogotá and Cali, where our partner presented the program, 
addressed questions, and promoted the use of alternatives such as carpooling, 
bicycles, and public transportation.
A significant milestone in 2025 was the accreditation of the Corporate 
Sustainable Mobility Plan by the Mobility Secretariats of Bogotá and Cali, 
successfully achieved in 2025. This recognition strengthens the alignment 
of our strategy with local public policies and validates the program’s 
comprehensive approach.
In the second half of the year, we expanded the program’s coverage to 
employees at the administrative offices in Medellín and Barranquilla,
joining those already in place in Cali and Bogotá. This expansion was 
accompanied by a campaign to award bicycles to the program’s most 
outstanding users and recognition activities, through which we celebrated 
our third anniversary alongside our employees.

Operational 
Eco-efficiency
Energy Management
| GRI 302-1; 302-3; 302-4 |
Energy management is a central pillar of our 
operational eco-efficiency and a key enabler for 
reducing emissions associated with our operations. 
At Banco de Occidente, we address this challenge 
through a comprehensive approach that combines 
responsible energy use, efficiency in electricity 
consumption, and a progressive shift toward 
renewable sources, with the goal of transitioning 
to an increasingly sustainable operating model.
Our approach prioritizes the implementation of 
technological solutions, process optimization, and 
continuous monitoring of energy performance, 
aligning daily management with the goals defined 
in the Eco-Efficiency Plan, the 2030 Agenda, and 
our decarbonization strategy. In this way, we seek 
to reduce dependence on non-renewable sources, 
improve energy efficiency, and strengthen an 
organizational culture focused on the conscious 
use of resources.
Looking ahead to 2030, we have set a goal to reduce 
our electricity consumption by 20%, using 2022 as 
the baseline year. To achieve this, we continuously 
promote eco-efficiency initiatives that enable us 
to achieve a minimum annual reduction of 2,5% in 
energy consumption. 
Achievements of Our 
Management in 2025
During 2025, the Bank’s energy management resulted 
in the following progress:
Sustained reduction in total energy consumption, 
in line with the defined eco-efficiency goals.
Reduction in electricity consumption as a result of 
energy efficiency projects implemented in offices 
and headquarters.
Increase in energy consumption from renewable 
sources, driven by the continuous operation of 
solar panel systems in our offices.
Significant reduction in non-renewable energy 
consumption associated with the vehicle leasing 
program and preventive maintenance of power 
plants.
Improvement in energy intensity, demonstrating 
greater energy efficiency relative to the number 
of employees.
Consolidation of energy consumption monitoring 
and control, strengthening the quality of information 
for decision-making.
SDG 6.4; 7.3; 13.1
Operational eco-efficiency is a key pillar of our 
environmental management, as it allows us to reduce 
the impact of our operations while enhancing resource 
efficiency. Through responsible management of 
energy, water, waste, and paper consumption, 
we seek to optimize processes, reduce associated 
emissions, and promote an organizational culture 
focused on the conscious use of resources.
Our approach combines the 
systematic measurement of 
environmental performance, the 
implementation of continuous 
improvement initiatives, and the 
participation of our employees. 
In this way, we are moving 
toward a more efficient and 
resilient operation, aligned with 
the Bank’s long-term goals, the 
Eco-efficiency Plan, and the 
commitments of the 2030 Agenda.

## Pagina 179

Measurement and Monitoring of Energy Consumption
Measuring and monitoring energy consumption are essential for guiding our decisions and evaluating 
the progress of eco-efficiency initiatives. At Banco de Occidente, we manage this information centrally 
through the Energy Master platform, where we consolidate the energy consumption of our operational 
sites based on invoices from various suppliers, ensuring 100% coverage of reported data.
Based on this information, we strengthen operational control, track goal achievement, and prioritize 
energy efficiency projects, ensuring more precise and timely energy management that is aligned with 
the Bank’s sustainability objectives.
Trend in total electricity consumption 
In 2025, we reached a total consumption of 10.616,90 MWh, representing a 5,84% reduction 
compared to 2024 and a cumulative decrease of 16,8% from our baseline. This performance, which 
exceeded the expected annual target, is the result of the consolidation of our energy efficiency project 
launched in 2023, through which we progressively installed energy-efficient lighting, solar control films, 
and state-of-the-art air conditioning equipment at our facilities.
We have implemented solutions that improve seasonal efficiency by up to 28% compared to conventional 
technologies. Since a large portion of these installations was completed in the fourth quarter of 
2023, we ensured that the most significant impact was maintained consistently throughout 2025, 
reaffirming our path toward long-term sustainability goals.
Energy consumption by source 
type
As part of our eco-efficiency and energy transition 
strategy, we manage energy consumption by 
distinguishing between renewable and non￾renewable sources, with the goal of moving toward 
a more efficient energy mix with a lower environmental 
impact.
In 2025, energy consumption from renewable sources 
reached 198,09 MWh, representing an 11,9% increase 
compared to 2024 and a cumulative 81% increase 
relative to the 2022 baseline. This performance is due 
to the continuous operation, throughout the twelve 
months of the year, of the solar panel systems installed 
at six of the Bank’s offices, as well as the progressive 
expansion of solar solutions at our locations. This 
trend reflects a planned transition toward the use of 
cleaner energy, which will continue to strengthen in 
the coming years.
Meanwhile, non-renewable energy consumption 
showed a significant reduction, standing at 85,94 
MWh in 2025, which equates to a decrease of 33,8% 
compared to 2024 and 51,26% compared to 2022. 
This reduction is primarily due to a structural change in 
vehicle fleet management through the leasing scheme 
implemented since 2022, which has allowed for the 
optimization of the use of company-owned vehicles. 
Additionally, in 2025 there was a 26,55% reduction 
in fuel consumption compared to 2024, associated 
with the strengthening of preventive maintenance 
at power plants located in different regions of the 
country.
*Figures in megawatt-hours (MWh).

Energy intensity
Energy intensity 
Energy intensity allows us to analyze energy consumption in relation to the number of employees, providing 
a more accurate view of the Bank’s operational efficiency. This indicator reflects how energy optimization 
measures translate into a more efficient use of resources, regardless of whether operations are growing or 
stable.
In 2025, energy intensity was 1,51 MWh per employee, representing a 6,21% reduction compared to 2024 
and a cumulative decrease of 15,64% compared to the 2022 baseline. This result demonstrates the positive 
impact of the energy efficiency projects implemented and reinforces the Bank’s progress toward a more 
efficient and sustainable operation, in line with its eco-efficiency and energy transition goals.
Water Resource 
Management
| GRI 303-5 |
Water is an essential resource for our operations, 
and therefore, at Banco de Occidente, we manage 
its use responsibly and efficiently as part of our 
operational eco-efficiency strategy. Our approach 
prioritizes optimizing consumption, preventing 
waste, and fostering an organizational culture 
focused on the conscious use of this resource.
At our facilities, the water supply comes from local 
water utilities in each municipality and city where 
we operate, and its use is intended exclusively for 
domestic purposes, such as sanitation, hygiene, 
and food preparation. Similarly, the wastewater 
generated consists of domestic sewage, which is 
treated and disposed of through municipal sewer 
systems, in compliance with current environmental 
regulations.
In line with our Eco-Efficiency Plan and the 
commitments of the 2030 Agenda, we have set a 
target to reduce water consumption by 10%, using 
2024 as the baseline. This approach provides us 
with a clear and technically sound starting point 
for tracking performance, guiding our operational 
decisions, and establishing more efficient and 
sustainable management practices over time.
Our Management 
Achievements in 2025
During 2025, we strengthened this management 
through the following actions:
Continuous monitoring of water 
consumption at operational sites, with 
tracking of significant variations.
Reporting and correction of leaks, based 
on early warnings identified in Energy 
Master.
A campaign promoting resource 
conservation and efficient use, carried 
out during the first half of the year, which 
encouraged responsible practices and 
recognized the offices with the best 
performance.
Implementation of water-saving 
technologies, such as water-saving faucets 
and toilets with flow control systems.
Environmental education programs aimed 
at strengthening a culture of responsible 
water use among employees.
While these initiatives contributed to a 
decrease in consumption at several locations, 
the overall performance of the indicator 
in 2025 was influenced by the addition of 
new measurement points, reinforcing the 
importance of continuing to advance targeted 
water efficiency actions in the coming periods.
*Figures in megawatt-hours per employee (MWh/
employee).

Water Consumption
Measuring water consumption is a central pillar of our water resource management. To this end, we consolidate 
data through the Energy Master platform, where we record and analyze consumption at our operational sites 
based on water utility bills, thereby enhancing data traceability and reliability for decision-making.
The trend in water consumption reflects the strengthening of our water resource management and 
the progressive improvement in the quality of reported information. In 2025, the Bank’s total water 
consumption was 0,0398 M³, representing a 19,52% increase compared to 2024.
This increase should be interpreted in the context of adjustments to data coverage and the consolidation 
of complete information from all operational sites. Specifically, in 2024, consumption at the Cali 
Main Building – Tower 1 was recorded for only six months, whereas in 2025, data for the full twelve 
months of the year was included, resulting in an upward variation compared to the previous period.
In this regard, the trend observed in the graph does not reflect a structural increase in water use, but 
rather a more accurate and representative measurement of actual consumption, strengthening the 
information base for implementing water optimization and efficient use measures in future periods.
*Figures in millions of cubic meters (M³).

## Pagina 183

Water Consumption in Water-Stressed Areas
As part of our responsible management of water resources, we conduct specific monitoring of water 
consumption in areas identified as water-stressed, based on information provided by environmental 
authorities. This approach allows us to better understand the potential risks associated with water use 
and to direct optimization efforts in regions with greater water sensitivity.
In 2025, water consumption in these areas was 0,0139 M³, representing an 8,43% decrease compared 
to 2024. This reduction demonstrates the positive impact of measures for efficient water use and 
continuous monitoring of consumption at facilities located in these regions.
During the 2021–2025 period, no direct water 
extraction or discharge activities were recorded, 
indicating that our operation does not place 
additional pressure on natural water sources.
Total net freshwater consumption remained stable 
between 2021 and 2023 (0,0275–0,0266 million m³), 
with an increase in 2024 (0,0333) and 2025 (0,0398), 
associated with higher occupancy at facilities and 
the normalization of in-person activities.
By 2025, consumption exceeded the established 
annual target (0,0328 million m³), reinforcing the 
need to continue strengthening our water efficiency 
strategies and internal awareness initiatives. 
100% data coverage across all years ensures the 
traceability and reliability of the reported information.
Goals, Challenges, and 
Opportunities
For 2025, we set a target of a 1,5% reduction in 
water consumption. Although the indicator showed 
an increase of 19,52%, this result is primarily due 
to improved coverage and quality of information, 
stemming from the inclusion of new consumption 
points, and not to a structural increase in resource 
use. This advancement in measurement constitutes, in 
turn, a significant milestone for future management.
Since this data lacks traceability from previous years, 
we have established 2024 as a new baseline without 
this affecting our 10% reduction target, aligned with 
our Eco-Efficiency Plan and the 2030 Agenda, which 
equates to an annual decrease of 1,5%. 
*Figures in millions of cubic meters (M³).
The areas considered in this analysis include, among others, the cities of Aguachica, Barrancabermeja, 
Barranquilla, Bogotá, Bucaramanga, Chía, Girardot, Girón, Guatapé, Medellín, Montería, Mosquera, 
Piedecuesta, Riohacha, San Gil, Siberia, Valledupar, and Zipaquirá, whose consumption is monitored 
through the Energy Master platform.
It is important to note that, as of 2025, some consumption figures are still being consolidated due to 
bimonthly billing schedules. However, the observed trend confirms a management approach focused 
on reducing consumption in contexts of increased water stress, thereby strengthening the Bank’s 
operational resilience.

## Pagina 184

Waste 
Management
Comprehensive Waste 
Management Model
Waste management at Banco de Occidente is 
structured around our Comprehensive Waste 
Management Plan (PGIR), which guides actions to 
prevent, minimize, recover, and properly dispose 
of the waste generated in our operations. This model 
is implemented at all locations, ensuring consistent 
management aligned with current environmental 
regulations.
The PGIR is based on four main pillars:
Prevention and minimization, through the reduction 
of waste at the source.
Internal waste management, through proper 
segregation and safe temporary storage.
External waste management, through delivery 
to authorized environmental service providers 
for recycling or final disposal.
Monitoring and evaluation, which allows us to 
verify compliance with actions and continuously 
improve management.
This management is complemented by awareness 
campaigns and environmental education programs 
aimed at employees, strengthening a culture of source 
separation and responsible use of resources—key 
to meeting our eco-efficiency goals.
Goals, Challenges, and 
Opportunities
By 2025, we achieved a 25,94% reduction in waste 
generated compared to 2024, regaining the 
optimization trend following the one-time increase 
associated with remodeling projects. This result 
reflects the strengthening of control, recovery, and 
reduction efforts at the source.
Moving forward, the main challenges center on 
managing waste resulting from infrastructure 
upgrades and implementing site-specific monitoring, 
while opportunities lie in increasing the reuse of 
recyclable materials, further digitizing processes, 
and consolidating a culture of source separation that 
enables continued reduction in waste generation.
Measurement, Scope, and 
Quality of Information
Information on waste generated and managed 
is compiled from the operational records of the 
Bank’s offices and reports issued by authorized 
environmental managers, ensuring traceability, 
reliability, and compliance with current environmental 
regulations. The coverage of the reported data is 
100% for the period analyzed.
Tracking is conducted by distinguishing between 
waste types (hazardous and non-hazardous) and 
their final disposition (recovery or disposal), which 
allows for the evaluation of management performance 
and the identification of areas for improvement. The 
variations observed in the indicators, particularly the 
increase recorded in 2024, are mainly due to building 
and office renovation activities, which generated 
higher volumes of construction and demolition waste. 
In 2025, the normalization of these activities and 
the strengthening of control measures allowed for 
a return to the path of reduction and optimization 
in waste management.
| GRI 306-3; 306-4; 306-5 |
Waste management is a key pillar of our operational 
eco-efficiency and our commitment to more 
sustainable operations. At Banco de Occidente, we 
focus this management on reducing waste generation, 
utilizing waste, and ensuring proper final disposal, 
in line with the principles of the circular economy,
the 2030 Agenda, and our Comprehensive Waste 
Management Plan (PGIR).
Our approach prioritizes prevention at the source, 
proper separation, and the strengthening of reuse and 
recycling practices, ensuring that waste that cannot 
be reused is managed safely through authorized 
environmental service providers, in compliance 
with current regulations. 
In line with this commitment, we 
have set a goal to reduce waste 
generation by 20% by 2030, 
equivalent to an annual reduction 
of 2,5%, thereby consolidating 
responsible management focused 
on continuous improvement.

Waste Generation
The trend in waste generated reflects the impact of the Bank’s operational activities and specific events, such 
as building and office remodeling projects. In 2025, total waste generated was 246,66 tons, representing 
a 25,94% reduction compared to 2024, a year in which a significant increase was recorded, primarily 
associated with facility adaptation and renovation projects.
During 2025, 98,11% of the waste generated was properly treated and recycled, maintaining a performance 
consistent with the past four years and demonstrating the effectiveness of our management. Given the nature 
of our operations, approximately 80% of the waste generated is non-hazardous, most of which is recycled 
or reused. Waste Not Sent to Landfill (Recovery)
Waste recovery is a central pillar of our management and a reflection of the circular economy approach we 
promote in our operations. In 2025, more than 95% of the waste generated was recovered, maintaining a 
performance consistent with recent years and demonstrating the effectiveness of the actions implemented.
Non-hazardous waste accounts for the largest proportion of recovery. In 2025, 220,94 tons of recovered 
non-hazardous waste were managed, primarily paper, cardboard, wood, metal, and plastic—materials 
largely associated with building and office renovation processes—which were reintroduced into recycling 
chains through authorized environmental management companies.
Regarding recycled hazardous waste, 21,06 tons were managed in 2025, with a notable reduction compared 
to 2024, particularly in Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE), as a result of the completion 
of technology renewal projects. Other waste, such as lamps and toner, continued to be managed under 
specialized recycling programs.
*Figures in tons (ton). *Figures in tons (ton).
Overall, the 2025 results confirm a return to the path of waste reduction and 
progress toward meeting the goals established in our Eco-Efficiency Plan.

Waste sent for disposal
Waste destined for disposal represents a smaller proportion of total waste generated, reflecting the Bank’s 
focus on reuse and reduction at the source. In 2025, there was a significant decrease in waste sent to final 
disposal, particularly that destined for landfills and containment cells.
During the year, 0,15 tons of non-hazardous waste were disposed of, reflecting a sustained reduction 
compared to previous years. Regarding hazardous waste destined for disposal, 4,51 tons were managed, 
representing a 29,29% reduction compared to 2024, primarily due to the completion of remodeling activities 
and improved control over the generation of this type of waste.
It is important to note that in 2025, no waste was incinerated, nor was there any waste with unknown disposal 
methods, and that all waste destined for disposal was managed through authorized environmental service 
providers, in compliance with current environmental regulations.

Following the increase recorded in 2024 
(333,06 tons), primarily associated with office 
and building renovation projects, in 2025 we 
managed to stabilize the indicator, reaching a 
total of 246,66 tons. This represents a 25,94% 
reduction compared to the previous year, 
demonstrating the effectiveness of the actions 
implemented to strengthen control, prevention, 
and responsible waste management.
During this period, we increased the amount 
of recyclable waste—particularly paper, 
metal, wood, and cardboard—generated 
by remodeling activities, ensuring its proper 
sorting and recycling. At the same time, we 
strengthened structural measures for source 
reduction, such as digitizing documents to 
reduce paper consumption and promoting 
remote work, contributing to lower operational 
waste generation.
Regarding hazardous waste, in 2025 we 
recorded 4,65 tons, representing a 40,54% 
reduction compared to 2024. This result 
reflects more efficient management within the 
framework of interventions carried out at our 
facilities and rigorous control of final disposal, 
always prioritizing regulatory compliance and 
the minimization of environmental impact.
Reduction and Circular Economy 
Initiatives
As part of our strategy to reduce waste generation 
and strengthen the circular economy, in 2025 
we continued to implement actions focused on 
prevention at the source, material reuse, and 
changing habits in our operations.
Key initiatives include:
Strengthening the reuse of waste, particularly 
paper, cardboard, wood, and metal, associated 
with office and building renovation processes.
Digitizing documents and processes, contributing 
to the reduction of paper consumption and waste 
associated with printing and logistics.
Promoting remote work as a complementary 
measure to reduce waste generation at 
administrative offices.
Source separation campaigns, accompanied by 
clear signage and guidelines in offices.
Environmental awareness and education 
programs for employees, focused on best practices 
in waste management.
Paper Consumption
Managing paper consumption is a key component of 
our operational eco-efficiency strategy, as it allows 
us to reduce environmental impacts associated 
with printing, logistics, and resource use, while 
strengthening the digitization of our processes and 
our customers’ experience.
At Banco de Occidente, we address 
this challenge from a comprehensive 
perspective, prioritizing digital 
transformation, the responsible use 
of supplies, and the optimization of 
information flows. This approach has 
allowed us to make steady progress 
in reducing paper consumption, 
aligning our operations with long￾term environmental goals and an 
increasingly efficient operating 
model.

## Pagina 190

Leverages for Reducing 
Paper Consumption
To advance the progressive reduction of paper 
consumption, in 2025 we strengthened a set of 
structural measures aimed at preventing the 
unnecessary use of this resource and promoting 
digital alternatives:
Digitization of the office supply ordering process
using the Ofix platform, facilitating the monitoring 
and tracking of office supply usage.
Review and control of stationery requests 
to avoid unnecessary volumes of supplies and 
promote more efficient use.
Implementation of certified text messaging 
for products such as vehicles, payroll, and 
rotating inventory, reducing the need for printed 
communications.
Continuation of the migration from physical 
statements to digital statements, consolidating 
electronic channels as the primary means of 
communication with customers.
Exclusive use of eco-friendly paper for office 
stationery supplies, as a measure to mitigate the 
environmental impact associated with residual 
paper consumption.
Key Results 2025
During the year, total paper consumption reached 
30,82 tons, reflecting the following results:
A 12,10% reduction compared to 2024.
A cumulative reduction of 44,7% compared to 
the 2022 baseline.
Consistent progress toward the goal of reducing 
paper consumption by 25% by 2030, as established 
in our Eco-Efficiency Plan.
These results are primarily due to the increased 
digitization of processes, more efficient control of 
office paper supplies, and the adoption of internal 
practices focused on the responsible use of this 
resource, consolidating an increasingly efficient 
operation with a smaller environmental footprint.
Breakdown of Paper 
Consumption
In 2025, the Bank’s total paper consumption 
amounted to 30,82 tons, with the majority consisting 
of eco-friendly paper, in line with our policy of 
standardizing supplies and reducing environmental 
impact.
The breakdown of consumption by paper type was 
as follows:
Eco-friendly letter-size paper: 27,0 tons 
(88,49% of total consumption).
General eco-friendly paper: 3,51 tons (11,5%
of total consumption).
Eco-friendly legal-size paper: 0,0004 tons 
(0,00131% of total consumption).
Custom white paper: 0,00014 tons (0,00046% 
of total consumption).
This breakdown shows that the use of non￾eco-friendly paper is marginal and meets 
specific needs, while operations rely primarily 
on supplies with a lower environmental impact.
Digitization of statements
This initiative established itself in 2025 as one of 
the main drivers of the Bank’s reduction in paper 
consumption. This progress reflects not only 
more efficient resource management but also an 
improvement in customer experience, by prioritizing 
more agile and sustainable digital channels.
As part of our sustainability strategy, the gradual 
shift of statements to digital formats significantly 
reduced the impacts associated with printing, the 
use of supplies, and distribution logistics. During 
2025, this trend strengthened compared to previous 
years, cementing a structural change in how we 
communicate with our customers.

Paper Management for Recycling
Responsible paper management focuses not only on reducing consumption but also on the proper 
use of the material used. In this regard, we maintain the best practice of delivering the paper 
generated in our operations to an authorized environmental management company, promoting 
its recycling and reintroduction into the production chain.
Although total paper consumption continued to decline in 2025, the amount of paper delivered for 
recycling increased compared to the previous year. This trend is primarily explained by building and 
office design, adaptation, and remodeling projects, which generated higher volumes of paper for 
disposal and reuse, without being associated with regular operational consumption.
The following chart shows the trend in paper sent for recycling in recent years, illustrating the 
management and reuse of this material within a circular economy framework:

Strengthening efforts to reduce the

Exploring new digital communication

Protection of 
biodiversity and 
ecosystems 
foundation for the well-being of present and future 
generations.
Our commitment is grounded in alignment with 
international frameworks and agreements such 
as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity 
Framework, the Paris Agreement, the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs), and the Colombia Carbon 
Neutral Strategy. Through our strategic focus on 
Environmental Stewardship, we integrate climate 
mitigation and adaptation actions, the efficient use 
of natural resources, and a positive relationship with 
the environment, progressively contributing to the 
protection and restoration of ecosystems.
The policy applies to Banco de Occidente, its 
subsidiaries, and its business relationships,
promoting awareness and shared responsibility 
among employees, suppliers, customers, and 
partners regarding sustainability and the protection 
of biodiversity.
Access to and Sharing 
of Benefits
At Banco de Occidente, we understand that 
biodiversity protection goes beyond ecosystem 
conservation and must generate shared benefits 
for the communities and territories where initiatives 
are carried out. Therefore, we have prioritized an 
ecological restoration approach using native 
species, which simultaneously contributes to 
environmental recovery, climate resilience, and the 
strengthening of the social fabric.
As part of this commitment, in 2022 we established a 
strategic partnership with the World Wildlife Fund 
(WWF Colombia), aimed at conserving strategic 
ecosystems within the National System of Protected 
Areas (SINAP). This partnership, which is voluntary 
and goes beyond our legal obligations, was initially 
conceived to last three years and remained active

the vulnerability of ecosystems to climate change

Since the partnership began, we have contributed to the planting of

the creation of local opportunities, and social ownership of the

Identifying Impacts on Biodiversity
At Banco de Occidente, we identify our actual and potential 
impacts on biodiversity by analyzing our strategic partnerships, 
environmental investments, and restoration projects, prioritizing 
territories with high ecological value and relevance for ecosystem 
conservation.
This approach has allowed us to concentrate our efforts in areas 
where our actions generate positive and measurable impacts, 
both in the recovery of degraded ecosystems and in strengthening 
climate resilience and biodiversity conservation. Through our 
partnership with WWF Colombia, we have focused our interventions 
within the SINAP, ensuring that restoration actions are carried out 
in strategic ecosystems and in accordance with technical and 
scientific criteria.
During the third year of this initiative’s implementation, we have 
supported ecological restoration processes in four key regions, 
contributing to ecosystem recovery and the strengthening of local 
communities:

efforts.

environmental impact, strengthening social ownership of the territories 
and our collaborators’ commitment to conservation.
Through this structured intervention, we contribute not only to the 
recovery of natural cover and the protection of ecosystem services—
such as water regulation and carbon sequestration—but also to the 
strengthening of local capacities and the consolidation of participatory 
conservation models in strategic areas of the country.

## Pagina 194

Farallones de Cali 
National Natural Park
The Farallones de Cali National Natural Park is one 
of the country’s largest and most biodiverse protected 
areas and plays a strategic role in providing ecosystem 
services to the Valle del Cauca region. At Banco de 
Occidente, we have prioritized this territory as a key 
intervention area, recognizing its importance for the 
conservation of Andean ecosystems and for climate 
change mitigation and adaptation.
Through our partnership, we have supported ecological 
restoration efforts using native species, focused on 
the recovery of degraded areas and the strengthening 
of ecosystem resilience.
During the partnership period, we carried out exclusively 
technical active restoration processes (excluding 
volunteer efforts), achieving:
7.750 native seedlings planted.
11,79 hectares restored.
Interventions defined in a participatory manner 
with local communities, landowners, and local 
organizations.
Ongoing technical support from Colombia’s National 
Natural Parks.
Sustained maintenance over the three years of the 
project was key to consolidating the plantations, 
increasing their resilience to extreme weather events, 
and ensuring the sustainability of the results, while 
strengthening local capacities for environmental 
management of the territory.
Environmental Volunteering 
and Conservation Education
Complementarily, we developed an environmental 
volunteer program in strategic sectors of the Park, 
such as Peñas Blancas and the Pance River basin, 
areas critical to the water security of more than 2,5 
million people in Valle del Cauca.
Through nine volunteer workdays held over three 
years:
568 volunteers actively participated
1.656 native seedlings were planted
1,2 hectares of Andean forest were restored
The sessions included 
planting activities, 
interpretive hikes, 
kokedama-making, and 
educational workshops, 
promoting knowledge about 
local biodiversity, water 
regulation, and soil stability.

La Playona and Loma La Caleta Integrated 
Management Regional District (Acandí, Chocó)
The La Playona and Loma La Caleta Regional Integrated Management District (DRMI), located 
in the municipality of Acandí (Chocó), is a strategic ecosystem for biodiversity conservation 
and ecological connectivity in the Colombian Caribbean. This area plays a fundamental role in 
protecting biological corridors, regulating ecosystem services, and strengthening the livelihoods 
of local communities.
As part of our partnership, we prioritized this territory for the development of ecological restoration 
processes, with a focus on community participation, the recovery of degraded areas, and the 
generation of social and economic benefits for the local population.
During the three years of intervention, actions in the La Playona and Loma La Caleta DRMI 
focused on active restoration processes, achieving significant results:
8.000 native seedlings planted
8 hectares restored
6 plant species incorporated into the restoration processes
Additional replanting of 150 and 350 seedlings to enhance the survival of the plantings
An 80% survival rate, reflecting the effectiveness of the implemented actions
The community-based approach was a central pillar of the project. Through the implementation 
of restoration activities:
Ten families benefited through employment opportunities and the provision of supplies
11 local jobs were created, boosting the community’s income
One local business or livelihood was established, contributing to the economic sustainability 
of the region

## Pagina 196

High Andean Forest 
– Chingaza National 
Natural Park buffer zone
The buffer zone of Chingaza National Natural 
Park represents a strategic area for ecological 
connectivity in the central part of the country 
and the provision of essential ecosystem services, 
such as water regulation and the conservation of 
Andean–Orinoco biodiversity. This ecosystem, 
located in the eastern Andes mountain range, plays 
a key role in protecting the habitat of emblematic 
species and maintaining biological corridors that 
connect Chingaza National Natural Park with the 
Eastern Hills of Bogotá.
We focused our efforts on Conservation Core 6, 
in the municipalities of La Calera and Choachí, 
prioritizing ecological restoration processes that 
would strengthen the connectivity of the Sumapaz–
Cruz Verde–Eastern Hills–Chingaza corridor 
and contribute to the recovery of degraded natural 
vegetation.
Ecological Restoration and 
Territorial Coordination
During 2024 and 2025, we carried out active 
restoration efforts with a comprehensive approach, 
combining environmental, social, and educational 
actions:
5.000 native seedlings planted, representing 9 
plant species of the high Andean forest.
5 hectares restored, contributing to the recovery 
of natural vegetation key to biodiversity and water 
recharge.
A survival rate of 92%, reflecting proper technical 
management and maintenance efforts.
Targeted replanting (250 seedlings) to reinforce 
the consolidation of the restored areas.
2 maintenance activities aimed at ensuring the 
stability and resilience of the plantations.
These actions were complemented by preventive 
measures to mitigate risks associated with forest 
fires and invasive livestock, such as the installation 
of perimeter fences, protecting the seedlings and 
ensuring the continuity of the restoration process.
The project actively engaged local communities and 
key stakeholders in the region, generating positive 
social impacts:
20 beneficiary families involved in project 
activities.
10 temporary jobs created during planting 
activities, using local labor.
8 agreements strengthened for the conservation 
and sustainable management of the territory.
3 strengthened enterprises or livelihoods, 
associated with environmental education, nursery 
operations, and home gardens.

## Pagina 197

PNN Via Parque Isla 
de Salamanca (VIPIS)
At Banco de Occidente, we contribute to 
the protection and restoration of strategic 
ecosystems in the Colombian Caribbean, such 
as the Isla de Salamanca Park Corridor (VIPIS),
a protected area of national and international 
significance due to its biodiversity and its key 
role in climate regulation, coastal protection, 
and the provision of ecosystem services.
VIPIS covers nearly 56.200 hectares, of which 
approximately 21% consists of mangrove 
ecosystems—essential habitats for migratory 
birds, fish, crustaceans, and reptiles. However, 
these ecosystems have faced historical 
pressures such as forest fires, prolonged 
droughts, channel blockages, increased salinity, 
and the loss of more than 56% of the original 
mangrove cover, making active and sustained 
intervention essential.
During the third year of the project, we made 
progress on an ecological restoration process 
focused on priority areas in Clarín Viejo, 
Clarín Nuevo, and the Kilometer 36 sector, 
with interventions covering approximately 3,5 
hectares, prioritizing areas with water deficits 
and high salinity.
The most significant actions included:
Planting of 2.500 mangrove seedlings, 
distributed as follows:
Rhizophora mangle (red mangrove): 1.350 
seedlings.
Laguncularia racemosa (yellow mangrove): 
1.150 seedlings.
Construction of ecological mounds:
500 mounds made from sediment and local 
organic material.
Designed to improve soil conditions, flood 
management, and seedling survival.
Community work and shared governance:
Partnership with the Clarín Canal Users 
Association.
Participation of community organizations, 
with an emphasis on women’s leadership.
Strengthening of the mangrove ecosystem, 
promoting the recovery of key habitats for fish, 
birds, crustaceans, and reptiles.
Positive social impact through the creation of 
local jobs, the strengthening of community ties, 
and the promotion of sustainable economic 
activities such as ecotourism.

## Pagina 198

Volunteering at Arví Park – Nare River 
Protected Forest Reserve
As part of our environmental volunteering strategy, we organize 
volunteer days at Arví Park, located in the Nare River Protected 
Forest Reserve, a key rainforest ecosystem for climate regulation, 
water supply, and ecological connectivity in the Aburrá Valley.
Although these activities are not part of the priority restoration 
areas of our partnership with WWF Colombia, they represent 
a complementary experience of high environmental, social, 
and educational value, strengthening the bond between our 
employees and the conservation of the country’s strategic 
ecosystems.
Over the three years of the program’s implementation, we 
achieved the following impacts:
223 employees participated in five volunteer days.
282 native seedlings planted during the first two years.
Adaptive replanting carried out in the third year, in accordance 
with site conditions and ecosystem needs.
Complementary conservation activities, which included:
Trail maintenance.
Wildlife monitoring.
Environmental education workshops with youth and visitors.
These actions were carried out in coordination with the Arví Park 
Corporation, promoting participatory restoration, responsible 
tourism, and social ownership of the territory.
Volunteering in Bogotá’s 
Eastern Forest – Las Moyas 
Trail
As part of our environmental volunteer initiatives, 
we organized workshops in the Bosque Oriental 
de Bogotá Protected Forest Reserve, specifically 
on the Las Moyas Trail, a strategic ecosystem for 
climate regulation, ecological connectivity, and the 
city’s air quality.
Although these events are not part of the priority 
restoration areas identified by the partnership with 
WWF Colombia, they represent a complementary 
initiative aimed at raising awareness and promoting 
environmental action, with a focus on employee 
participation and fostering a sense of ownership 
of the local area.
Volunteer Results
560 native seedlings planted.
1 hectare restored.
Activities carried out exclusively through volunteer 
events.
Focus on participatory restoration and 
environmental education. 
Implementation of the Environmental Education 
Program for employees, focused on best practices 
for saving and efficiently using natural resources.
Development of the “Together It’s Possible – 
WWF” course, aimed at biodiversity conservation 
and the adoption of responsible actions by all 
employees.

## Pagina 199

Planeta Azul National 
Ecology Award
SDG 6.3; 17.5; 13.2
The Planeta Azul National Ecology Award is 
one of our flagship initiatives to recognize, 
highlight, and strengthen projects that 
contribute to water conservation, biodiversity, 
and sustainable development in Colombia.
This award, held every two years, has 
established itself as a platform for bringing 
together companies, startups, social 
organizations, and academia, promoting 
innovative and replicable solutions to the 
country’s environmental challenges.
Beyond the award itself, the Planeta Azul 
Award seeks to:
Promote initiatives that generate a positive 
impact on water resource management and 
ecosystem conservation.
Foster environmental innovation and the 
adoption of sustainable technologies.
Promote education and social ownership 
of knowledge regarding environmental 
stewardship.
Bring together public, private, and community 
actors around a common sustainability 
agenda.
In 2025, we will continue to strengthen 
this platform as a space for inspiration 
and connection, consolidating the 
Planeta Azul Community as a 
network for exchange and learning 
among winners and applicants from 
previous editions. In this way, the Award 
transcends one-time recognition and 
becomes a mechanism for collective 
mobilization toward the protection of 
water and biodiversity.

## Pagina 201

Human capital 
and talent 
management
in the areas of human capital, well-being and 
motivation, talent development and performance, 
diversity, equity, and inclusion, labor relations, 
occupational health and safety, as well as our 
commitment to communities and customers. Together, 
these elements reflect a coherent and coordinated 
management approach, aligned with our vision of 
responsible growth, innovation, and sustainability.
At Banco de Occidente, the development of people, 
their families, and communities is the central pillar 
of our sustainability strategy and long-term value 
creation. We believe that the development of human 
talent, the holistic well-being of our employees, 
and responsible engagement with the communities 
where we operate, including our commitment to 
social and financial inclusion, in are fundamental to 
building trust, enhancing productivity, and delivering 
a personalized, high-quality service experience to 
our customers.
Throughout 2025, we continued to strengthen 
a comprehensive human capital management 
approach, aimed at creating inclusive, safe and 
motivating work environments where every employee 
can develop their potential and contribute their 
experience to achieving the Bank’s objectives. This 
approach is based on principles of equity, respect, 
non-discrimination and inclusion, and recognizes 
that people’s well-being and development are key 
to business sustainability.
This chapter presents the main advances and results 
From an age perspective, the workforce in 2025 is characterized by a significant 
presence of people under 30, who account for 30% of the total. This composition 
reflects a young and dynamic workforce that coexists with other life stages 
and career paths, fostering the exchange of experiences and the long-term 
development of talent.
National and 
International Presence
GRI 2-1; 2-7; 2-8; 2-9; 2-23; GRI 2-30
The information for 2025 shows a solid national and 
international presence, supported by a workforce of 
7.054 employees in our own operations who enable 
the Bank’s operations in the various regions where it 
operates. Bogotá, Cali, Medellín, and Barranquilla 
account for the majority of our workforce, reflecting 
a distribution aligned with the Bank’s operational 
structure. Overall, 38% of employees are covered 
by collective bargaining agreements, in line with 
the right to collective bargaining and freedom of 
association, demonstrating structured labor relations 
based on social dialogue and trust.
The workforce composition reflects a majority of 
women, who account for 59% of all employees (4.180 
women). This trend is consistent across all regions 
and is particularly pronounced in cities such as 
Barranquilla (69%) and Medellín (62%), reaffirming 
the Bank’s commitment to gender equality and equal 
opportunity, and the creation of diverse and inclusive 
work environments.

## Pagina 203

Employee 
Well-being
Well-being and Motivation: Caring for Our People
BdO 13
At Banco de Occidente, we view well-being as an essential component of the employee experience and a 
key factor in engagement and performance. Therefore, we manage well-being from a holistic perspective 
that integrates the work environment, work-life balance, benefits, initiatives related to workplace stress 
management, flexible working arrangements, and organizational culture, with the goal of creating work 
environments where people feel valued, heard, and supported.
This approach is grounded in principles of equity, respect, and care, and recognizes that each employee 
contributes based on their own experience and unique circumstances. Through practices focused on physical, 
mental, and social well-being, we seek to strengthen a sense of belonging, foster work relationships based 
on trust, and promote a positive and collaborative work environment.
At Banco de Occidente, talent management is a 
fundamental pillar for business sustainability and the 
strengthening of organizational culture. We recognize 
that the commitment, well-being, and development 
of our employees are critical to achieving strategic 
objectives and delivering a consistent, high-quality 
service experience to our customers.
Throughout 2025, we continued to consolidate an 
integrated approach to talent management, which 
combines holistic well-being, skills development, 
performance evaluation, equity, and inclusion as 
complementary components of the employee 
experience. This approach allows us to support 
individuals throughout their career lifecycle and 
strengthen the alignment between individual goals 
and the Bank’s strategic priorities.
Talent management is supported by structured 
processes for structured employee development 
programs, performance management and appraisal 
systems –including management by objectives 
frameworks and ongoing performance evaluations-, 
compensation schemes, and social dialogue 
mechanisms, aimed at promoting labor relations 
based on respect, transparency, non-discrimination, 
and continuous improvement. Through these 
practices, we seek to create work environments 
that foster professional growth, commitment, and 
our employees’ contribution to the Bank’s results.
In 2025, Banco de Occidente was recognized for the third consecutive year 
by Great Place to Work as the best place to work in Colombia, reflecting an 
organizational culture based on trust, respect, and equity. 99% of employees 
report being treated fairly, regardless of their gender, age, race, or sexual 
orientation, which reinforces corporate values and a sense of belonging.

As a result of the measures implemented, workplace 
environment metrics showed a positive and 
sustained quantitative improvement throughout 
2025. The engagement, satisfaction, and well-being 
index reached 95, exceeding the goal set for the 
year, while participation in the survey remained 
at high levels (93,00%). These results demonstrate 
a culture of employee feedback and continuous 
improvement, as well as the impact of initiatives 
aimed at strengthening the well-being and experience 
of our employees.
Well-being is also strengthened through a 
comprehensive range of benefits, including flexible 
working arrangements and well-being initiatives, 
activities, and opportunities for integration, aimed at 
promoting work-life balance. The high participation 
and satisfaction levels recorded in well-being 
initiatives, supported by measurable engagement 
indicators, along with the introduction of new 
flexibilities, reflect the ownership of these actions 
and their contribution to strengthening camaraderie 
and motivation among employees.
Overall, the management of well-being and motivation 
in 2025 helped consolidate an organizational 
culture based on trust, respect, and recognition, 
strengthening the commitment of our talent and 
positioning the Bank as a leading employer in terms 
of employee experience and workplace practices.
Our workforce is characterized by significant 
generational diversity, bringing together different

our daily work by integrating multiple perspectives, 
styles, and experiences, and allows us to build 
environments where, regardless of age or tenure, all 
employees enjoy equitable conditions, development 
opportunities, and an inclusive work experience.
Employee and Skills 
Development Programs
SDG 4.3; 10; GRI 404-2;404-3
At Banco de Occidente, employee development is 
a key pillar for talent development and business 
sustainability. Through the corporate university “La 
U,” the Bank manages and systematically tracks 
training hours in a structured manner, consolidating 
a learning and development offering aligned with 
strategic priorities and the needs of the environment.
In 2025, training indicators showed a positive trend 
with consistent quantitative improvement compared 
to 2024. Total training hours increased by nearly 
16%, while the average number of training hours per 
employee rose by a similar proportion, reflecting 
greater learning intensity and increased adoption 
of learning and development programs as part of 
the employee experience. This growth was driven, 
among other factors, by the introduction of the Blue 
Hour, an institutional initiative designed to promote 
continuous learning during the workday.
The Blue Hour, an institutional learning initiative, made 
it possible to expand access to learning content 
and development opportunities, facilitate employee 
participation, and reinforce the learning culture, 
complementing the offerings managed through “La 
U.” Its implementation directly contributed to an 
increase in training hours and the strengthening of 
employee capabilities and skills at various levels of 
the organization.
This growth was accompanied by an increase of 
nearly 5% in investment allocated to training, which 
demonstrates an efficient allocation of resources and 
a focus on high-impact programs. The increase in 
classroom hours is largely explained by the expanded 
coverage of training programs, the strengthening of 
virtual offerings, the incorporation of Hora Azul, and 
greater participation by employees in administrative, 
operational, and commercial roles.
Taken together, the results confirm the role of La U 
and the Blue Hour as key enablers of organizational 
learning and reflect the Bank’s commitment to the 
continuous development of talent as the foundation 
for performance, innovation, and long-term 
sustainability.

The trend in average training hours per employee 
confirms the consolidation of training as a strategic 
lever for the Bank’s capacity development and 
sustainability. Following a gradual decline between 
2022 and 2024, associated with prioritization 
processes, operational adjustments, and changes 
in the workforce composition, a significant recovery 
in training intensity is observed in 2025.
Taken together, these results confirm a positive 
evolution of the training model, which is shifting 
from a coverage-focused approach to one of 
greater depth and impact, aligned with leadership 
development, employability, and preparing talent to 
respond to the Bank’s strategic challenges.
Performance Evaluation
The performance evaluation process we manage at 
Banco de Occidente is based on management by 
objectives, which allows us to assess individual and 
organizational performance in a structured manner, 
in alignment with the Bank’s strategic goals. This 
process is carried out using the Success Factors 
module, a tool we make available to our employees 
to facilitate objective, clear, and efficient evaluations.
During 2024 and 2025, the management of the 
performance evaluation process was structured 
around key milestones, integrating pedagogical, 
technological, and analytical strategies that 
strengthened its adoption and quality. During the 
planning phase and initial meeting, we promoted 
the clear definition of functional objectives, ensuring 
their alignment with corporate goals. This rollout was 
supported by internal communication campaigns, 
open orientation sessions, digital guides, and live 
sessions designed to support employees at every 
stage of the process.
Complementarily, support was reinforced for 
employees who joined outside the established 
deadlines through personalized sessions and digital 
materials that facilitated their effective integration 
into the process. Additionally, a structured incident 
management system was established, enabling 
timely case handling and the generation of relevant 
analytical information for decision-making.
During the closing phase of the process, training 
sessions were held for leaders and teams, focusing 
on objective evaluation, effective feedback, reducing 
bias and promoting fair and objective performance 
assessments. These actions were complemented by 
the strengthening of soft skills such as communication, 
leadership, teamwork, and adaptability—essential 
for performance management consistent with the 
organizational culture.
In 2025, the Bank consolidated the implementation of 
the Mi Desarrollo 360 platform, which is a 360 degree 
performance appraisal system, available in the BdeO 
Development Universe, as an evolution of the pilot 
conducted in 2024. This tool was created with the 
purpose of strengthening talent development and 
organizational culture by enabling a multidimensional 
evaluation that integrates self-assessment, leader 
assessment, peer assessment, and, where applicable, 
employee assessment. Through this comprehensive 
view of performance and organizational behaviors, 
the Bank seeks to promote constructive feedback, 
identify development opportunities, and guide actions 
that strengthen leadership, collaborative work, and 
alignment with the Bank’s values and strategy.
The platform incorporates advanced reporting 
features, individual access to downloadable reports, 
and automatic consolidation of results, enhancing 
traceability, data quality, and the user experience. 
This evolution represents a significant advancement 
in performance management by facilitating more 
agile, transparent processes focused on continuous 
learning.
Overall, the performance evaluation 
and career development process 
reflects Banco de Occidente’s 
commitment to talent management 
based on management by 
objectives, ongoing feedback, and 
multidimensional performance 
appraisal, contributing to 
the strengthening of a high￾performance culture and the 
organization’s sustainability.

At Banco de Occidente, these extra-legal benefits 
complement statutory social protection mechanisms 
and reflect a long-term vision focused on supporting 
employee well-being and social protection, 
strengthening talent retention, and supporting 
employees through the various stages of their working 
lives.
The design and administration of these benefits 
are based on equity, regulatory compliance, and 
financial sustainability criteria, prioritizing initiatives 
that generate a positive impact on the economic, 
personal, and family well-being of employees in 
our own operations with permanent contracts and 
that contribute to building a relationship of trust and 
long-term commitment.
Together, these benefits help strengthen employees’ 
financial and personal well-being, providing 
greater liquidity throughout the year, savings 
opportunities, better expense planning, and access 
to social protection mechanisms beyond statutory 
requirements. In 2025, benefits management was 
consolidated through efficient administration, 
continuous portfolio adjustments, and communication 
and support initiatives, which ensured their proper 
implementation and understanding by employees.
This comprehensive approach reinforces commitment, 
satisfaction, and retention of talent, and helps foster 
a balanced, supportive work environment aligned 
with Banco de Occidente’s sustainability strategy.
With the aim of enhancing the well-being and quality 
of life of our employees and their families, Banco 
de Occidente offers a benefits portfolio designed 
to support personal and family development. These 
initiatives contribute to building a work environment 
that promotes work-life balance and enriches the 
employee experience within the Bank.
Within this framework, we promote practices that 
prioritize holistic well-being through benefits such 
as flexible work arrangements that include flexible 
working hours, remote work options, and part-time 
work arrangements. These alternatives allow us to 
adapt to employees’ diverse needs and support them 
throughout the different stages of their professional 
life cycle.
We also promote physical and mental health through 
initiatives such as sports activities, wellness programs, 
and events that encourage healthy lifestyle habits, 
including nature walks, marathons, and sports 
tournaments. In compliance with maternity and 
paternity leave regulations, we have paid parental 
leave policies that include 18 weeks for the primary 
caregiver and 2 weeks for the secondary caregiver, as 
well as adequate spaces for breastfeeding/lactation 
facilities, which facilitate a balance between family 
responsibilities and professional development.
Together, these benefits reflect our commitment to creating a flexible, 
inclusive, and healthy work environment where people can fully develop 
and contribute to the Bank’s goals through their well-being.

Employee Well-being and Quality of Life Benefits
The information presented demonstrates the 
positive impact of benefits and financial support on 
strengthening employees’ overall well-being. During 
2025, increases were recorded in both coverage and 
investment allocated to benefits related to education, 
housing, and support during key moments in the 
personal and family life cycle. These advances reflect 
a management approach aimed at providing greater 
stability, encouraging retention, and improving the 
quality of life for our talent.
In this context, benefits are established as a key 
tool to support employees at different stages of 
their lives and contribute to fostering a balanced, 
inclusive work environment aligned with the Bank’s 
sustainability strategy. To encourage participation 
in these benefits and continue strengthening the 
work environment within teams, Banco de Occidente 
implemented several key strategies:
Benefit awareness and accessibility programs:
Internal campaigns were developed targeting 
different work teams and institutional onboarding 
sessions, with the aim of raising awareness of the 
benefits portfolio and access mechanisms. These 
actions included internal communications and 
group socialization meetings.
Monitoring and support for leaders:
Training sessions were held with leaders and 
managers, aimed at strengthening their role in 
promoting, guiding, and supporting the proper 
use of benefits within their teams.
Employee feedback mechanisms:
Satisfaction surveys were conducted during various 
activities to gather feedback and suggestions 
from employees. This information was used as a 
key input to refine initiatives and respond more 
effectively to the needs of our workforce.
Continuous optimization of the benefits portfolio:
Based on the feedback received and trends 
in workplace well-being, adjustments and 
improvements were made to the benefits portfolio, 
including the addition of new activities and the 
expansion of those that were most popular.

Variable Compensation
Our Variable Compensation Model is designed to 
recognize and reward high performance in commercial 
areas, strengthening a performance-driven culture 
aligned with the Bank’s strategy. Through this scheme, 
we seek to incentivize the achievement of commercial 
objectives, while reinforcing measurement discipline 
and teams’ commitment to achieving clear, shared 
goals.
Variable compensation is conceived as a recognition 
tool that directly links individual and collective 
effort to the results achieved. Its design allows us 
to support commercial management, motivate 
consistent performance, and recognize employees’ 
contributions to business growth, while maintaining 
criteria of equity, transparency, and sustainability.
This model applies to sales teams and other strategic 
roles linked to value creation, and is managed 
according to the operational cycles of each function; 
additionally, it includes variable compensation 
components linked to short and long term performance 
outcomes. In this way, variable compensation not 
only contributes to the achievement of business 
objectives but also strengthens motivation, a sense 
of accomplishment, and employees’ alignment with 
the Bank’s strategic priorities.

employees and staff turnover are fundamental 
components for maintaining a healthy, productive 
work environment aligned with business objectives. 
Through structured and efficient selection processes, 
we seek to attract and integrate talent with the 
necessary skills to effectively contribute to the 
fulfillment of the Bank’s strategy. Complementarily, 
we proactively manage turnover with the aim of 
preserving organizational knowledge, promoting 
stability, and strengthening long-term commitment.
This approach is not only focused on attracting talent 
but also on building an environment where employees 
feel valued, supported, and have real opportunities 
for development. In this way, we strengthen a solid

## Pagina 219

Collective 
Bargaining
At Banco de Occidente, collective bargaining is 
a fundamental pillar of labor relations and a key 
mechanism for promoting fair, stable, and equitable 
working conditions. Through formal social dialogue 
processes, the Bank seeks to build agreements that 
recognize employees’ interests, strengthen trust, and 
contribute to a work environment based on respect 
and shared responsibility.
Collective bargaining is conducted within a 
framework of regulatory compliance, transparency, 
and good faith, guaranteeing the exercise of the right 
to association and freedom of association. Current 
collective agreements cover a representative portion 
of the workforce and establish conditions related 
to compensation, benefits, well-being, job stability, 
and other relevant aspects of the employment 
relationship, contributing to employee retention and 
satisfaction.
During the reporting period, the Bank maintained the 
applicable collective agreements and labor pacts 
in force, ensuring their proper implementation and 
compliance with the commitments made.

In addition, the Bank promotes ongoing communication channels with labor unions and employee representatives, 
which allows us to anticipate situations, resolve concerns in a timely manner, and foster a work environment 
based on dialogue and cooperation. This preventive approach contributes to stable labor relations and the 
operational continuity of the business.
Overall, the Bank de Occidente’s approach to collective bargaining reinforces a model of mature and 
constructive labor relations, aligned with business sustainability, respect for labor rights, and the comprehensive 
well-being of employees. These processes enable the establishment of balanced agreements, strengthen 
trust between the parties, and support talent development in a stable and predictable work environment.
