## Pagina 220

Diversity, 
Equity, and 
Inclusion
Throughout 2025, we continued to strengthen DEI as a 
structural component of our culture, fostering diverse 
work environments free from discrimination, violence, or 
harassment. Under a managed meritocracy approach, we 
promoted selection, evaluation, and promotion processes 
centered on skills and performance, actively reducing the 
risks associated with conscious or unconscious biases.
As part of this process, we continue to promote initiatives 
that reinforce respect for individuality and inclusion 
in the Bank’s day-to-day operations. Notable among 
these are the “Mi Estilo BdeO” dress code, which 
eliminates gender-based guidelines and promotes the 
free expression of identity, as well as the adaptation of 
employee benefits to recognize diverse family structures 
in an inclusive manner, including the extension of marriage 
leave to unmarried couples.
At Banco de Occidente and our subsidiaries, we focus 
on talent rather than labels, in line with the principles 
established in our People’s Manifesto, designed as part 
of the action plans derived from our Human Rights Due 
Diligence exercise and launched in 2025. Guided by 
this conviction, we promote selection and development 
processes based on a managed meritocracy, in which 
hiring and professional growth are based exclusively on 
competencies and skills, ensuring that gender, sexual 
orientation, or other personal characteristics do not 
represent barriers to accessing job opportunities. These 
actions help close the inclusion cycle, reinforcing a 
clear message: at the Bank, merit is the primary driver 
of professional development and growth.
In 2025, the launch of the People’s Manifesto established itself as a significant 
milestone in the management of diversity, equity, and inclusion, translating 
human rights commitments into a living cultural guide that shapes our decisions, 
behaviors, and relationships, both within the organization and in our interactions 
with our clients and other stakeholders.
SDG 8.5; 10.2
At Banco de Occidente, we view diversity, equity, 
and inclusion (DEI) as an essential part of how we do 
business and interact, both within the organization 
and with our customers. Throughout 2025, this 
approach went beyond mere principles, translating 
into concrete actions aimed at strengthening our 
organizational culture, preventing any form of 
discrimination, harassment and unequal treatment, 
and promoting work and service environments that 
are safe, equitable, and accessible to everyone.
This path is grounded in a clear and coherent 
framework that integrates our Human Rights Policy 
and Human Rights Due Diligence framework, Code 
of Ethics and Conduct, Internal Work Regulations, 
and the People’s Manifesto. These guidelines 
reflect a shared conviction: respect for human 
rights and human dignity and the valuing of merit 
and competencies as the foundation for hiring, 
development, and professional growth, ensuring 
equal opportunities at every stage of the employment 
cycle.

## Pagina 221

In this context, we continue to actively participate in Asobancaria’s Social Protocol, a sector-wide initiative 
that promotes best practices in equity, diversity, and inclusion within the Colombian financial system. 
Through this initiative, we strengthen our work on four key fronts: internal culture, financial education 
and inclusion, the development of a more inclusive value proposition, and the responsible management 
of financial risks.
Complementarily, during 2025 we took a step forward in training, evolving from general awareness-raising 
processes toward more specialized and technical training programs. This progress has allowed us to 
put the principles of diversity and inclusion into daily practice, strengthening our teams’ capabilities to 
provide attentive, respectful service that meets our clients’ needs.
Key initiatives include:
Specialized training for strategic 
areas, such as the Processes and 
Projects team (40 employees), 
addressing the identification of 
unconscious biases, the adoption 
of the People’s Manifesto, and the 
integration of DEI criteria into the 
design of processes and products.
These actions help strengthen the Bank’s capacity 
to prevent discriminatory practices and promote 
equitable and respectful treatment in all our 
spaces, both within the organization and in our 
relationships with our customers.
In this same vein, gender equity remains a priority 
focus of our management, approached from 
a comprehensive perspective that combines 
strengthening organizational culture with creating 
economic opportunities, recognizing that both 
aspects are key to advancing toward fairer and 
more inclusive environments.
Internally, we launched the #MujeresQueInspiran 
campaign, accompanied by forums for dialogue and 
reflection on women’s leadership, monitoring and 
adressing the gender pay gap, and participation in 
decision-making spaces. In 2025, women accounted 
for 59,22% of the total workforce, 42,64% of 
management positions, and 25,92% of senior 
leadership roles, demonstrating sustained progress 
in women’s participation in leadership roles.
Externally, we strengthened our value proposition 
for women-led companies, highlighting:
A working capital line for Women-Owned SMEs, 
with special terms to foster their growth.
Access to the Banco de Occidente Business 
Community, along with business intelligence tools 
such as the Business Environment Report and 
sector reports.
Training and support initiatives, such as the 
“Lecciones Pyme” podcast, focused on women’s 
leadership, digital transformation, and business 
competitiveness.
Complementarily, we participate in high-impact 
initiatives such as Women Working for the World and 
Women in Connection, platforms that allow us to 
strengthen women’s leadership networks, exchange 
insights, and adopt best practices to continue 
promoting equity at the senior management level.
In line with the principles of the People’s Manifesto, 
we do not use diversity hiring quotas. However, we 
promote proactive measures aimed at expanding 
access to job opportunities and reducing structural 
barriers, convinced that inclusion is built by creating 
real conditions for talent to develop on an equal 
footing.
“Diverse and Inclusive Service – 
Friendly Biz” course, in which 2.286 
employees were trained, strengthening 
their skills in engaging with diverse 
populations, including older adults, 
people with disabilities, the LGBTIQ+ 
community, and ethnic groups.
Technical course on Service for 
People with Disabilities, in which 6.016 
employees participated, focused on 
recognizing different types of disabilities 
and implementing reasonable 
accommodations for dignified and 
accessible service.

In 2025, indicators show that Banco de Occidente 
maintains a solid and stable female workforce, with 
women accounting for 59% of the total workforce. 
The presence of women at various management 
levels remains consistent, reflecting a sustained 
base of female leadership and responsible talent 
management.
Women’s representation in management positions 
remained around 42% throughout 2025, reflecting 
stability at leadership levels and the continuity of a 
solid base of female talent in the succession pipeline. 
This trend demonstrates that, while progress in 
representation requires time and consistency, the 
Bank has succeeded in maintaining a significant 
presence of women in decision-making roles.
At the senior management level, female representation 
stood at 25% in 2025. The period was marked by 
significant qualitative advances in leadership,
such as the appointment of the first woman to 
the Bank’s Executive Committee, Ángela Maria 
Ceballos, as well as the appointment of Juana 
Beltrán Echeverri as Head of the Legal Division. 
These milestones reflect a significant step toward 
opening strategic spaces for women in leadership 
and reinforce the Bank’s commitment to increasingly 
diverse and inclusive decision-making, beyond the 
annual evolution of the indicators.
Positive progress stands out in revenue-generating 
functions and STEM roles, where female participation 
continues to strengthen compared to previous years, 
demonstrating concrete efforts to reduce gaps in 
strategic business areas. At the senior management 
levels, although challenges remain in accelerating 
parity, structural progress continues, laying the 
groundwork for further advancement.
Overall, the results confirm that 
the Bank is making gradual and 
consistent progress in managing 
gender diversity, prioritizing the 
sustainability of these advances 
and the creation of increasingly 
equitable and inclusive work 
environments, in line with its human 
rights approach.
Looking ahead to the coming years, we identify as 
challenges the deepening of external partnerships 
that promote workplace inclusion and the 
strengthening of metrics that allow us to measure, 
in a more comprehensive manner, the impact of 
DEI actions in the medium and long term. At the 
same time, we recognize significant opportunities 
in the progressive incorporation of diversity and 
inclusion criteria into the design of products, services, 
and channels, with the aim of continuing to build a 
banking experience that is increasingly accessible, 
equitable, and people-centered.

## Pagina 224

Human rights
SDG 5.5 | 8.5 | 10.2 | 16
At Banco de Occidente, human rights management made significant progress in 2025 
regarding its Human Rights Due Diligence approach: we shifted from an approach 
focused primarily on commitment and compliance to a more structured model of 
management, prevention, mitigation, addressing human rights impacts and continuous 
improvement, integrated across our own operations, subsidiaries, processes and 
business relationships, progressively including suppliers and partners. This progress 
stems from the strengthening of our social governance and the consolidation of 
human rights due diligence as a strategic tool to anticipate risks, manage impacts, 
and promote responsible and sustainable relationships throughout our value chain.
In 2025, the Bank reaffirmed and deepened its commitment to respecting and 
promoting human rights, backed by a current Human Rights Policy approved 
by the Board of Di rectors and applicable to all our operations, subsidiaries, and 
business relationships. In line with this, this commitment translated into greater 
integration into the Bank’s day-to-day operations, strengthening the incorporation 
of a human rights approach into key instruments such as the Code of Ethics and 
Conduct, the Internal Work Regulations, and decision-making forums related to 
sustainability and risk management.
Our management remains aligned with widely recognized international standards, 
such as the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the 
ILO Core Conventions, the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, and 
the Sustainable Development Goals, as well as with applicable national regulations 
in the jurisdictions where we operate.
Human Rights 
Due Diligence
In 2025, the Bank established a structured 
and ongoing Human Rights Due Diligence 
process, which allowed us to move from a 
more general identification of risks to a more 
systematic and evidence-based management 
approach. This process covers 100% of our 
operations and progressively incorporates 
suppliers, contractors, partners, clients, and 
new business relationships. Due diligence is 
carried out through the following stages:
Analysis of the regulatory, sectoral, and 
institutional context.
Proactive identification of risks and impacts 
through internal consultations, analysis of 
external information, and benchmarking 
exercises.
Assessment and prioritization of risks, 
consider ing their severity, probability, and 
the Bank’s level of involvement.
Definition and implementation of action 
plans aimed at preventing, mitigating, and 
remedying impacts.
Monitoring and periodic updating of the risk 
mapping and the measures adopted.
Current Human Rights Policy

Identification of 
Potentially Vulnerable 
or At-Risk Groups and 
Impact Assessment
The due diligence exercise allowed us to deepen 
our understanding of the main actual and potential 
human rights risks, both in our direct operations and 
throughout the value chain.
Among the prioritized issues are:
Decent working conditions, occupational health 
and safety.
Prevention of workplace and sexual harassment.
Diversity, equity, inclusion, and non-discrimination.
Freedom of association and collective bargaining.
Protection of personal data and privacy.
Access to clear information and financial services 
under fair conditions.
Potential social impacts associated with funded 
projects.
Labor practices of suppliers and partners.
The stakeholders prioritized in this analysis include our 
employees, supplier employees, individual customers, 
and local communities, considering their level of 
exposure, vulnerability, and the potential severity of 
impacts.
The Bank maintains a zero￾tolerance policy toward any form 
of human rights violation, including 
discrimination, harassment, 
forced and child labor. In line 
with this commitment, we work to 
prevent, identify, and mitigate
risks associated with human 
trafficking, forced labor, and 
child labor, both in our operations 
and in our supply chain, guided 
by international standards such 
as the United Nations Guiding 
Principles on Business and Human 
Rights, the OECD Guidelines for 
Multinational Enterprises, and the 
ILO Core Conventions.
As a result of this process, traceability of identified risks and consistency between 
findings, implemented actions, and monitoring mechanisms were strengthened 
during the period.

## Pagina 226

Mitigation and Remediation 
Measures
In 2025, the Bank strengthened its framework of 
preventive, mitigation, and remediation measures in 
human rights, with the aim of ensuring comprehensive 
coverage across the entire operation. Among the 
main actions implemented are:
Updating and strengthening internal policies 
related to workplace and sexual harassment, work￾life balance, and ethical conduct.
Ongoing training programs for employees and 
leaders on human rights, diversity, equity, and 
inclusion, freedom of association, and personal 
data protection.
Operation of specialized committees, such as 
the Workplace Relations Committee and the 
Sustainability Committee, which support monitoring 
and decision-making on these issues.
Integration of human rights criteria into key 
processes, including supplier management, 
environmental and social risk assessment (SARAS), 
and due diligence for clients and funded projects.
Reporting and Complaint 
Mechanisms
In 2025, we took a significant step toward strengthening 
our response and redressing mechanisms by explicitly 
incorporating a human rights approach into the Ethics 
Hotline. This advancement allowed us to improve 
the classification, traceability, and monitoring of 
reports related to potential human rights violations, 
complementing other existing mechanisms such 
as the Workplace Relations Committee, Human 
Resources channels, and the workplace environment 
suggestion box.
Compliance with our human rights standards is 
monitored through an integrated approach that 
combines the monitoring of action plans, the 
functioning of internal committees, the analysis of 
reporting channels, and the verification of compliance 
with applicable policies and procedures, ensuring 
confidentiality and non-retaliation.
Progress, Challenges, and 
Opportunities
In 2025, significant progress was made in 
institutionalizing the human rights approach, 
particularly in consolidating the due diligence system 
and integrating the issue into corporate governance 
processes.
At the same time, we identified challenges related to deepening management 
throughout the value chain and strengthening impact measurement. These 
opportunities will guide our next steps as we continue to move toward management 
that is increasingly preventive, traceable, and aligned with international best 
practices.

## Pagina 227

Occupational 
Safety and 
Health
We have protocols for emergency prevention 
and response, as well as periodic internal 
inspections and audit processes—both internal 
and external—conducted in accordance with 
national and international standards and regulations. 
These audits allow us to verify compliance with the 
requirements of the Occupational Health and Safety 
Management System (SG-SST), identify opportunities 
for improvement, and continuously strengthen our 
practices. Based on the monitoring of key indicators 
and the results of these evaluation exercises, we guide 
the implementation of corrective and improvement 
actions, ensuring OSH management that is consistent 
with our sustainability strategy and with the well￾being of the people and communities with whom 
we interact. 
Our Occupational Health 
and Safety OHS 
programs
The Occupational Health and Safety department 
is responsible for developing, managing, and 
strengthening the Occupational Health and Safety 
Management System (SG-SST) through planning, 
implementation, monitoring, and continuous 
improvement, in compliance with Law 1562 of 2012, 
the Single Regulatory Decree for the Labor Sector 
1072 of 2015, and Resolution 0312 of 2019. This system 
guides our decisions and practices to protect the 
health, safety and well-being of our employees, 
contractors, and other stakeholders involved in our 
operations. 
At Banco de Occidente, we understand that 
protecting employee health, safety and well-being 
is a fundamental pillar of business sustainability.
Therefore, we promote safe, healthy, and supportive 
work environments that foster the physical, mental, 
and social well-being of our employees, as well as 
the continuity of our operations and the fulfillment 
of our responsibilities as an employer. 
Based on this vision, we comprehensively manage 
Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) through a 
preventive, risk-based and continuous improvement 
approach, which allows us to anticipate risks, 
strengthen a culture of prevention and risk 
awareness, and respond in a timely manner to 
challenges related to the health, safety, and mobility 
of the people who are part of our organization. This 
approach is supported by the systematic monitoring 
of performance indicators that, in addition to guiding 
internal decision-making, underpin the reporting 
of our progress in international benchmarks such 
as the Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI), 
contributing to management that is increasingly 
robust, transparent, and aligned with industry best 
practices. 
Our OSH management is structured around 
different lines of action aimed at preventing 
accident s, promoting health, and 
strengthening safe work environments: 
System planning and 
management 
Definition of the OSH management 
system’s policy, objectives, and indicators. 
Development and implementation of 
annual work plans. 
Prevention and health care 
Epidemiological surveillance systems 
for psychosocial risk factors and 
musculoskeletal disorders. 
Occupational medicine, return-to-work, 
and rehabilitation programs. 
Program for the protection of pregnant 
women and support for breastfeeding/
lactation.

## Pagina 229

Scope of the SG-SST 
In 2025, we strengthened the implementation of 
the Occupational Safety and Health Management 
System (SG-SST), ensuring 100% comprehensive 
coverage for all individuals associated with our 
operations, regardless of employment status or work 
arrangement—whether on-site, remote, hybrid, or on 
assignment. The system covered all 7.054 of our direct 
employees, as well as 37 contractors and third-party 
workers whose work or place of service provision is 
controlled by the Organization, ensuring in all cases 
the application of the defined OSH standards and 
controls. 
The OSHMS was implemented across all of the Bank’s 
offices and workplaces, ensuring the consistent 
application of programs, controls, and actions 
aimed at preventing workplace accidents and 
occupational diseases. Similarly, its scope was 
extended to contractors and suppliers with personnel 
on assignment who carry out activities within our 
facilities, to whom we provide guidelines, support, 
and verification of compliance with occupational 
safety and health requirements. 
During the period under review, no employees, 
activities, or workplaces were identified as being 
excluded from the OSHMS. In cases where operations 
are carried out through third parties, we apply the 
coordination and control mechanisms defined 
by current regulations to ensure compliance with 
minimum OSH standards. 
OSH Policy 
At Banco de Occidente, we promote a culture of 
care, prevention, and shared responsibility regarding 
Occupational Safety and Health, in which open 
dialogue and active participation are fundamental 
to risk management. Our policy guides decisions and 
practices aimed at protecting the life, health, and 
well-being of those who are part of our operations, 
as well as contractors and associated third parties. 
In line with this approach, we ensure work environments 
where employees can identify, report, and warn 
about unsafe conditions in a timely manner, with the 
assurance that there will be no retaliation or negative 
consequences for doing so. Likewise, we guarantee 
the right to withdraw from situations that pose an 
imminent risk, always prioritizing the protection of 
physical and mental well-being. 
Employee Participation and 
OSH Committees 
At Banco de Occidente, we promote an Occupational 
Health and Safety management approach based 
on participation, ongoing consultation, and open 
communication with our employees. We believe 
that early risk identification, incident prevention, 
and continuous improvement of the OHSMS are 
strengthened when the people who are part 
of the operation participate in an informed and 
co-responsible manner in its development, 
implementation, and evaluation. 
This approach is realized through formal participation 
forums, accessible reporting channels, and joint 
committees that allow us to gather proposals, address 
concerns, and make decisions aimed at protecting 
life, health, and well-being in the workplace.
Mechanisms for Participation 
and Oversight in Occupational 
Safety and Health 
Our employees have access to various mechanisms 
that enable active participation in the management 
and continuous improvement of the OSH Management 
System and access relevant information regarding 
occupational safety and health, including: 
Participation in formal committees, where risks 
are analyzed, preventive actions are proposed, 
and improvement plans are monitored. 
Channels for reporting unsafe conditions, unsafe 
acts and incidents, as well as suggestions for 
This framework strengthens incident 
prevention, drives continuous 
improvement of the Occupational Health 
and Safety Management System, and 
consolidates an organizational culture 
based on trust, transparency, and self￾care as pillars of the Bank’s well-being 
and sustainability.

Hazard identification, 
risk assessment, and 
continuous improvement
We conduct hazard identification and risk assessment 
on a regular basis at all our locations and workplaces 
through in-person or virtual exercises involving 
employees, area leaders, COPASST, and technical 
support from the Occupational Risk Management 
Company (ARL). This process allows us to anticipate, 
prevent, and control the risks associated with our 
activities, protecting the safety, health, and well￾being of our employees, contractors, and other 
individuals involved in the operation.
This analysis comprehensively considers the 
processes, activities, and tasks carried out by the 
Organization, including:
Routine and non-routine activities.
In-house and subcontracted tasks.
Different stages of service delivery.
Operational conditions and geographic contexts 
where the operation takes place.
Participation in hazard 
identification and 
risk assessment
Employee participation is also directly integrated 
into the technical processes of the SG-SST. During 
2025:
Employees actively participated in safety 
inspections at facilities and workstations.
Process and job analyses were conducted, 
incorporating the experience of those performing 
the work.
The annual update of risk identification, 
assessment, and control was strengthened, 
validating the effectiveness of the measures 
implemented.
OSH Risk Management 
and Application 
of Controls
Identified risks are managed by applying the 
hierarchy of controls, prioritizing hazard elimination 
and, when this is not possible, the implementation 
of controls at the source, in the environment, and 
for the worker, supplemented by administrative 
measures. This approach allows us to effectively 
reduce the likelihood of workplace accidents and 
occupational illnesses, fostering safe and healthy 
work environments.
Based on this information, we periodically 
update the hazard identification and 
risk assessment matrix, which allows 
us to prioritize those scenarios with the 
highest level of exposure and potential 
impact.

In addition, we conduct safety inspections aimed 
at identifying unsafe conditions requiring priority 
intervention. These inspections are carried out 
according to prioritization criteria defined by the 
Organization, considering the risk level of the sites, 
the activities performed, and the results of previous 
assessments, and are supported by technical 
assistance from the ARL when necessary.
We use the results of hazard identification, risk 
assessment, inspections, and incident investigations 
to measure the performance of our SG-SST, in 
accordance with GTC 45 standards and complementary 
specialized methodologies. This process allows 
us to identify opportunities for improvement and 
implement preventive and corrective actions in a 
timely manner. Additionally, we share these findings 
with our employees, the COPASST, process leaders, 
and Senior Management, which strengthens informed 
decision-making and our commitment to continuous 
improvement.
Hazard Identification 
Methodology
In 2025, we maintained full coverage in hazard 
identification and risk assessment processes, 
ensuring the implementation of controls at 100% 
of our sites. This result consolidates our preventive 
management and allows us to focus our 2026 efforts 
on strengthening the consistency and depth of risk 
analyses. This comprehensive approach is based on 
the systematic application of the following processes 
and tools:
Hazard identification and risk assessment (GTC 
45).
Psychosocial risk assessment.
Biomechanical tools (OCRA and RULA checklists).
Scheduled safety inspections.
Analysis of workstations and work processes.
Major occupational risks 
identified
In 2025, the main occupational hazards identified as 
having the potential to cause ailments and illnesses 
were psychosocial and biomechanical risks, which 
were primarily associated with diagnoses related 
to the musculoskeletal system and the mental 
and behavioral health system. These risks have 
been addressed as a priority through preventive 
measures, epidemiological surveillance programs, 
and adjustments to working conditions, aimed at 
mitigating their impact and strengthening the overall 
well-being of employees.
No incidents resulting in serious injuries occurred 
in 2025.
The identified risks are managed by applying 
the hierarchy of controls, prioritizing preventive 
measures that reduce exposure and the likelihood 
of adverse events occurring:
Elimination of the hazard, when technically 
feasible.
Substitution with safer alternatives.
Engineering controls, such as physical or 
environmental modifications.
Administrative controls, including procedures, 
signage, and training.
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), as a last 
line of defense.
This approach helps foster safe 
and healthy work environments, 
effectively reducing the risks 
associated with operations.

Prevention and protection of 
customers and third parties
Our preventive approach also extends to customers, 
suppliers, contractors, and visitors who interact with 
our facilities, through:
Visible signage for hazards and traffic areas.
Adaptation of physical spaces to prevent falls and 
other incidents.
Procedures for responding to emergencies and 
physical security incidents.
Continuous monitoring of reported unsafe 
conditions.
Accident and incident 
management and continuous 
improvement in OSH
At Banco de Occidente, we manage workplace 
accidents and incidents with a preventive and 
continuous improvement approach, focused on 
identifying root causes, strengthening existing 
controls, and preventing the recurrence of events. 
Each incident is analyzed to identify root causes 
and prevent recurrence, and as an opportunity to 
reinforce the culture of self-care, risk management, 
and comprehensive protection of our employees, 
contractors, and third parties.
Accident and Incident 
Investigation Process
All reported workplace accidents and incidents 
are investigated in accordance with the SG-SST 
guidelines, following a structured process that 
includes:
1. Composition of the Investigation Team
Composed of the immediate supervisor, 
a representative from COPASST, and the 
Occupational Safety and Health team. In serious 
or fatal incidents, a licensed OSH professional 
and specialized technical staff participate.
2. Information gathering
This is conducted in person or virtually, depending 
on the severity of the incident, using ICT tools. The 
investigation is carried out within fifteen (15) days 
of the incident.
3.Root cause analysis
Immediate and underlying causes are identified 
using the cause tree methodology, in accordance 
with NTC 3701.
4.Definition of Corrective and Preventive Actions
A prioritized action plan is developed, applying 
the hierarchy of controls to eliminate or mitigate 
the identified risks.
5.Documentation and dissemination of lessons 
learned
Reports are documented, approved, and shared 
with the relevant departments to prevent the 
recurrence of similar incidents.
6.Follow-up and verification
The completion of actions and their effectiveness 
over time are monitored.

Trends in OSH indicators
To analyze OSH performance over time, we track the evolution of workplace accidents, the accident rate, 
and occupational illness incidents during the 2022–2025 period. This analysis allows us to identify trends, 
evaluate the effectiveness of implemented preventive measures, and guide decision-making for the continuous 
strengthening of OSH management.
At the consolidated level, the reduction in the total rate in 2025 confirms the effectiveness of the prevention 
strategies implemented and reinforces the importance of continuing to deepen root cause analysis, strengthening 
the culture of self-care, and implementing differentiated risk management, to sustain and improve this 
performance in the coming periods.

Key occupational health 
services and programs
Our occupational health services are 
delivered through a comprehensive approach 
that allows us to anticipate risks, reduce the 
severity of health events, and strengthen the 
Bank’s preventive capacity. This approach is 
implemented through the following strategic 
activities:
Comprehensive rehabilitation program, 
with monitoring and support for employees 
with health conditions that result in 
prolonged disabilities (longer than 30 days) 
or work restrictions.
Periodic occupational medical 
examinations, administered to the entire 
employee population, in accordance with 
identified risks.
Annual health assessment, which 
consolidates the main findings of 
occupational medical evaluations and 
guides the planning of preventive actions 
in occupational medicine.
Follow-up on special cases, with the 
involvement of occupational health 
professionals to facilitate return-to-work 
and job adaptation processes.
The absenteeism rate remained stable and within controlled levels during the 2022–2025 period, with 
consistent levels among direct employees (between 13,16 and 14,30) and greater volatility among contractors, 
explained by the operational and temporary nature of their activities. In 2025, the total rate stood at 14,35, 
in line with the corporate target of 14,29%, demonstrating effective management of working conditions, 
health, and well-being, as well as effective monitoring of absenteeism at the organizational level.

and Occupational

work environments.

Confidentiality and responsible 
use of health information
The quality of occupational health services is ensured 
through the participation of specialized occupational 
health professionals, led by an occupational 
physician, who is responsible for the custody and 
management of employees’ clinical information.
To protect the confidentiality and appropriate use 
of personal health data:
Clinical information is held exclusively by the Bank’s 
occupational physician.
Access to the information is limited to the 
Occupational Safety and Health team (physician, 
psychologist, physical therapist, or occupational 
therapist).
Any use of the information is made with the 
employee’s informed consent, following a clear 
explanation of its scope and purpose.
Confidentiality agreements are in place with 
healthcare providers who support evaluations 
and interventions nationwide.
Under no circumstances is health information used 
to grant favorable or unfavorable treatment, nor 
is it shared with other areas of the Bank, including 
Human Resources, ensuring ethical and responsible 
handling in accordance with current regulations.

programs.

Training for care and 
prevention
At Banco de Occidente, we view training as a 
cornerstone of risk prevention, the promotion 
of self-care, and the fostering of a culture of 
occupational safety and health. Through ongoing 
training programs, we strive to ensure that our 
employees, suppliers, and contractors have the 
knowledge and skills necessary to perform their 
duties safely and responsibly.
Our OSH training strategy is designed to meet the 
needs of different stakeholders, considering the 
risks associated with each role, activity, and work 
environment. This approach allows us to ensure 
comprehensive and consistent coverage nationwide. 
Training is delivered through in-person, virtual, 
and hands-on sessions and includes the following 
processes:
Induction and periodic refresher training on the 
OSH Management System.
General and specialized training based on the 
level of risk exposure.
Mandatory and voluntary training, in accordance 
with regulations and internal guidelines.

Goals, 
performance,

In 2025, we achieved 100% compliance with

of employees and contractors, establishing training

Promotion of Health and 
Holistic Well-being
At the Bank, we promote a holistic well-being 
approach that recognizes health as an essential 
component of quality of life, productivity, and 
organizational sustainability. Beyond occupational 
risk prevention, we facilitate timely access to health 
services and develop voluntary programs aimed 
at strengthening healthy lifestyle habits, disease 
prevention, and self-care among our employees.
Access to non-work￾related health services
We ensure that all employees have timely access 
to medical and healthcare services not directly 
associated with their work. To this end, we grant 
the necessary leave and time to attend medical 
appointments, exams, and procedures, in accordance 
with each individual’s schedule, regardless of whether 
these services are provided through:
La Entidad Promotora de Salud (EPS).
Planes complementarios o medicina prepagada.
Pólizas de salud contratadas de manera 
independiente.
Voluntary health promotion programs: As part of our 
commitment to prevention and well-being, we develop 
voluntary programs aimed at mitigating significant 
non-work-related health risks and promoting healthy 
lifestyles throughout the Organization:
Occupational Safety and Health Day: We hold an 
annual nationwide company-wide event focused 
on:
Health promotion and self-care.
Healthy eating.
Prevention of common diseases.
Healthy lifestyle habits.
The most recent edition took place in September 
2025, featuring educational and experiential activities 
open to all.
Blood donation drives: We organize voluntary blood 
donation drives at our facilities in coordination 
with authorized healthcare providers, who supply 
medical staff, equipment, and safe conditions for 
blood collection and storage, thereby promoting 
solidarity and public health.
Executive Health Screening Program: aimed 
at employees in Senior Management, Middle 
Management, and Department Heads, this program 
seeks to strengthen the early detection of health 
risks through:
Routine and specialized laboratory tests.
Medical evaluations by specialists.
Professional guidance for interpreting results.
Nutrition Challenge: a program designed for 
employees who are overweight or obese, focused 
on:
Professional nutrition counseling.
Education on balanced eating.
Regular progress monitoring.
Improved well-being and quality of life.
In 2025, we achieved high levels of compliance in health 
promotion activities, including the implementation of 
company-wide health days, preventive programs, 
and medical evaluations, establishing these 
initiatives as a pillar of organizational well-being.
Looking ahead to 2026, the main 
challenge is to increase employee 
attendance and engagement 
in preventive activities,
strengthening communication 
and participation strategies that 
expand the impact of health and 
wellness programs.

access channel for facilitating access to financial

Banco de Occidente’s customer experience

the CAMEL Model, which consists of measuring and 
analyzing five fundamental parameters: capital 
(C), asset quality (A), management (M), earnings

used in the financial sector to measure corporate 
risk, and Banco de Occidente adapts it to analyze 
customers for the purpose of assigning credit limits. 
This maintains financial stability by granting loans 
based on repayment capacity.
Through this comprehensive approach, Banco de

strengthens trust, promotes financial inclusion, 
and contributes to the sustainable development of

Our Commitment to 
Inclusion and Accessibility
Financial inclusion and accessibility are fundamental 
pillars of the customer experience at Banco de 
Occidente. Under this approach, throughout 2025 
we continue to strengthen a comprehensive service 
model aimed at ensuring equitable, dignified, and 
timely access to our financial products and services, 
with a special emphasis on people with disabilities 
and groups in situations of greater vulnerability.
This model is managed in a coordinated manner 
through the Financial Customer Service System 
(SAC), which establishes processes, guidelines, 
and monitoring mechanisms that ensure inclusive, 
respectful service centered on the specific needs of 
each customer, in accordance with current regulations 
and the principles of fair treatment promoted by the 
Bank.
As part of this approach, the Bank has a specialized 
protocol for serving people with disabilities,
designed to ensure adequate, efficient, and respectful 
service delivery across all service channels. This 
protocol guides employees on how to interact 
appropriately with customers who have hearing, visual, 
or physical disabilities or other conditions, promoting 
clear, empathetic, and effective communication.
In addition, the Bank offers a Colombian Sign 
Language interpretation service, provided by a 
specialized vendor, with coverage at 100% of its 
physical branches. This service facilitates interaction 
with people with hearing impairments, ensuring timely 
and equal access to information, and the proper 
delivery of financial services.
In terms of infrastructure, by 2025, 100% of the 
Bank’s branches had Braille signage indicating 
operating hours, while 99% had physical accessibility 
features, such as ramps, stair lifts, or level entrances, 
enabling customers to access services safely and 
independently.
In addition, the Bank makes contracts available 
to people with visual impairments in audio format, 
accessible digitally, to promote understanding of 
contractual information and the informed exercise of 
their rights as financial consumers. Similarly, subtitles 
were added to financial education audiovisual 
content published on institutional websites and 
channels, strengthening access to information and 
inclusive learning.
The inclusive service model is reinforced by a 
nationwide institutional policy on guide dog access, 
which authorizes their entry into all Bank branches. 
This policy is uniformly communicated and applied 
across the network, in accordance with current 
regulations, ensuring equal conditions for guide 
dog users.
The Bank promotes an organizational culture based 
on fair treatment, respect, and empathy through the 
periodic dissemination of guidelines and practical 
recommendations for employees. These actions aim 
to strengthen quality, inclusive service that aligns with 
corporate values as well as customer expectations.
In addition, compliance with inclusive service 
processes is monitored periodically, providing 
support to the various service channels to ensure their 
proper implementation and the consistent delivery 
of accessible, high-quality service throughout the 
country.
With the aim of consolidating a culture centered on 
inclusion, in 2025 the Bank continued to develop 
training programs for its employees, designed to 
strengthen the skills necessary for the proper care of 
people with disabilities and other vulnerable groups.
Among the main training initiatives are:
An online course on serving people with 
disabilities, which provides practical tools for 
assisting individuals with hearing, visual, and 
physical disabilities through clear guidelines, 
simulations of real-life situations, and best practices 
aimed at delivering an inclusive, respectful, and 
efficient service.
Online course on the Financial Consumer Service 
System (SAC) and the Financial Consumer 
Ombudsman (DCF), focused on strengthening 
knowledge regarding the protection of financial 
consumers’ rights, with an emphasis on the most 
vulnerable populations.
Basic sign language workshop, available on 
the Bank’s digital platform, aimed at improving 
communication with people with hearing 
impairments and raising employees’ awareness 
of functional diversity.

Banking Correspondence: 
In 2025, Banco de Occidente consolidated the 
banking correspondent network as one of the main 
enablers of the customer experience by strengthening 
proximity to users, expanding territorial coverage, 
and ensuring continuous access to financial services 
in areas where there is no physical branch presence. 
This channel is positioned as a strategic pillar for 
financial inclusion, operational continuity, and the 
generation of social and economic value in these 
regions.
As a result of the efforts made during the year, 
transaction volume grew by 4,2% compared to 
2024, and the bank achieved 95% compliance with 
the strategic objectives defined for the channel, 
demonstrating its relevance within the customer 
service model.
During the reporting period, the banking correspondent 
channel strengthened its contribution to financial 
inclusion by expanding its territorial coverage 
and integrating new networks of correspondents 
with significant national and regional impact. Learn 
more about the banking correspondent network at 
the following link.
In this context, the bank partnered with nationwide 
networks featuring high brand recognition and 
significant customer traffic, such as OXXO, with 
nearly 500 locations, and Farmatodo, with 18 stores, 
as well as strategic regional networks like GANA in 
Antioquia, which has approximately 3.000 locations 
spread across all of the department’s municipalities, 
establishing itself as one of the networks closest to 
local communities. Additionally, through the Punto 
de Pago correspondent, the CONRED network was 
enabled, adding nearly 1.000 additional locations 
to the Bank’s network.
These integrations allowed the Bank to expand its 
presence to more than 350 municipalities across 
the country, benefiting both banked and unbanked 
customers, local businesses, microentrepreneurs, 
self-employed workers, and citizens in general, in 
both urban and rural areas.
Through its banking correspondent network, Banco 
de Occidente facilitated access to essential financial 
services, such as payments for public and private 
utilities, PILA and tax payments, withdrawals, and 
deposits, reducing geographic and economic barriers 
and promoting financial inclusion in historically 
underserved areas.
The Bank maintained the standardization of 
transactional processes to ensure that operations 
are easy for any user to understand and execute, 
regardless of their educational level or prior 
experience with financial services. This effort 
was complemented by scheduled and organic 
communication campaigns on social media, aimed 
at raising awareness of the correspondent network 
and educating users on how to conduct transactions 
safely and easily.
Additionally, practical recommendations on 
conducting transactions were developed and 
disseminated, facilitating access to clear, visual, and 
easy-to-understand information, which indirectly 
contributed to strengthening financial literacy and 
inclusion in the communities served. These results reflect Banco de Occidente’s commitment to continuously improving the customer experience, 
eliminating barriers to access, and complying with Law 1328 of 2009, ensuring that all individuals, regardless 
of their circumstances, can access financial solutions equitably and with dignity.

As a result of these actions, 587 comprehensive 
accident insurance policies were sold, facilitating 
access to low-cost financial protection products 
for populations such as security guards, motorists, 
informal self-employed workers, micro-entrepreneurs, 
and SMEs, who have traditionally been excluded from 
the insurance system.
In fulfillment of its contractual responsibility to the 
correspondent networks, a national knowledge 
survey was conducted in August 2025 among staff 
serving at the service points, with the aim of assessing 
the adoption of lessons taught in previous years and 
strengthening the quality of service provided to users.
This assessment involved 1.150 employees nationwide 
and identified opportunities for improvement in 
user guidance, promotion of the channel’s use, and 
service delivery. As part of the initiative, the five 
most outstanding participants were recognized with 
symbolic incentives, strengthening motivation and 
commitment to service quality.
Aware of the operational challenges associated with 
providing financial services in areas without a physical 
branch presence, during 2025 the Bank continued 
working on the development of technological solutions 
aimed at ensuring uninterrupted service delivery 
through banking correspondents.
In this context, progress was made on the Stand-in 
initiative, which, starting in February 2026, will allow 
customers to make payments and other transactions 
even in scenarios of operational unavailability, 
reducing the need for travel, strengthening service 
sustainability, and protecting the customer experience.
The social impact of the banking correspondent 
channel is measured using indicators such as 
growth in transaction volume, territorial coverage, 
the availability of financial services in areas without 
bank branches, and effective access to financial 
resources by vulnerable populations.
In 2025, Banco de Occidente had approximately 175 
branches nationwide, so banking correspondents 
played a fundamental role in the distribution 
and payment of subsidies targeted at high-risk 
populations, ensuring that funds reached communities 
in remote and hard-to-reach regions in a timely and 
secure manner. In this context, more than 10.000 
payments were made to third parties totaling 
approximately $5,6 billion, demonstrating the 
growing use of this channel for delivering funds to 
beneficiaries of social programs, business clients, 
SMEs, and public entities.
In addition, special payment and collection days 
were held at banking correspondents for large￾scale agreements, facilitating compliance with 
civic obligations and reducing the need to travel to 
municipal capitals or intermediate cities.
This year, the Bank advanced the evolution of the 
banking correspondent channel toward a model with 
greater added value, progressively incorporating 
products and services that go beyond transactional 
execution.
Historically, Payment Points have been viewed 
primarily as collection points; in 2025, the bank—
through marketing campaigns, training, coaching, and 
incentives—encouraged operators at these points 
to develop sales skills for promoting and selling 
comprehensive accident insurance in partnership 
with SURA.
Additionally, innovations were implemented to 
improve the channel’s efficiency, such as the direct 
connection with Efecty for PILA collections, 
the launch of PowerPage for the digital filing 
of correspondent Mechanisms for Requests, 
Complaints, Claims, and Suggestions – PQRs,
and the technological integration of new networks 
through transactional platforms interoperable with 
Grupo Aval’s infrastructure.
The performance of the banking correspondent 
channel is measured through key indicators such 
as transaction volume, territorial coverage, and 
digital banking penetration. In this regard, in 2025 
the channel recorded an overall 4,2% increase in 
the number of transactions compared to 2024, and 
the adoption of the Dale! digital wallet through 
payment points grew by 15%, driven by network 
expansion, the addition of new correspondent 
networks, and the diversification of services offered.
Taken together, these results reflect the positive 
impact of the banking correspondent network on the 
quality of life in the communities it serves, by ensuring 
continuous, accessible, and reliable access to 
financial, collection, and protection services, thereby 
strengthening financial inclusion, local economic 
stability, and user confidence in the financial system.

Customer 
Experience 
Awards - 
Recognizing 
Excellence 
The Customer Experience Awards are held annually 
through a structured and transparent process that 
ensures the objective evaluation of the submitted 
initiatives. The call for entries is open to all areas of the 
Bank, inviting teams to submit projects implemented 
during the year that have significantly contributed 
to improving customer experience.
In the first stage, departments submit their initiatives, 
which are evaluated by a specialized team that 
analyzes their scope, impact, and alignment with 
the Bank’s strategic objectives. Subsequently, the 
selected initiatives advance to an evaluation phase 
by a judging panel, which determines the winning 
projects based on pre-established criteria, such 
as impact on the customer experience, innovation, 
sustainability, and scalability.
In 2025, the awards were organized into six 
categories, each designed to recognize a key aspect 
of the transformation of customer experience:
Best Projects: recognizes teams that implemented 
innovative solutions and transformed key moments 
in the customer journey, generating tangible 
impacts on the Bank’s profitability and customer 
satisfaction.
Best ENSI (Internal Satisfaction Level): highlights 
the areas that achieved the highest levels of internal 
customer satisfaction, demonstrating collaborative, 
accessible, and empathetic management.
WOW Branches: rewards branches that stood 
out for their exceptional performance in customer 
service, based on satisfaction surveys, mystery 
shopper results, participation in customer 
experience campaigns, and the implementation 
of improvement plans.
WOW Employees: recognizes employees who 
exceeded expectations in customer service, 
creating memorable experiences for customers and 
leaving a positive impression in every interaction.
| SDG 9.3 | 
At Banco de Occidente, we understand that a 
memorable customer experience is built on an 
organizational culture centered on people, 
collaborative work, and continuous improvement. 
In this regard, throughout 2025 we continued to 
strengthen the Customer Experience Awards as a 
key mechanism to recognize, highlight, and promote 
the initiatives, projects, and behaviors that generate 
a positive and tangible impact on the experience of 
our internal and external customers.
This initiative has established itself as a strategic tool 
to drive innovation, reinforce a culture of service, and 
align the efforts of the Bank’s various departments 
around a common purpose: to deliver consistent, 
personalized, and high-value experiences at every 
customer touchpoint.
Best Managers: Honors sales managers with 
the highest levels of customer recommendation, 
highlighting their advice, support, and 
approachability.
Best Directors: Recognizes the Fiduciaria’s 
directors who stood out for their guidance, 
effective responses, consistent approachability, 
and sensitivity to client needs, as well as for their 
contribution to creating positive experiences and 
making strategic decisions.

Net Promoter Score (NPS)
| BdO-17 |
At Banco de Occidente, measuring customer 
experience is a fundamental pillar of management, 
organizational learning, and strategic decision￾making. In 2025, we strengthened our measurement 
and active listening model to gain a deeper 
understanding of customers’ perceptions of 
our products, services, and channels, identify 
opportunities for improvement, and guide segment￾specific actions.
We measure customer experience using quantitative 
indicators, standardized methodologies, and 
specialized tools, which allow us to consistently 
evaluate changes in satisfaction, recommendation, 
and the key factors that influence customers’ 
relationships with the Bank.
In 2025, Banco de Occidente’s Net Promoter Score 
(NPS) stood at 64%, representing a 4-percentage￾point decrease from 2024 (68%), in a challenging 
environment for the financial sector characterized 
by regulatory changes, increased competition, and 
rising customer expectations.
Despite this change, the indicator remained at 
favorable levels and allowed for the identification 
of specific improvement opportunities by segment, 
which guide the actions defined for the coming 
periods.

These results show that, although the satisfaction level varied from the target set for the year, data coverage 
increased in 2025, rising from 0,46 in 2024 to 0,61, reflecting an improvement in the representativeness of 
the measurement and in the quality of the information collected.
Indicator 2025 Target 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021
NPS for Businesses (%) 76 69 74 72 73 72
NPS People (%) 51 47 45 46 50 47
In the Corporate Banking segment, the NPS reached 69% in 2025; the indicator remained at solid levels, 
reflecting a positive perception among corporate clients regarding the support, advice, and solutions offered 
by the Bank.
Meanwhile, in Retail Banking, the NPS stood at 47%, showing a 2-percentage-point change from the previous 
year. This result helped identify opportunities for improvement aimed at strengthening recommendations, 
particularly in areas related to response times, process clarity, and proactive communication.
With the aim of deepening its understanding of customer perception, in 2025 the Bank consolidated an 
active listening model through the implementation of the Qualtrics Voice of the Customer (VoC) tool. This 
model operates with samples defined according to statistical criteria that guarantee representativeness and 
a margin of error of 5% or less.
Analysis of the collected data allowed us to classify 
customers into three main groups—promoters, 
passives, and detractors—and identify the factors 
that influence their perception:
Promoters: They particularly value 
personalized service, prompt resolution 
of requests, and the ease of use of 
the digital portfolio and transactional 
channels.
Passive customers: i d e n t i f y 
opportunities for improvement related 
to response times in after-sales service, 
the clarity of processes, and more 
proactive communication regarding 
changes and updates.
Detractors: highlight friction associated 
with more complex processes, such 
as product applications, complaint 
management, and the need for better 
integration between channels, as well as 
the reduction of repetitive procedures.
The results of the satisfaction survey and the NPS serve 
as a key input for Banco de Occidente’s decision￾making. Throughout 2025, these findings enabled 
the prioritization of actions aimed at enhancing the 
customer experience in a differentiated manner by 
segment, channel, and type of interaction.
The methodology used is endorsed by IZO, an international provider specializing 
in quantitative customer experience measurements, which supports the 
reliability and consistency of the results obtained.

Although some goals were not fully achieved, the 
stability of the indicators, the increase in survey

Mechanisms for Requests, 
Complaints, Claims, and 
Suggestions – PQRS
At Banco de Occidente, handling Requests, 
Complaints, Claims, and Suggestions (PQRS) is 
a fundamental component of customer experience 
and a key mechanism for strengthening trust, 
transparency, and the continuous improvement of the 
Bank’s processes and services. Through the Financial 
Consumer Service System (SAC), the Bank ensures 
timely, traceable, and effective handling of requests 
submitted by customers through various channels.
In 2025, the Bank continued to strengthen the 
management of PQRS as part of its commitment 
to quality, customer-centric service aligned with 
current regulations on financial consumer protection. 
This approach allows the Bank not only to resolve 
customer requests but also to identify opportunities 
for improvement in products, processes, and service 
channels.
Throughout the year, 244.855 PQR requests were 
received, 100% of which were resolved, corresponding 
to a 100% resolution rate.
Breaking down the data by type of request, 219.401 
inquiries were handled, there were 0 claims, and 
25.454 complaints, of which, as mentioned above, 
100% were resolved satisfactorily.
These results reflect the Bank’s efforts to ensure 
clear, timely, and consistent responses to customers, 
in accordance with the timeframes and guidelines 
established by applicable regulations and the 
Customer Service Center (SAC).
The information derived from PQRS management 
is analyzed periodically to identify trends, recurring 
causes, and opportunities for improvement in customer 
experience. This analysis allows for providing feedback 
to the responsible departments, strengthening internal 
controls, and prioritizing actions aimed at preventing 
the recurrence of situations that could affect customer 
satisfaction.
Additionally, PQRS management is integrated with 
other mechanisms for measuring customer experience, 
such as the Net Promoter Score (NPS) and the active 
listening model, providing a comprehensive view of 
customers’ expectations, perceptions, and main pain 
points in their relationship with the Bank.
In 2025, the Bank made progress in strengthening the 
channels and tools available for PQRS management, 
with the aim of facilitating customer access to these 
mechanisms and improving service efficiency. Notable 
among these actions is the implementation of digital 
solutions that promote self-service, the traceability 
of requests, and reduced response times, in line with 
the strategy for digital transformation and improving 
customer experience.
PQRS management is also conceived as a strategic 
input for decision-making, continuous improvement, 
and the consolidation of a customer-centric culture, 
in which the voice of the financial consumer is a 
key element for strengthening trust and long-term 
relationships.
Through this approach, Banco 
de Occidente reaffirms its 
commitment to rigorously 
measuring customer experience, 
transparency in results, and the 
implementation of continuous 
improvement actions that 
strengthen trust and long-term 
relationships with its customers.

Training Excellence in Customer 
Experience 
| SASB FN-CB-240a.4 | SDG 4 y 8|
At Banco de Occidente, we understand that a 
positive and sustainable customer experience 
is built not only on service quality but also on 
capacity building, access to knowledge, and 
informed decision-making. Therefore, in 2025 we 
continue to promote a comprehensive strategy for 
financial training and education aimed at different 
customer segments, with the goal of supporting their 
development, strengthening their competitiveness, 
and consolidating long-term relationships based 
on trust and shared value.
This strategy is designed to address the specific 
needs of each segment—corporate banking, 
government, businesses, SMEs, and individuals—
through specialized training programs, relevant 
content, and technical support frameworks that 
help improve customer experience and enhance 
the economic and social impact of their activities.
Corporate Banking Training
In 2025, Banco de Occidente expanded and 
deepened its training programs for the Corporate 
Banking segment, with the goal of keeping business 
owners informed about the main challenges and 
opportunities in the economic, financial, and 
regulatory environment, and strengthening their 
decision-making capacity in highly volatile contexts.
Over the course of the year, two in-person training 
sessions were held in various cities across the country, 
including Cali, Barranquilla, and Medellín, with an 
average duration of two to three hours per session. 
These initiatives were attended by 241 participants 
and represented an approximate investment of 
$28.397.614.
The content covered was focused on:
Sharing key information for business decision￾making.
Strengthening relationships with corporate clients.
Promoting awareness and use of the Bank’s 
financial solutions, such as payment systems and 
treasury solutions.
These training sessions helped strengthen the Bank’s 
value proposition for the corporate segment and 
consolidate long-term strategic relationships.
Government Banking Training
As part of Banco de Occidente’s commitment 
to institutional strengthening and the efficient 
management of public finances, training sessions 
were developed for local and national government 
entities, aimed at strengthening the technical and 
financial capabilities of public sector teams.
Throughout the year, multiple training sessions were 
held, with an average duration of two hours per 
session, reaching more than 512 public servants 
from provincial governments, departments, districts, 
and municipalities across different regions of 
the country. These initiatives represented a total 
investment of $24.685.423.
The training sessions focused primarily on:
Tax regulations and fiscal strengthening, including 
updates on tax stamps, the unified property tax, 
registration tax, and territorial taxes.
 Financial and budgetary management, addressing 
issues related to budgeting, funding sources, and 
financial diagnostics for local governments.
 Public procurement and digital tools, with an 
emphasis on the use of platforms such as SECOP 
II and processes in the health sector.
 Territorial planning and sustainability, including 
development plans, land use planning, and 
multipurpose cadasters.
 Pension liability management, through training 
on reducing pension liabilities (FONPET).
These actions strengthened public 
management, financial planning, 
and regulatory compliance among 
the entities served.

Corporate Banking and SME 
Training
In 2025, Banco de Occidente promoted a 
comprehensive training portfolio aimed at 
strengthening the competitiveness, sustainability, 
and growth of companies and SMEs through training 
programs designed to address their strategic and 
operational needs.
In total, 12 certificate programs were offered, each
lasting an average of 16 to 18 hours. These initiatives 
addressed key topics in business management and 
attracted a large number of participants.
Among the main programs offered, the following 
stand out:
Tax Update 2025: A program designed to train 
participants on reforms and regulatory updates 
to the Colombian tax system, facilitating the 
correct interpretation and application of current 
regulations; it reached 1.624 companies and 1.392 
SMEs, with 1.030 attendees.
Strategic Talent Management: Training 
focused on developing competencies for the 
comprehensive management of human talent, 
including performance evaluation, leadership, 
and strengthening high-performance teams; 
involving 1.219 companies and 266 SMEs, with 
313 attendees.
How to Increase Sales with Artificial Intelligence: 
A training program focused on the use of artificial 
intelligence tools to optimize business processes, 
data analysis, and sales strategies, reaching 374 
companies and 257 SMEs, with 218 participants.
Financial Management for High-Impact 
Companies: A program aimed at strengthening 
advanced financial capabilities, addressing 
topics such as financial planning, cost analysis, 
and strategic decision-making, involving 481 
companies and 329 SMEs, with 309 attendees.
Corporate Leadership for Women: Training 
focused on empowering women’s leadership in the 
business environment, promoting equity and the 
development of management skills, impacting 356 
companies and 193 SMEs, with 249 attendees.
Digital Marketing and Analytics: A program aimed 
at strengthening capabilities in digital strategies, 
data analysis, and brand positioning in digital 
environments, involving 505 companies and 162 
SMEs, with 153 attendees.
Labor Law for Non-Lawyers: A program designed 
to provide business owners and talent managers 
with essential knowledge of labor law, facilitating 
regulatory compliance and the proper management 
of labor relations; reaching 775 companies and 
474 SMEs, with 293 participants.
Project Management and Agile Methodologies:
Training focused on the implementation of agile 
methodologies and best practices for the efficient 
management of business projects, involving 912 
companies and 663 SMEs, with 281 attendees.
Digital Business Innovation: A program aimed 
at developing strategic and technological 
competencies for the adoption of digital solutions 
and innovative business models, impacting 239 
companies and 292 SMEs, with 118 participants.
Performance evaluation and performance 
management: Training focused on the design 
and implementation of systems for measuring 
and monitoring organizational performance, with 
participation from 244 companies and 257 SMEs, 
and 113 attendees.
Experience Design and Customer Loyalty: A 
training program aimed at enhancing customer 
experience through service design tools and loyalty 
strategies, reaching 133 companies and 129 SMEs, 
with 85 participants.
Soft Skills for Team Leaders: A program aimed 
at developing key soft skills, such as effective 
communication, collaborative leadership, and 
change management, involving 205 companies 
and 274 SMEs, with 119 participants.
In total, these training sessions saw 
the active participation of 3.289 
attendees and represented a 
total investment of $339.342.912,
allocated to ensuring academic 
quality, the participation of 
specialized experts, and the 
use of technological tools for a 
comprehensive learning experience.

Maestros del Hacer
In line with its commitment to financial inclusion 
and economic empowerment, Banco de Occidente 
continued to strengthen the Maestros del Hacer 
program, designed as a comprehensive financial 
education platform aimed at customers and 
communities.
The program expanded its reach by developing 
five specialized financial education forums, 
primarily aimed at customers in the Retail Banking 
segment, with a focus on investment, financial 
planning, and setting goals for 2026. These forums 
were organized through Hacertivos, a free virtual 
platform offering educational content such as 
forums, podcasts, and training modules.
In total, the forums had 1.878 registered 
participants and 471 actual attendees, 
representing an approximate investment of 
COP 50 million, aimed at strengthening financial 
education and the quality of the content.
The forum with the widest reach was “Discover 
Bre-B: Instant Payments, No Waiting,” which had 
1.187 registered participants and 240 attendees, 
demonstrating customers’ interest in instant 
payment solutions and financial digitization.
In 2025, Maestros del Hacer directly impacted 
471 beneficiaries, consisting of customers who 
actively participated in the training sessions.
The training and educational initiatives carried 
out in 2025 contributed to:
Strengthen clients’ ability to make informed 
decisions.
Improving the use and understanding of financial 
products and services.
Increasing trust and fostering long-term 
relationships with the Bank.
Enhancing the competitiveness and sustainability 
of companies, SMEs, and public entities.
Through this comprehensive capacity-building 
strategy, Banco de Occidente reaffirms its role as a 
strategic partner to its customers, promoting an 
experience that goes beyond the transaction and 
is established as a process of support, learning, 
and the creation of shared value.

## Pagina 252

Responsible marketing and 
financial consumer protection
| GRI 417 | 
At Banco de Occidente, we view responsible marketing 
as a key element in building relationships of trust with 
our clients and other stakeholders. In this regard, we 
manage our commercial communications based on 
principles of transparency, clarity, accuracy, and 
timeliness, ensuring that information about financial 
products and services is understandable, sufficient, 
and aligned with current regulations.
This approach seeks to protect the rights of financial 
consumers, promote informed decisions, and prevent 
practices that may be misleading, in accordance 
with the Financial Consumer Service System (SAC), 
applicable regulations, and the guidelines defined 
by Grupo Aval.
Responsible marketing management at the Bank is 
carried out through internal processes for reviewing, 
validating, and controlling commercial materials, 
campaigns, and messages directed at customers, 
systematically considering aspects such as:
The characteristics, conditions, and costs of 
financial products and services.
The associated risks and the financial consumer’s 
responsibilities.
The appropriate use of communication channels 
and responsible audience segmentation.
Compliance with applicable regulations regarding 
financial advertising and consumer protection.
This approach is implemented differently depending 
on the type of product, recognizing the specific 
characteristics of the Transactions and Loans 
segments, and tailoring messages and content to 
the risks and impacts associated with each.
Transactions Clan
In the Transactions Clan, responsible marketing is 
geared toward ensuring that customers receive clear, 
accurate, and easily accessible information about the 
features, terms, and use of transactional products, 
such as savings and checking accounts, transfers, 
payment methods, banking correspondents, and 
digital channels.
Communications associated with this cluster explicitly 
include:
A detailed description of the features of 
transactional products and services, including 
their scope, limitations, and terms of use.
Transparent information on fees, commissions, 
and operating costs, presented in a way that is 
understandable and visible to customers.
Preventive and educational messages regarding the 
safe use of channels, the protection of personal 
data, and fraud prevention.
Clear information on the rights and obligations of 
financial consumers in transactional operations, 
in accordance with current regulations.
All marketing materials, campaigns, and informational 
content from the Transactions division undergo 
internal review and validation processes to avoid 
ambiguous messages or those that may create false 
expectations regarding benefits, service availability, 
or preferential terms.
Information regarding the Transactions Clan’s 
products is available to customers through the 
following institutional channels:
The Bank’s transactional portal and 
informational pages (Products and Services 
section).
Official fee schedules published on digital 
channels.
Informational communications sent to 
customers and distributed at branches and 
correspondent locations.
Contractual documentation and 
informational material validated by the 
Customer Service Center (SAC).

## Pagina 254

Commitment to 
communities 
Social Investment 
At Banco de Occidente, social investment is a key 
driver of inclusive and sustainable development of 
the communities where we operate. Throughout 
2025, we operated in accordance with our Social 
Investment Policy, a framework that guides our 
decisions and ensures that every contribution is 
made voluntarily, responsibly, ethically, and in 
alignment with our Sustainability Strategy and the 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in order to 
create measurable social impact.
More than just financial support, we seek to be a 
strategic partner for these regions, strengthening 
local capacities and helping to improve people’s 
quality of life. We are convinced that well-managed 
social investment generates shared value, fosters 
more inclusive and resilient environments, and lays a 
solid foundation for the country’s long-term economic 
and social development.
SDG 10.2; 13.2; 
15.1; 17.5
At Banco de Occidente, we view our engagement 
with communities as a fundamental pillar of our 
sustainable management. In 2025, we strengthened 
our approach toward a more structured and 
measurable social impact approach, aimed at 
generating positive and sustainable impacts in the 
regions where we operate and have a presence.
Our commitment to communities is realized 
through social investment programs, corporate 
volunteering, and strategic partnerships, which seek 
to bridge social gaps, strengthen local capacities, 
and promote social, environmental, and economic 
well-being, in line with our Sustainability Strategy 
and the Sustainable Development Goals.
Throughout the year, we made progress in 
consolidating a social management model that 
prioritizes transparency, shared responsibility, and 
impact measurement, allowing us to direct our 
resources toward initiatives aligned with the needs 
of the region and our corporate purpose.
Environmental Conservation:
Through this pillar, we support programs 
and projects aimed at protecting natural 
resources, conserving biodiversity, and 
strengthening resilience to climate change. 
We promote initiatives that contribute to the 
adaptation to and mitigation of environmental 
impacts and to the development of a culture 
of caring for the natural environment in local 
communities.
Social Investment Policy
Our Social Investment Pillars
Our Social Investment Policy defines three strategic 
pillars that guide our decisions and ensure that every 
initiative we support has a clear purpose, a verifiable 
impact, and aligns with our Sustainability Strategy.
Inclusive social development:
This pillar brings together programs aimed at 
improving quality of life and promoting social 
progress in communities. Through these 
initiatives, we seek to foster social inclusion, 
well-being, and the strengthening community 
resilience and social cohesion, with a special 
focus on vulnerable populations.
Education for development:
We believe that education is a key tool for 
creating opportunities. Therefore, we support 
initiatives that strengthen knowledge 
and skills among different populations, 
contributing to personal, family, work, and 
professional development, and promoting 
inclusion and social mobility.

Strengthening Impact 
Monitoring and 
Measurement
As part of the evolution of our social investment 
model, in 2025 we took an important step toward 
strengthening the mechanisms for monitoring and 
measuring the impact of our donations and social 
contributions. This progress allowed us to improve 
the traceability and accountability of resources and 
gain a deeper understanding of the results of the 
initiatives we support.
To this end, we implemented standardized monitoring 
reports through which partner organizations share 
information on project progress, challenges faced, 
and lessons learned during implementation, as well 
as the quantification and characterization of the 
impacted population. This information allows us to 
assess the actual scope of our actions and strengthen 
continuous improvement processes.
Coordination with 
Corporate Volunteering
At the same time, in 2025 we began developing a new 
value proposition for our Corporate Volunteering 
program, with the aim of ensuring that every 
initiative generates a significant impact for both 
the communities and the volunteers themselves.
This approach seeks a shared benefit among the 
community, the organization, and our employees, 
and is structured around the three pillars of our 
Social Investment Policy: environment, education 
for development, and conscious social growth.
The development of this framework, which continued 
to advance throughout the year, lays the groundwork 
for us to consolidate a volunteer program in 2026 
that is fully aligned with our social and environmental 
impact goals, ensuring that every hour of volunteer 
work contributes directly and measurably to 
community development.
In addition, we conducted verification visits to partner organizations, which 
allowed us to see firsthand the progress made, validate evidence of the impact 
generated, and strengthen our relationship with implementing organizations, 
based on a spirit of support and shared responsibility.
