## Pagina 256

Strengthening access to 
water and sanitation in 
vulnerable communities 
with UNICEF
| BdO-14 |
As part of our commitment to regional development 
and the reduction of structural disparities, in 2025 we 
continued to strengthen our strategic partnership 
with UNICEF, aimed at improving sustainable access 
to safe drinking water, basic sanitation, and hygiene 
practices in rural areas of the department of La 
Guajira, through the WASH (Water, Sanitation, and 
Hygiene) program.
We recognize that La Guajira faces conditions of 
high social, environmental, and climate vulnerability, 
associated with water scarcity, the geographic 
dispersion of rural communities, high poverty rates, 
and limited coverage of basic services.
In this context, the collaboration between Banco de 
Occidente, UNICEF, and local implementing partners 
is established as a high-impact social intervention, 
focused on guaranteeing fundamental rights and 
strengthening community resilience.
In terms of social investment, in 2025, Banco de 
Occidente allocated a total of $223.881.446 COP 
to this program with the valuable contribution of 824 
customers, and since 2022 we have donated a total 
of $2.134.110.976 COP—resources directed toward 
implementing sustainable solutions that have tangibly 
improved the living conditions of the beneficiary 
communities and strengthened their resilience in 
the face of the region’s social, environmental, and 
climate challenges. These interventions were carried 
out primarily in rural communities in the municipalities 
of Manaure, Uribia, and Maicao—areas prioritized 
by UNICEF due to their high levels of vulnerability 
and existing gaps in access to WASH services.
Access to safe drinking water:
In 2025, progress was made in rehabilitating 
and improving water supply systems in priority 
communities. A significant milestone was the 
installation of a drinking water production station 
equipped with a Drinking Water Treatment System 
(DWTS) in the community of Campamento (Maicao), 
ensuring water safe for human consumption for 
399 families (1.595 people) and 487 students.
This intervention helps reduce health risks and 
strengthen water security in an area affected by 
climate variability.
Basic sanitation:
In the sanitation component, the program made 
progress in implementing the SAHTOSO methodology, 
resulting in 11 communities being certified as open￾defecation-free. As a result, 523 people, including 
254 children, now have self-built latrines in their 
homes, improving sanitary conditions and reducing 
the risks associated with waterborne diseases.
In addition, we supported 103 families (523 people) 
in strengthening hygiene practices through 
behavior change strategies promoted by UNICEF, 
with an emphasis on handwashing with soap and 
the adoption of social norms that promote the 
sustainability of these practices over time. These 
actions are essential for disease prevention and the 
enhancement of community well-being.
The program’s implementation faced challenges 
related to climate variability, the geographic 
dispersion of rural communities, and, in some cases, 
cultural resistance to changes in traditional practices. 
However, these challenges helped strengthen the 
program’s participatory approach, promoting 
community dialogue and the joint development of 
solutions tailored to the local context.
As an opportunity, the program has demonstrated 
high potential for:
Empower communities in the sustainable 
management of WASH services.
Strengthen the climate resilience of the territories.
Contribute to the development of local livelihoods 
associated with the operation and maintenance 
of water and sanitation systems.
The partnership with UNICEF reflects our commitment 
to a territorial development model based on 
strategic alliances, which integrates social 
investment, technical expertise, and community 
management. This initiative aligns with the 
Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDGs 
6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), 3 (Good Health and 
Well-being), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), 13 (Climate 
Action), and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), and 
reinforces our role as a stakeholder committed to

Environmental education and 
community empowerment
In 2025, at Banco de Occidente, we strengthened 
our approach to environmental education and 
community capacity building, consolidating initiatives 
aimed at knowledge transfer and awareness, 
environmental awareness, and the empowerment 
of local actors as pillars for long-term sustainability 
in the territories where we operate.
This approach took shape through training activities, 
community coordination platforms, and educational 
processes that integrate educational content, active 
participation from partners, and mechanisms for 
measuring the social impact generated.
Within this framework, the production of the Ecolibros 
was consolidated in 2025 as one of the Bank’s 
main initiatives to promote reading, knowledge of 
Colombian biodiversity, and awareness of ecosystem 
protection, integrating environmental education, 
culture, and social action.
During the reporting period, the following results 
were achieved:
19.500 Ecolibros produced, corresponding to 
the edition “Colombia: The Orchid Garden,” 
dedicated to an emblematic species of the 
country’s biodiversity.
550 Ecolibros delivered to partner organizations 
for educational and cultural initiatives, distributed 
as follows:

Planeta Azul Community

the Planeta Azul Community, conceived as a 
coordination platform that brings together companies, 
social organizations, foundations, clients, NGOs, 
educational institutions, and individuals committed 
to environmental sustainability.
This process helped consolidate the community as 
a space for gathering, knowledge exchange, and 
collective action, aimed at promoting collaborative 
efforts to care for the environment and foster 
sustainable development.

the role of the Planeta Azul Community as a catalyst 
for collaborative projects.
Additionally, in 2025 we made progress in designing 
a mentoring program, in partnership with ICESI 
University, aimed at strengthening the technical 
and management skills of finalists and winners 
of the Planeta Azul Award. The goal is to launch 
this program in 2026, as part of the community’s 
consolidation and outreach efforts.

Environmental Volunteering
Corporate volunteering is a key component of our 
sustainability strategy, as it allows us to translate 
our environmental and social commitments into 
concrete actions in the regions where we operate. 
Within this framework, the environmental education 
component was strengthened through workshops 
that incorporated experiential learning processes for 
our employees and local communities, promoting 
greater environmental awareness and culture within 
the Bank.
In 2025, we carried out environmental volunteer 
initiatives in partnership with WWF Colombia,
aimed at contributing to the ecological restoration 
of the country’s strategic ecosystems. These actions 
were coordinated with environmental authorities and 
local partners and were framed within the Nature￾Based Solutions (NbS) approach, contributing 
to national objectives for restoration, adaptation 
to climate change, and biodiversity protection. 
In this way, the initiatives were primarily aligned 
with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 15 
(Life on Land), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 8 
(Decent Work and Economic Growth), by promoting 
employee participation in environmental actions 
with a territorial impact.
The workshops included activities such as planting, 
maintenance, and restoration of vegetation cover in 
key areas for water security, ecological connectivity, 
and climate resilience, viewing these interventions 
as part of a long-term conservation strategy that 
goes beyond one-off actions.
Key Results for 2025:
Three days of environmental volunteering in 
strategic ecosystems:
Barranquilla – Isla Salamanca National Park.
Cali – Farallones National Natural Park.
Bogotá – Las Moyas Trail.
Participation of 164 volunteer employees.
1.028 volunteer hours, of which 938 hours were 
spent planting trees and 90 hours on social 
volunteer work.
440 seedlings planted, as a direct contribution 
to ecological restoration efforts.
Initiatives in areas of high environmental value, 
raising awareness about biodiversity, conservation, 
and climate change.
Additionally, the social component of corporate 
volunteering helped create more inclusive 
environments and meaningful experiences for 
vulnerable children and communities, strengthening 
community cohesion and our employees’ participation 
in the region’s social development. These actions 
align with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 
10 (Reduced Inequalities), and SDG 17 (Partnerships 
for the Goals).
Together, these initiatives not only contributed to 
environmental restoration but also strengthened the 
Bank’s internal environmental culture, promoting 
shared responsibility and our employees’ commitment 
to sustainability and long-term social transformation.

In 2025, we consolidated our social contribution 
strategy as a key mechanism for addressing priority 
needs in vulnerable communities and strengthening 
programs led by strategic partners. These voluntary 
contributions, aligned with our Social Investment 
Policy, prioritize education, well-being, and inclusion, 
integrating a vision of social, environmental, and 
economic impact across all initiatives.
This approach allowed us to respond quickly to the 
needs of urban and rural communities, reaffirming our 
role as a committed stakeholder in the development 
of the regions where we operate. We carried out 
these actions primarily through the distribution of 
school kits, toys, food and hygiene aid, items for 
people with disabilities, and kits for farmers, helping 
to improve the living conditions of children, rural 
families, and other socially vulnerable populations.
Contributions made in 2025 generated a direct social 
impact on thousands of people, primarily children 
and families in vulnerable situations, contributing to:
Promote the emotional and social well-being of 
children.
Facilitate access to education by providing school 
supplies.
Strengthen rural productivity and farmers’ 
livelihoods.
Address social and health emergencies.
Promote the inclusion of people with disabilities, 
improving their quality of life.
We measure the impact of our actions through the 
number of beneficiaries, the type of contribution 
provided, and the geographic reach. This monitoring 
allows us to evaluate the relevance of our donations 
and optimize resource allocation in future periods, 
ensuring that each investment generates the greatest 
possible value for communities.
In 2025, we established a structured and measurable 
social management framework, aligned with the 
needs of local communities and strengthened 
through development programs, volunteer initiatives, 
environmental education, and strategic partnerships. 
We have evolved from isolated initiatives toward a 
comprehensive approach to creating shared value, 
enabling us to report on our contributions with greater 
rigor and clarity. This progress reaffirms our commitment 
to inclusion and sustainability, and lays the groundwork 
for deepening impact measurement and building lasting 
relationships with the communities where we operate.

Donations
In line with this approach, during the year we 
made donations to partner organizations working 
in different regions of the country, contributing 
to the strengthening of local capacities, support 
for vulnerable populations, and the promotion 
of conscious social development. Through these 
partnerships, we seek to expand the reach of our 
actions and generate positive and sustainable 
impacts in the communities where we operate.
Among the supported organizations are:
ProPacífico - Foundation 
for the Comprehensive 
Development of the Pacific
In 2025, we supported ProPacífico, a foundation that 
advances the comprehensive development agenda of 
Cali, Valle del Cauca, and the Pacific region through 
the mobilization of partnerships and coordination 
among the public, private, and academic sectors. Our 
contribution was aimed at strengthening strategic 
initiatives with a territorial and long-term focus
that promote social, educational, environmental, 
infrastructure, and health development.
With this donation, we seek to support a regional 
agenda that contributes to the sustainable 
development of the territory by strengthening 
institutional capacities, promoting social equity, and 
helping to improve the quality of life for the population, 
especially in contexts of greater vulnerability.
Amount donated in 2025: $158.000.000 COP
The donation aligned with the following lines of work:
Education: promotion of initiatives to expand 
coverage and improve educational quality, as well 
as strengthening of socio-emotional, pedagogical, 
and technical skills.
Health: support for strengthening the health 
system, in accordance with Statutory Law 1751 
of 2015, and improving timely access to women’s 
health diagnostics.
Social development: protection and promotion 
of the rights of vulnerable populations, and 
strengthening of social control, transparency, and 
peacebuilding.
Environment: conservation, restoration, and 
sustainable use of natural resources.
Infrastructure and competitiveness: promotion 
of strategic infrastructure, logistics, and mobility 
projects.
Business development: promotion of 
entrepreneurship and strengthening of the business 
sector.
Human rights and global goals: alignment with 
the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.
Support for non-profit organizations: 
strengthening organizations that carry out 
commendable activities throughout the country.
Our partnership with ProPacífico helps generate structural and sustainable impacts in the region, strengthening 
public-private coordination, improving the quality of social services, and promoting more equitable, competitive, 
and resilient regional development.

dimension Key impacts

Departmental scope throughout the Valle del

## Pagina 263

As part of this partnership, in 2025 we also supported the Compromiso Valle initiative, led by ProPacífico 
and aimed at helping to close socioeconomic gaps in priority municipalities in Valle del Cauca —Cali, 
Buenaventura, Palmira, Yumbo, Buga, Jamundí, Candelaria, and Tuluá—through a comprehensive 
approach focused on populations facing the greatest challenges.
Amount donated in 2025: $350.000.000 COP
This initiative coordinates actions in food security, life transformation, entrepreneurship, employability, 
leadership, and education, with cumulative results of high social impact. Between 2021 and 2025, more 
than 77.000 people have participated in its programs, of whom 12.344 were in 2025, reflecting an 
inclusive approach with high participation by women (74%), youth, and the Afro-descendant population.
During the year, the following results stood out, among others:
Food security: distribution of more than 43.800 food rations and establishment of 44 urban gardens, 
strengthening access to food and the productive use of community space.
Life-changing projects: 2.030 early conflict mediations, with a 91% success rate in achieving 
positive resolutions.
Entrepreneurship and employability: participation of more than 6.000 people, 658 startups 
in formation, and the creation of 604 inclusive jobs, promoting sustainable income and formal 
employment opportunities.
Leadership and social empowerment: support for community initiatives and social organizations 
with the participation of 380 people, with projected and self-managed resources exceeding $1,7 
billion, strengthening local leadership and citizen participation.
Nuevo futuro - Asociación 
de Nuevo Futuro de Colombia
In 2025, we supported the Nuevo Futuro Association 
of Colombia, located in Bogotá, an organization 
dedicated to the well-being and holistic development 
of children and adolescents through support 
processes that strengthen skills, life plans, and the 
creation of protective environments.
Our contribution was allocated to supporting the 
implementation of training programs and to funding 
the maintenance and development of activities aimed 
at the young people associated with the organization, 
with the goal of promoting their emotional, social, 
and educational development. The young people 
receiving support come from highly vulnerable and 
psychosocially risky backgrounds and require 
comprehensive and sustained support to advance 
in their educational and life trajectories.
As part of this support, 16 university students served 
at the University House directly benefited; they are 
currently enrolled in higher education institutions, 
in undergraduate programs and, in some cases, 
graduate programs.
 Amount donated in 2025: $7.393.400 COP
The funds provided made it possible to:
Carry out facility repairs aimed at improving the 
physical and structural conditions of the University 
House.
Strengthen safety and health conditions at the 
facility, as well as the livability of common and 
private spaces.
Make progress toward meeting minimum 
infrastructure standards that promote the physical 
and emotional well-being of young people.
Through this partnership, we contribute to creating 
more suitable conditions for students to remain in 
higher education and for the holistic development of 
young people facing greater challenges, reaffirming 
our commitment to education for development and 
social inclusion.
Thanks to this support, the Nuevo Futuro 
Association of Colombia was able 
to sustain and strengthen its support 
processes, contributing to the creation 
of safe and protective environments for 
the young beneficiaries. These actions 
contribute to the holistic development of 
children and adolescents and reinforce 
our commitment to education for 
development and conscious social 
growth, in line with our Social Investment 
Policy.

from the armed conflict.
Families with incomes below the minimum wage 
and limited educational levels.
Thanks to the support provided throughout the year, 
significant results were achieved:
45.696 hours during which children remained in 
a protective and educational environment.
3.210 people indirectly impacted.
96% of children strengthened their cognitive and 
socio-emotional skills.
64% improved their grades in four or five subjects.
41% ranked in the top five at their schools.
100% of the children remained in their family 
environments, without being placed in foster 
homes.
0% of children were involved in recruitment 
situations.
Qualitatively, the program fostered the development 
of children who were more secure, with greater 
confidence to take on challenges and express 
their opinions; more sociable, with better skills for 
interaction and group work; and more autonomous, 
as reflected in their ability to perform tasks 
independently.
PRODEIN - Asociación 
Benéfico Cristiana Promotora 
de Desarrollo Integral
In 2025, we supported PRODEIN – Christian 
Charitable Association for Integral Development, 
located in Valle del Cauca, an organization committed 
to promoting the integral development of children in 
contexts of high social vulnerability. Our contribution 
was aimed at supporting the construction of an 
educational institution in the Potrero Grande 
neighborhood, in the Aguablanca District of the 
city of Cali, an area characterized by high rates of 
poverty and social exclusion.
The main purpose of this investment was to expand 
access to decent, quality education by creating 
appropriate educational environments that help 
reduce social risks and generate development 
opportunities for children and their families.
Amount donated in 2025: $400.000.000 COP
The funds provided enabled progress in the 
construction and renovation of educational 
infrastructure, including:
Partition walls and facades, ensuring safe and 
functional spaces.
Electrical, voice, and data networks that support 
modern educational processes.
Water, sanitation, pressurized water, and fire 
protection systems, enhancing safety and health 
conditions.
Interior finishes, designed to create environments 
conducive to learning.
Metalwork, ensuring durability and protection of 
the spaces.
Exterior work, improving accessibility and the 
institution’s surroundings.
The construction of this educational institution 
directly benefits 565 girls and boys from vulnerable 
communities characterized by:
Poverty or extreme poverty.
Limited access to quality education.
Risk of social exclusion and rights violations.
Through this support, we help 
create the conditions necessary 
for the holistic development 
of children, reaffirming our 
commitment to education for 
development and the creation 
of more equitable and protective 
environments.

## Pagina 267

Universidad de los Andes
In 2025, we supported the Universidad de los Andes 
through the “Vamos Pa’lante” program, an initiative 
aimed at promoting the retention and graduation 
of university students in Colombia who are at risk 
of dropping out due to financial difficulties.
Our contribution was directed toward reducing 
financial barriers that affect the academic continuity 
of talented young people, reaffirming our commitment 
to education for development and the creation of 
opportunities for social mobility through access to 
and retention in higher education.
Amount donated in 2025: $150.000.000 COP
The funds provided made it possible to:
Support the academic retention of students in 
economically vulnerable situations.
Reduce the risk of college dropout by mitigating 
financial factors that contribute to students leaving 
their studies.
Support vocational training programs, strengthening 
long-term educational trajectories.
The program directly benefited 14 students, whose 
main characteristics are:
Young people between the ages of 16 and 21.
Belonging to socioeconomic strata 1 through 4.
Students in academic programs other than 
medicine.
Individuals facing economic vulnerability that 
jeopardizes the continuity of their studies.
Through this support, we contribute to:
Preventing college dropout rates by strengthening 
student retention.
Eliminating financial barriers that limit access to 
and continuity in higher education.
Promote graduation of college students, 
expanding their opportunities for personal and 
professional development. Sponsorships with a social and business focus
We promote initiatives that generate social value, strengthen the business community, and 
contribute to the development of the regions where we operate through our sponsorship strategy. 
We direct this support toward fostering spaces for dialogue, training, and leadership, as well as 
supporting companies and startups that stimulate the economy and promote responsible practices.
In this way, we consolidate our sponsorships as a strategic tool to strengthen our relationships 
with our stakeholders and expand our positive impact in the social and productive spheres.
For details on the sponsorships we have undertaken, their scope, and 
main beneficiaries, we invite you to consult the Annex on Corporate 
Sponsorships and the Annex on Social Sponsorships.

## Pagina 268

Banca Gobierno and 
Its Social Impact
At Banca Gobierno, we support public entities in 
fulfilling their functions, convinced that responsible 
financial management also has a direct impact 
on the well-being of communities. Through our 
social contributions, we help strengthen the social, 
environmental, and economic development of the 
regions where these entities provide their services.
Our approach is based on voluntary contributions 
aimed at supporting initiatives that address the real 
needs of the population, especially in vulnerable 
contexts. These contributions take the form of 
actions such as the distribution of school supplies, 
toys, food aid, basic necessities, items for people 
with disabilities, and support during humanitarian 
emergencies, helping to improve the quality of life 
for children, families, and communities.
Main areas of social 
contribution:
Education and child welfare: distribution of school 
kits and toys, promoting school retention, inclusion, 
and access to recreational spaces.
Support for vulnerable populations: assistance 
to communities affected by emergencies, forced 
displacement, and adverse socioeconomic 
conditions.
Inclusion and disability: provision of items that 
enhance the autonomy, well-being, and inclusion 
of people with disabilities.
Support for rural communities: distribution of 
basic supplies and tools that help improve living 
conditions and local productivity.
Focus on Integrity and 
Transparency
All social contributions made through Banca 
Gobierno comply with the Bank’s internal policies, 
including the guidelines of the ABAC program, 
and are aligned with our strategic focus on social 
growth. This allows us to ensure that our actions are 
carried out in accordance with criteria of legality, 
transparency, and accountability, and that they 
contribute to generating a positive and sustainable 
impact on society.
Key Impacts Generated by 2025
 Relevant population coverage: positive 
impact on approximately 7.700 children aged 
3 to 15 who are socially and economically 
vulnerable, in both urban and rural areas 
across different regions of the country.
 Access to education and school retention: 
distribution of school kits, educational 
materials, and support for libraries, 
contributing to improved access to education 
and reduced risk of school dropout in 
communities in socioeconomic strata 1, 2, 
and 3.
 Emotional well-being and social inclusion:
strengthening the emotional well-being and 
social inclusion of at-risk children, victims of 
armed conflict, and the migrant population 
through the distribution of toys, Christmas 
gifts, and recreational activities.
 Comprehensive care for vulnerable 
communities: support for communities 
affected by poverty, emergencies, and 
limited access to basic services through the 
distribution of food aid, hygiene kits, and 
essential items.
 Inclusion of people with disabilities: 
distribution of wheelchairs and assistive 
devices, improving the mobility, autonomy, 
and quality of life of people with disabilities 
and older adults.
 Strengthening educational environments: 
equipping and renovating educational 
institutions, combining infrastructure, 
technology, volunteerism, and training to 
create safe, modern, and suitable spaces for 
learning.
 Wide territorial reach: impacts across 
multiple departments and municipalities 
nationwide, including Bogotá, Valle del Cauca, 
Atlántico, Bolívar, Boyacá, Cauca, Caquetá, 
Huila, Meta, Nariño, La Guajira, Santander, 
Norte de Santander, Quindío, Tolima, San 
Andrés, Cesar, and Sucre, among others.
 Fundación Educambio– Library Re￾equipping: provision of books with a 
differentiated approach, technological 
equipment, teaching materials, shelves made 
of recycled plastic, and training and follow￾up processes, benefiting 120 people.
We allocated 1.175.523,400 COP 
in donations nationwide
We directly impacted 19.888 
beneficiaries

Acknowledgments
At Banco de Occidente, we know that sustainability cannot be achieved 
alone: it is built on trust, purpose, and the daily efforts of many people. In a 
challenging year, the constant support of our stakeholders drove us to keep 
moving forward with responsibility, empathy, and a vision for the future.
We thank our employees for their commitment; our customers for their trust; 
our shareholders for supporting our strategy; our suppliers and strategic 
partners for their outstanding collaboration; the communities for allowing us 
to grow alongside them; and the authorities for their guidance and ongoing 
coordination.
This report is our commitment to transparency and accountability: a way 
of sharing where we stand, what we have learned, and where we are headed. 
We will continue to contribute to a more sustainable transition and to our 
blue planet, convinced that every responsible decision counts and that the 
future is built better when we do it together. Thank you for being part of this 
journey.

Independent Practitioner’s Limited Assurance Report 
Scope
We have performed a limited assurance engagement over the 
information detailed in Appendix A of this document (hereinafter, 
the “information subject to assurance”) of Banco de Occidente 
S.A. (hereinafter, the “Bank”), which will be included in the 
Management and Sustainability Report for the period from January 
1 to December 31, 2025.
Our limited assurance engagement was performed solely with 
respect to the selected sustainability information included in 
Annex A. Our assurance report does not extend to information 
from prior periods nor to any other information in the Management 
and Sustainability Report not included in Annex A, nor to any other 
information related to that Report which may contain images, 
audio, or video content. Accordingly, we do not express a 
conclusion or any other form of assurance on such information.
Responsibility of Banco de Occidente S.A. Management
Management is responsible for preparing the information subject 
to assurance in accordance with the following applicable criteria 
effective in 2025:
• Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards – Option of 
use: GRI‑Referenced.
• Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) 
Standards for the Commercial Banks sector.
• Criteria of the Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) 
questionnaire of S&P ESG – Sustainable1. 
• Criteria defined by the Bank for the review of the current 
double materiality analysis.
Management is also responsible for selecting the applicable 
criteria used.
The preparation of the information subject to assurance requires 
Management to establish and interpret the criteria, determine the 
relevance of the information to be included, and make estimates 
and assumptions that affect the reported information. 
Management’s selection of different, yet acceptable, 
measurement techniques, estimates, or assumptions could have 
resulted in materially different amounts or metrics. Obtaining 
sufficient and appropriate evidence to support our limited 
assurance conclusion does not reduce the inherent uncertainty in 
the amounts and disclosures.
Management is also responsible for the internal control it deems 
necessary to enable the preparation of the information subject to 
assurance that is free from material misstatement, whether due 
to fraud or error.
Our Independence and Quality Management
We have complied with the Code of Ethics for Professional 
Accountants issued by the International Ethics Standards Board for 
Accountants (IESBA), together with the relevant ethical 
requirements in Colombia, and we have fulfilled the other 
applicable ethical responsibilities, which are based on the 
fundamental principles of integrity, objectivity, professional 
competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional 
behavior.
The firm applies the International Standard on Quality 
Management 1 (ISQM 1) – Quality Management for Firms that 
Perform Audits or Reviews of Financial Statements, or Other 
Assurance or Related Services Engagements, which requires the 
firm to design, implement, and operate a system of quality 
management that includes policies or procedures related to 
compliance with ethical requirements, professional standards, and 
applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
Our Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express a limited assurance conclusion on 
the information subject to review, based on the procedures we 
have performed and the evidence we have obtained. We 
conducted our limited assurance engagement in accordance with 
the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 
(Revised), Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of 
Historical Financial Information, issued by the International 
Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB). This standard 
requires us to conclude whether anything has come to our 
attention that causes us to believe that the information detailed 
in Annex A has not been prepared, in all material respects, in 
accordance with the applicable criteria.
A limited assurance engagement is substantially narrower in scope 
than a reasonable assurance engagement, both in terms of the risk 
assessment procedures—including the understanding of internal 
control—and in the procedures performed in response to the 
assessed risks.
Our engagement included, among others, the following 
procedures performed:
a) Through inquiries, we obtained an understanding of the Bank’s 
relevant control environment and information systems; 
however, we did not evaluate the design of specific control 
activities, nor did we obtain evidence regarding their 
implementation, nor did we test their operating effectiveness.
b) Understanding of the tools used to generate, aggregate, and 
report the information subject to assurance through inquiries 
with those responsible for the related processes.
c) Understanding, inquiry with management‑designated 
representatives, and verification of the process carried out by 
the Bank in 2025 for the review of its double materiality 
analysis, including the participation of its stakeholders in this 
process. 
d) Interviews with Bank personnel to understand its business and 
the process for preparing the 2025 Management and 
Sustainability Report.
e) Interviews with corporate‑level Bank personnel responsible for 
the information to be reported, to understand the process for 
collecting, consolidating, and presenting the information 
subject to assurance.
f) Verification of the calculation criteria and their appropriate 
application in accordance with the methodologies described in 
the criteria for the indicators subject to assurance, as defined 
in the scope indicated in Annex A.
g) Performance of analytical procedures to support the 
reasonableness of the data.
h) Comparison of the information presented in the Management 
and Sustainability Report with the corresponding underlying 
sources to determine whether such information has been 
included in the 2025 Management and Sustainability Report.
1. Assurance 
Letter
Página 2 de 6
i) Analysis of the data collection processes and internal controls 
over the quantitative information reflected in the Report, in 
terms of the reliability of the information, using analytical 
procedures and verification tests based on sampling.
j) Reading of the information to be included in the 2025 
Management and Sustainability Report to compare it against 
the criteria defined by GRI 1 – Foundations, GRI 2 – General 
Disclosures, and GRI 3 – Material Topics, applicable according 
to the declaration of use applied by the Bank. These 
procedures were performed based on the version of the 
Management and Sustainability Report provided by the Bank to 
BDO on March 10, 2026.
k) Application of substantive procedures on a selective, random 
basis over the information subject to assurance, prepared by 
Management, to determine the standards and indicators and to 
corroborate that the data were measured, recorded, 
compiled, and reported appropriately through:
i. Inspection of policies and procedures established by 
the Bank.
ii. Inspection of supporting documents from internal and 
external sources.
iii. Recalculations.
iv. Comparisons of the information presented by 
Management with what is established in the criteria 
referenced in this report.
The information subject to assurance included within the scope of 
our work is detailed in Annex A.
The procedures performed in a limited assurance engagement vary 
in nature and timing and are less extensive than those performed 
in a reasonable assurance engagement. Consequently, the level of 
assurance obtained is substantially lower than the assurance that 
would have been obtained had a reasonable assurance engagement 
been performed.
We consider that the evidence obtained is sufficient and 
appropriate to provide a reasonable basis for our conclusion.
Significant Inherent Limitations
The selected sustainability information is subject to inherent 
uncertainty due to the use of non‑financial information, which is 
subject to greater inherent limitations than financial information, 
given the nature of the methods used to determine, calculate, 
sample, or estimate such information. In preparing the selected 
information, the entity makes qualitative interpretations 
regarding the relevance, materiality, and accuracy of the 
information, which are subject to assumptions and judgments.
Conclusion of Limited Assurance
Based on the procedures performed and the evidence obtained, 
nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe that 
the information subject to assurance, as indicated in Annex A of 
this report—and which will be included in the Bank’s 2025 
Management and Sustainability Report for the period from January 
1 to December 31, 2025—has not been prepared, in all material 
respects, in accordance with the applicable criteria referenced in 
Annex A.
Other Matter
Our assurance engagement does not extend to information relating 
to prior periods.
Restriction on Use of This Report
This report is issued exclusively for the purpose described in the 
first paragraph and must not be used for any other purpose nor 
distributed separately to other parties. This report relates solely 
to the matters addressed in the preceding sections and the
information subject to assurance included in Annex A, and does 
not extend to any other financial or non‑financial information 
included in the Bank’s Management and Sustainability Report for 
the period from January 1 to December 31, 2025, nor to its 
financial statements taken as a whole.
Action Plans
BDO Audit S.A.S BIC provides the Bank, through an additional 
report, with recommendations for the future preparation of the 
Management and Sustainability Report. These recommendations 
do not modify the conclusion expressed in this report and are 
intended to strengthen the Bank’s processes for developing, 
managing, measuring, reviewing, reporting, and communicating 
its sustainability indicators.

Dow Jones 1.5.3 - 
CSA
Crime Prevention: Business Policy/ Procedures
Crime Prevention: Corporate Policy and Procedures
Assured text: 
During 2025, we continued safeguarding one of the Bank’s most important assets: trust. We reaffirmed our commitment to 
transparency, financial security, and the protection of our clients against risks associated with fraud and other practices that 
may compromise the integrity of the system. To this end, we maintained and strengthened prevention, detection, and 
incident‑management strategies aligned with regulatory standards and industry best practices. Our approach combines 
preventive actions with timely response measures, not only to protect clients but also to contribute to the stability of the 
financial system—one of the key pillars of our sustainable management.
By promoting a secure and trustworthy environment, we strengthen market confidence and facilitate financial inclusion, 
ensuring that more individuals and businesses can access financial services under safe conditions. To maintain these results, we 
operate under internal controls and compliance policies that reinforce the prevention of misconduct and the mitigation of risks. 
This management is grounded in principles of integrity, transparency, and accountability, and seeks to ensure that employees,
clients, and strategic partners operate within a trustworthy financial environment fully aligned with applicable regulations.
In parallel, we have specific mechanisms for managing legal risk, enabling us to monitor and anticipate situations that may 
result in litigation. When we receive notification of a legal proceeding, a report is immediately sent to the Operational Risk 
area for analysis, follow‑up, and the definition of mitigation measures.
At Banco de Occidente, we operate under strong ethical principles, understanding that integrity is not only a compliance 
requirement but the foundation of trust and the way we conduct business. This commitment contributes to building a more 
equitable society and a more transparent economic system, fostering responsible practices that reinforce our values across the 
organization. This approach is supported by our Internal and External Fraud Management Process Policy and forms part of the 
ABAC program. Our Fraud Management Process Policy and the associated compliance initiatives aim to prevent and mitigate 
legal and financial risks while strengthening market confidence and relationships with our stakeholders.
We implement rigorous internal controls; conduct periodic training on corporate values and business ethics for our employees;
develop awareness activities for suppliers to promote a culture of integrity across the value chain; and provide confidential
reporting channels that facilitate the timely detection and management of any irregularities. In this way, we consolidate a 
transparent business environment aligned with our ESG strategy and continuously improving to address the challenges of a 
demanding and constantly evolving regulatory landscape.
The ABAC policy also enables us to prioritize activities that, due to their nature, may involve greater exposure to corruption 
risk. These include donations, sponsorships, contributions to social programs under the sustainability model, the acceptance 
and/or offering of gifts and invitations, public or political contributions, and merger or acquisition processes.
Oversight of this management is carried out by the management teams under the Risk and Collections Vice‑Presidency, which 
report results to the various committees. Furthermore, the Board of Directors’ Comprehensive Risk Committee (CIR)—chaired 
by an independent member—meets quarterly to supervise management, monitor the risk profile, and verify that policies and 
procedures remain adequate. The CIR also advises the Board of Directors on operations, events, or activities that may affect 
risk exposure and profile, approves adjustments to the SIAR, and promotes continuous monitoring of risk culture.
The Compliance Officer oversees the risk of money laundering and reports directly to the President, presenting detailed reports 
to the Board of Directors each quarter.
Independent Audits and Evaluation
Annually, KPMG performs an internal audit of the management of the different types of risks. The results of these audits have
generally been satisfactory; when improvement opportunities are identified, each risk specialty develops action plans to address 
gaps, which are monitored and reported to the corresponding committees. In addition, our Holding has a Corporate 
Comptroller’s Office that periodically evaluates the risk management processes of the various entities.

Privacy Policy: Systems/ Procedures
Assured text:
Communication to clients regarding privacy and data protection
For us, transparency is also a form of protection. Therefore, we inform our clients clearly and in a timely manner about our 
Personal Data Processing Policy, which is available for consultation on our institutional website. Additionally, when a security 
incident occurs that may compromise personal data, we activate the necessary mechanisms to inform potentially affected clients,
in compliance with Law 1581 of 2012 and under an approach centered on care and timeliness.
Regulatory compliance and normative reference
• In matters related to personal data, we conduct our management in alignment with Law 1581 of 2012, strengthening practices 
for the responsible processing of information.
• To guide our model and ensure consistency, we use recognized frameworks such as ISO 27001:2022 and NIST (v2.0) as 
reference points. These frameworks help us evaluate and enhance our capabilities without relying solely on formal 
certification.
External assessments and monitoring
• To complement our internal management, we conduct assessment exercises: in 2024, we shared the results of an external 
evaluation performed by EY.
• During 2025, we advanced in an evaluation with Deloitte, which was still in progress at the close of the reporting period, as
part of our effort to understand our maturity level, prioritize gaps, and strengthen action plans.
Critical third parties: compliance verification
• Although we do not perform vulnerability analyses on third parties using internal Bank tools, we do carry out compliance 
verification visits to critical third parties in information security and cybersecurity, with support from Incocrédito, including 
questions related to vulnerability management.

Verification procedures were performed through observation, inquiry, 
and inspection of documentation related to the review of the

the Bank’s key portfolio.

• A survey addressed to the Vice Presidents to obtaining an updated 
and strategic perspective on institutional priorities.
These procedures enabled a more structured review of the most 
relevant ESG matters within the current business context and its 
operating environment, thereby supporting alignment between the 
sustainability strategy and the Bank’s organizational purpose.

line with DJSI guidelines and current accounting standards. This methodology considers total revenue, operating 
expenses, and employee-related expenses.

range compared to previous years and, although it shows a slight decrease from 2024 (3,91), reflects stability 
in the efficiency of human capital utilization and the continuity of strategies focused on productivity, labor cost 
optimization, and the strengthening of talent management, in line with international sustainability standards.

Chapter on Responsible Growth and Comprehensive Risk Management, we have a section titled "Information 
Security, Cybersecurity, and System Availability" 
In 2025, the bank did not experience any data breach incidents or accidents; however, one of its suppliers did: 
there was a data breach incident involving a vendor acting as the processor of the bank’s customer database, 
which suffered a ransomware attack; 26.533 pieces of customer personal data were compromised. As a corrective 
measure, direct communication between the vendor and the bank was suspended until the vendor was certified as 
secure, and the internal security protocol and crisis management team were activated.
107 X
Information 
security, 
cybersecurity, and 
system availability 
SASB 
FN-CB-230a.2 Description of 
the approach to identifying 
and addressing data security 
risks
Cybersecurity
Our management is supported by an information security framework that brings together guidelines, practices, and 
controls to protect our clients’ and the Bank’s information. To remain aligned with recognized best practices, we use 
international standards such as ISO 27001:2022, NIST 800-53 (v2.0), and local regulations such as the regulatory 
circulars issued by the Colombian Financial Superintendency regarding compliance with security and cybersecurity 
controls. We periodically review our approach to adapt it to changes in the environment and the evolution of our digital 
services.
We also test our capabilities. We complement our internal audit and corporate compliance functions with assessment 
exercises that help us identify opportunities for improvement and prioritize actions. In recent processes, we shared the 
results of an external assessment conducted in 2024 with the consulting firm Ernest & Young (EY), and during 2025 we 
made progress on a new assessment with Deloitte, which was ongoing at the end of the period.
Under the leadership of the Vice Presidency of Operations and Technology, together with the Vice Presidency of Risk, 
technical and risk management teams are coordinated, taking into account the risk assessment model (ANX-APY-1186). 
Monthly follow-ups are managed with the Information Security Committee, guided by the principle of continuous 
improvement.
In 2025, we strengthened our prevention efforts with a simple principle: “the earlier we identify a risk, the lower its 
impact.” That is why we combine controls, monitoring, and continuous improvements to protect information and 
maintain the stability of our services. This approach allows us to act before a threat becomes an incident and to 
support the growth of our digital channels with confidence.

FN-CB-550a.1 Score in

Important Bank (G-SIB) 
assessment, by category
Chapter: Responsible Growth and Comprehensive Risk Management 
Subchapter: Strategic Management of Financial and Non-Financial Risks 
Section: Global Systemically Important Banks 
In accordance with Circular Letter 068 of 2025 from the Financial Superintendency of Colombia (SFC) and in 
compliance with paragraph 2.1.1.4.3 of Decree 2555 of 2010, the SFC published the list of Systemically Important 
Institutions (SIIs) for fiscal year 2026, based on the methodology defined for their identification. For this calculation, 
information as of June 30, 2025, submitted to the Financial System Coordination and Monitoring Committee, was 
used. 
With these results, we ranked third, with a score of 9,58%, above the threshold of 6,45%, meaning that for the first 
time we were considered a systemically important bank. It is important to note that this classification does not 
represent a risk assessment or rating of the institutions. 
In this context, the Bank must continue to build the additional buffer for systemic institutions, equivalent to 1% of 
assets weighted for credit, market, and operational risk, in accordance with the instructions and deadlines issued by 
the SFC in Resolution No. 2629 of December 27, 2024.

consequences. The accident rate was 3,0, showing a decrease compared to 2024. The severity and frequency rates 
also decreased, standing at 1,67 and 0,60, respectively. Psychosocial and biomechanical risks associated with 
administrative activities were primarily identified. The Bank maintains 100% coverage of employees and contractors 
under the SG-SST and continues to strengthen prevention, training, and epidemiological surveillance programs.

At Banco de Occidente, we distinguish ourselves by promoting respect for the differences that define us as human 
beings. Thanks to this culture, to date it has not been necessary to implement specific actions to mitigate or resolve 
situations related to discrimination for any reason. 
However, we have clear provisions in our Code of Ethics and Conduct that expressly prohibit all employees from 
engaging in discriminatory conduct. Additionally, we continuously review our processes to ensure that inclusive and 
respectful language is used. An example of this is the update to our dress code protocol, “Mi Estilo BdeO,” which now 
uses gender-neutral language.

## Pagina 306

4. TCFD Report
Task Force on Climate￾related Financial 
Disclosures (TCFD)
A Strong Commitment 
to Addressing the 
Climate Crisis
At Banco de Occidente, we recognize that climate 
change is one of the most complex and urgent 
challenges facing humanity in the 21st century. We 
view it not merely as an environmental risk, but as 
a critical variable that is reshaping markets, public 
policy, and social behavior. For this reason, we 
have taken on the responsibility to act not merely 
as observers of this transformation, but as financial 
catalysts driving resilience and sustainability in every 
sector we support.
Our commitment is not new; since 2022, we have 
rigorously implemented our roadmap for adopting 
the Task Force on Climate-related Financial 
Disclosures (TCFD) framework. This process has 
marked a turning point in our organizational culture, 
allowing us to transition from a traditional view of 
social responsibility toward a technical and strategic 
integration of climate risk into our governance 
structure and credit decision-making.
Through this report, we share the progress made in 
identifying and assessing the physical and transition 
risks that could affect our portfolio. At the same time, 
we highlight the opportunities emerging from the 
green economy, which allow us to design innovative 
financial products that support our clients in their 
own transition toward decarbonization. We are 
convinced that transparency in the disclosure of 
this data is essential to building trust and stability 
in the Colombian financial system.
Looking ahead, we reaffirm that 
our strategy is aligned with global 
mitigation and adaptation goals. At 
Banco de Occidente, we continue 
to strengthen our metrics and 
objectives to ensure that every 
investment and every loan granted 
contributes to a development 
model that is economically viable, 
socially just, and, above all, climate￾responsible.

Sustainability Strategy
Occidente, we integrate climate change management 
across the board into our sustainability strategy and 
into the way we create long-term value. Through 
Planeta Azul, we focus our actions on mitigating 
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and adapting 
to climate change, the responsible use of natural 
resources, and environmental conservation, consistent 
with responsible management of climate-related 
risks and opportunities.
We align our strategy with the pillars of transparency, 
profitable growth, social value creation, and the 
development of our people. Additionally, we align with 
international frameworks such as the United Nations 
Global Compact, the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs), and industry best practices, strengthening 
the resilience of our business and our contribution 
to the country’s sustainable development. We create 
meaningful experiences for our customers and build

Climate Governance 
Structure
We base our climate governance on a clear and well￾defined organizational structure, where we assign 
specific roles and responsibilities to manage the risks 
and opportunities associated with climate change 
and sustainability. This structure allows us to integrate 
climate and ESG criteria into strategic decision￾making, risk management, and business operations. 
Thus, we ensure oversight from the highest levels of 
corporate governance and coordinated execution 
across all key areas of our institution.

## Pagina 313

In 2025, Banco de Occidente 
began strengthening its climate 
governance through a structured 
process of defining and formalizing 
strategic roles, aimed at more 
consistently integrating climate 
change management into existing 
risk management, internal control, 
and strategic decision-making 
systems. This process included 
consultation sessions with key 
departments and the design and 
refinement of an updated climate 
governance model, which will be 
submitted for approval by Senior 
Management.
As part of this process, six two-hour training and 
awareness-raising sessions were held for employees 
and key decision-making bodies such as risk, credit, 
and sustainability committees and teams, with the 
aim of strengthening internal capabilities regarding 
climate change, environmental risks, and sustainable 
finance. The sessions addressed fundamental 
concepts of climate change, physical and transition 
risks, regulatory trends, and climate analysis tools, 
promoting a consistent and cross-functional 
understanding of climate risks and opportunities 
within the organization.
These activities were attended by more than 30 
employees from areas such as sustainability, credit 
risk, market, liquidity, and operations, as well as 
financial planning and commercial units within 
Corporate Banking and Retail Banking, helping to 
strengthen ownership of the climate approach and 
support the progressive implementation of the Bank’s 
climate governance model.
Lines of Defense in Climate 
Governance
To strengthen the management and control of climate 
risks, Banco de Occidente has adopted a three￾line-of-defense governance model, which enables 
an appropriate separation of duties, greater control, 
and comprehensive management aligned with the 
General Risk Management System.
First line of defense: The Bank’s operational areas 
that integrate climate change considerations into 
the execution of processes, in accordance with 
corporate governance guidelines and current 
regulations, to prevent the materialization of risks.
Second line of defense: The Vice Presidency 
of Risk and its departments, responsible for 
assessing, measuring, monitoring, and mitigating 
risks—including those associated with climate 
change—to support comprehensive management 
and decision-making.
Third line of defense: Audit Department, responsible 
for conducting independent assurance activities 
to verify the effectiveness of the internal control 
system and its alignment with the Bank’s strategy.

Climate Policies and 
Enablers 
Environmental and Climate 
Change Policy of Banco de 
Occidente and Subsidiaries
Environmental and 
Climate Change 
At Banco de Occidente, we have a set of commitments, 
policies, and guidelines that guide our decisions and 
operations regarding ESG issues and enable us to 
progressively integrate climate change management 
into our strategy, risk management, and business 
operations.
The Sustainability Strategy serves as the guiding 
framework for these policies and directs the Bank’s 
ESG initiatives, contributing to its positioning as a 
leader in sustainability within the financial sector. 
This Strategy was updated in 2025 to establish 
clear, measurable objectives aligned with current 
challenges, structured around five strategic 
commitments:
We contribute to climate change mitigation and 
adaptation by reducing our environmental impact. 
We strengthen corporate governance through 
ethical and responsible practices.
We promote sustainable businesses that contribute 
to the country’s economic, social, and environmental 
development. 
The Environmental and Climate Change Policy 
constitutes the primary institutional framework for 
climate change management at Banco de Occidente 
and its subsidiaries. This policy establishes the 
general principles that guide the development of 
initiatives aligned with the Sustainability Strategy, 
integrating environmental management into business 
operations, decision-making, and risk management.
This policy defines guidelines related to regulatory 
compliance and voluntary commitments, the 
measurement and offsetting of the carbon footprint, 
the implementation of eco-efficiency practices, 
the promotion of thematic financing, climate risk 
management, and the strengthening of internal and 
supply chain capabilities.
1Support compliance with the country’s current 
environmental regulations applicable to our

subsidiaries operate, as well as the voluntary 
commitments to which it adheres.
We create meaningful experiences for our 
customers and build partnerships to support 
regional development. 
We foster a work environment where we promote 
the comprehensive development of talent.
It also defines procedures with a direct impact, 
such as measuring and offsetting the carbon 
footprint, setting climate targets, and managing 
risks associated with climate change, all of which 
support the Bank’s comprehensive risk management. 
In addition, it includes actions with an indirect 
impact, such as measuring indirect emissions and 
participating in climate mitigation, adaptation, and 
financing initiatives.

At Banco de Occidente, we have a 
set of policies and guidelines that 
support the progressive alignment 
of our environmental, social, 
and corporate governance 
(ESG) management with climate 
challenges. While these frameworks 
were not created exclusively for 
climate management, we have 
consolidated them as strategic 
enablers that allow us to integrate 
sustainability considerations 
into every decision and the daily 
operations of our business.
Social Investment Policy
It recognizes Banco de Occidente’s role as a key 
player in the development of people, regions, 
and the country. This policy defines a strategic 
approach to prioritize, implement, and monitor social 
investments, ensuring their alignment with corporate 
objectives, the Sustainability Strategy, the Sustainable 
Development Goals, and the principles of ethics and 
transparency. It also highlights the importance of 
having indicators and methodologies to measure 
the impact of these investments and establishes 
clear approval mechanisms and guidelines for 
unauthorized practices.
Human Rights Policy
This policy defines Banco de Occidente’s commitment 
to respecting, protecting, and remedying the 
human rights of its stakeholders. It establishes 
specific guidelines for employees, customers, and 
partners, promoting a respectful work environment, 
equal opportunities, access to clear and accurate 
information, the protection of personal data, and 
treatment free from discrimination in all interactions.
Sustainable Finance Guidelines
These guidelines direct the incorporation of ESG 
criteria into project financing, asset financing, and 
working capital financing operations across all of 
the Bank’s segments. These guidelines aim to offer 
financing opportunities that promote responsible and 
sustainable practices and incorporate the Bank’s 
Sustainable Taxonomy—based on Colombia’s 
Green Taxonomy—as a tool for classifying and 
monitoring operations.
Environmental and Social Risk 
Management System (SARAS) 
Policy
This policy establishes the Bank’s commitment to 
managing environmental and social risks in the credit 
evaluation and origination process, with the aim 
of minimizing the likelihood of negative impacts 
and directing financial flows toward activities 
that demonstrate responsible stewardship of the 
environment and society.

This policy applies to the commercial portfolio and 
is grounded in principles such as respect for human 
rights, protection of nature, and prevention, mitigation, 
and adaptation to climate change. SARAS includes 
a list of excluded activities, the categorization of 
clients according to their level of environmental 
and social risk, assessment using specific tools, and 
monitoring of clients with the highest risk exposure.
SARAS Manual
It makes the Environmental and Social Risk 
Management System operational by defining 
clear roles, responsibilities, and tools for the areas 
involved. The manual outlines six stages, from the 
initial screening based on the exclusion list to the 
final evaluation of results and details the steps and 
components necessary to ensure the system functions 
properly.
This set of policies and internal frameworks enables 
the Bank to manage the risks and opportunities 
associated with climate change in a cross-cutting 
manner, strengthening the coherence between 
strategy, risk management, and business operations.
Climate Strategy and 
Long-Term Horizon
At Banco de Occidente, we have made steady progress 
in adopting and implementing a comprehensive 
climate strategy aimed at identifying, managing, 
and mitigating climate risks, as well as seizing 
opportunities for decarbonization and strengthening 
resilience. Our roadmap operates in phases and 
integrates risk management, the identification of 
opportunities, and the implementation of actions 
aligned with national goals and international best 
practices.
Our approach seeks to contribute 
to the country’s climate goals, 
maintain the carbon neutrality of 
our operations, and strengthen 
the resilience of our clients and the 
financed portfolio, with a long-term 
vision toward 2050.

## Pagina 319

Risks arising from 
climate change
As part of our climate strategy and in line with 
TCFD recommendations, at Banco de Occidente we 
conduct a comprehensive analysis of risks arising from 
climate change. Our goal is to anticipate potential 
impacts on our operations, our portfolio, and our 
long-term strategy. This process has enabled us to 
strengthen risk management, guide decision-making, 
and advance the implementation of GHG mitigation, 
adaptation, and climate resilience measures.
For the analysis of climate risks, we consider two 
broad categories, based on their nature and how 
they materialize:
Physical Risks
These are risks associated with the direct and indirect 
effects of climate change on assets, operations, and 
the regions where both we and our clients operate. 
These risks are classified into two main groups:
1.
Acute physical risks: associated with 
sudden-onset extreme weather events, 
such as floods, landslides, cyclones, 
heat waves, and flash floods, which 
can immediately affect operational 
continuity and the portfolio.
Chronic physical risks: related 
to gradual, long-term changes in 
climate patterns, such as variations in 
precipitation patterns, rising average 
temperatures, increased climate 
variability, and sea-level rise, with 
progressive impacts on economic 
sectors and regions. 2.
In this process, we identified eight physical risks, 
of which 62% are acute risks and 38% are chronic 
risks. Since most of these events are expected 
to materialize in the short and medium term, we 
prioritize strengthening our prevention, mitigation, 
and adaptation measures to protect the stability of 
our portfolio.
Distribution of physical risks by 
time horizon
In our analysis of climate risks, we consider different 
time horizons, thereby assessing their potential 
occurrence in the short, medium, and long term, 
as well as their potential financial impact.

## Pagina 321

Transition risks 
These are risks arising from changes in the political, 
technological, and market environment associated 
with the transition to a low-carbon economy. 
Depending on the nature, speed, and scope of these 
changes, transition risks can have varying impacts 
on organizations and economic sectors.
According to the TCFD framework, these risks are 
classified into four main categories: political and 
legal, technological, market, and reputational 
risks, which may affect the strategy, operations, and 
financial performance of the Bank and our clients.
In this process, we identified 12 transition risks, of 
which 62% correspond to market, policy, and legal 
risks, primarily associated with current regulatory 
changes, emerging regulatory requirements, as 
well as shifts in demand and adjustments to the 
business models of the sectors we finance; 23% 
correspond to reputational risks; and the remaining 
15% correspond technology risks.

already materialized recently in 
the country through events such

accounting for 54%. This highlights 
the importance of anticipating them 
and progressively integrating them 
into our strategy, risk management, 
and financial planning.

Financial Impact Assessment 
Methodology
We strengthen our climate assessment methodologies, 
tools, and criteria, aligning them with regulatory 
and market best practices. To this end, we have 
implemented a specialized tool that allows us to 
assess the criticality level of climate risks using a 
stochastic, non-deterministic approach, which 
has remained in effect and unchanged since its 
adoption, ensuring the consistency and comparability 
of the analyses conducted.
Unlike point estimates, this model accounts for future 
uncertainty and assigns probability distribution 
functions to the analyzed variables. This allows us 
to simulate ranges of outcomes in terms of frequency 
and severity, significantly strengthening our analytical 
capabilities.
For each prioritized risk, we identify the climate 
parameters associated with its cause, integrating 
historical trends and future projections specific
to Colombia. These projections are based on highly 
rigorous technical sources, such as the scenarios 
from the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors 
for a Greener Financial System (NGFS) and the 
models from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate 
Change (IPCC), available through the platform of the 
International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis 
(IIASA).
Finally, we link climate data to our operational and 
financial variables, which allows us to estimate the 
financial impact on two fronts: opportunity costs 
(lost revenue) and direct impacts (potential losses in 
our portfolio due to extreme events that compromise 
our customers’ ability to pay).

Climate Change 
Management 2025
Throughout 2025, at Banco de Occidente we 
continue to make decisive progress in our climate 
management. Currently, we are consolidating the 
integration of climate risk into our comprehensive 
risk management system, working to incorporate it 
more consistently into strategic decision-making.
Key Progress and 
Actions 2025
Approximately 36,49% reduction 
in paper use in offices compared 
to the 2022 baseline; this result is 
due to the strengthening of digital 
channels and platforms.
A 28,9% reduction in total 
emissions compared to 2024 and 
approximately 44% compared to 
the 2022 baseline. 
Manufacturing 100% of credit cards 
with 85% recycled PVC, promoting 
circular economy practices.

Possible – WWF” course, aimed 
at biodiversity conservation and the 
adoption of responsible actions.
Strengthening of the Planeta Azul 
Community as a space for raising 
awareness and fostering citizen 
engagement in environmental.
Promotion of sustainable mobility

with the participation of more than

Exposure of the portfolio 
to climate risks by sector

As part of the implementation of the TCFD 
recommendations and in accordance with the 
guidelines of the Colombian Banking Association, 
at Banco de Occidente we conducted a detailed 
classification of our loan portfolio by economic 
sector, based on the International Standard 
Industrial Classification (ISIC). This analysis aims 
to assess and manage sectoral exposure to climate 
risks, considering the nature of the financed activities 
and their level of vulnerability to physical events 
and transition risks. We segment our portfolio into 
three exposure levels—high, medium, and low—
which allows us to prioritize support efforts for risk 
management and the exploitation of opportunities 
with a positive fiscal impact in the short, medium, 
and long term for our clients. 
This segmentation enables us to precisely identify 
the areas requiring greater attention and proactive 
management, facilitating strategic decision-making 
and the development of policies that strengthen our 
resilience and sustainability in the face of climate 
challenges. In line with these efforts, during 2024 
we conducted stress tests by geography and sector, 
identifying latent risks in the portfolio that allowed 
us to establish mitigation plans to minimize our 
exposure.
As a result of this process, we found that the cost 
of provisions is significantly higher in an adverse 
scenario involving risks stemming from climate 
change than in the other scenarios evaluated, which 
reaffirms the need to integrate these variables into 
our long-term financial planning.
To strengthen this process, in 2025 the Bank 
developed a structured tool for identifying, assessing, 
and prioritizing physical and transition climate risks, 
applicable at both the sectoral and client levels. 
This methodology considers variables of exposure, 
sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, as well as 
geographic location, economic sector (ISIC), and 
reference climate scenarios, including scenarios 
for the transition to net-zero emissions. This allows 
for the estimation of inherent risk and its consistent 
classification, enhancing comparability and informed 
decision-making.
Additionally, the tool incorporates a risk management 
component that enables the identification of existing 
controls, the estimation of residual risk, and the 
assurance of traceability between identified climate 
risks, implemented mitigants, and remaining gaps. 
This approach facilitates the integration of climate 
risk into traditional risk management processes—
such as credit analysis and sectoral assessment—in 
line with TCFD recommendations and international 
best practices.

Trend Analysis of Climate 
Exposure (2022–2025)
To identify trends in the portfolio’s exposure, we 
conducted a comparative analysis for the years 
2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, revealing the following 
findings:
The percentage of the portfolio classified as 
medium climate risk increased by 10 percentage 
points in 2024 compared to the levels observed 
in 2022 and 2023, and remains stable in 2025.
This increase is due to a greater concentration in 
divisions associated with:
Water collection, treatment, and distribution, 
including the operation of irrigation canals, 
water purification, and the supply of water for 
domestic and industrial use, which is linked to 
the water crisis currently affecting the country, 
as evidenced by water rationing in Bogotá.
Installation, maintenance, and specialized 
repair of machinery and equipment.
Manufacture of other non-metallic mineral 
products, activities related to the gradual 
recovery of the construction sector following 
the COVID-19 pandemic.
Key sectors at high climate risk 
in 2025
In 2025, the five divisions with the highest exposure 
to climate risk account for nearly 25% of the total 
portfolio value, with the same categories identified 
in 2024 remaining, although with changes in their relative order. Civil engineering works now ranks first in 
terms of exposure, while food manufacturing drops to third place. The Transportation, Building Construction, 
and Electricity, Gas, Steam, and Air Conditioning Supply sectors remain within the group with the highest 
exposure, demonstrating a consistent sectoral concentration regarding climate risk.

A. Civil Engineering and 
Building Construction
The civil engineering and building construction 
sectors account for a significant portion of the Bank’s 
portfolio and share significant exposure to climate 
risks, given their dependence on physical assets, 
natural resources, and environmental conditions. 
In 2025, the civil engineering sector reached a 
criticality level of 6,40%, ranking first, up from third 
place in 2024, indicating an increase in its relevance 
within the portfolio’s climate exposure. Meanwhile, 
the building construction sector remained in fifth 
place, with a criticality of 3,61%, showing relative 
stability compared to the previous year.
From a transition risk perspective, both sectors 
face growing pressure to incorporate low-emission 
construction technologies and energy efficiency 
criteria, which implies greater investments and 
adjustments to business models. Added to this is a 
greater market preference for sustainable projects, 
which may affect demand for projects that do not 
incorporate stricter environmental standards and limit 
access to financing for carbon-intensive activities.
Regarding physical risks, exposure to extreme 
weather events such as heavy rains, floods, droughts, 
and, in the long term, sea-level rise can lead to 
project delays, higher construction, insurance, 
and maintenance costs, as well as impacts on the 
productivity and viability of infrastructure. These 
factors underscore the need to advance resilient 
designs and construction practices adapted to 
current and future climate conditions.

B. Electricity, Gas, 
Steam, and Air 
Conditioning Supply
The electricity, gas, steam, and air conditioning 
supply sector is strategic for the functioning of the 
economy and the well-being of society, as it provides 
essential services to households, industry, and regions. 
In Colombia, this sector includes the generation, 
transmission, and distribution of electricity, the 
production and distribution of gas, and the supply 
of thermal services, all of which are highly relevant 
to the continuity of economic operations.
From a transition risk perspective, the sector faces 
challenges associated with rapid technological 
transformation and shifts in market preferences. 
The decline in renewable energy costs and the 
need to transition away from fossil fuel-based 
technologies create risks of asset obsolescence, 
pressure on profitability, and a reconfiguration of the 
energy supply. Additionally, volatility in energy and 
commodity prices, along with regulatory uncertainty, 
can affect the viability of certain business models, 
while reputational risks associated with carbon￾intensive activities influence the decisions of investors 
and consumers.
Regarding physical risks, the country’s high 
dependence on hydroelectric generation exposes the 
sector to climate events such as prolonged droughts, 
water stress, floods, and heat waves, which can affect 
resource availability, operational efficiency, and the 
integrity of energy infrastructure. In the long term, 
chronic risks such as rising average temperatures, 
changes in precipitation patterns, and sea-level 
rise may cause structural disruptions in the energy 
supply chain and higher adaptation costs.
As a result of this analysis, in 2025 this sector is 
classified as high-risk, representing 5,53% of the 
Bank’s portfolio, which reinforces the need for 
continuous monitoring, proactive management of 
climate risks, and support for clients in their transition 
toward more resilient and sustainable energy models.

Decrease in energy demand for heating and increase 
in demand for cooling. Conflicts with communities 
over scarce resources such as water. 
Changes in seasonal energy demand and increases 
in peak demand during periods of extreme heat or 
other conditions. 
Water stress and higher water temperatures reduce 
energy production and operational capacity in thermal 
generation.
Increased electricity losses in transmission and

C. Food Processing
Food processing is a key sector for the country’s 
food security and economic development, but it is 
highly exposed to climate risks that can impact its 
financial and operational performance. In 2025, this 
sector accounted for 5,42% of the Bank’s portfolio, 
ranking third in terms of criticality, down from first 
place in 2024, reflecting a shift in risk composition 
and concentration.
From a transition risk perspective, the sector faces 
pressures associated with the adoption of lower￾emission technologies, shifts in consumer preferences 
toward more sustainable products, and commodity 
price volatility—factors that directly affect costs, 
demand, and business models. In terms of physical 
risks, exposure to droughts, floods, and heat waves 
remains significant, with potential impacts on 
production cycles, the availability of inputs, and 
the stability of supply chains.
Additionally, the legal and reputational risks 
associated with compliance with environmental 
regulations and market expectations reinforce the 
need for proper management of these factors to 
preserve the sector’s competitiveness. During 2024, 
the Bank developed climate resilience tests specific 
to the agri-food sector, considering scenarios of 
drought and variability in precipitation. In 2025, the 
criteria, assumptions, and results of this assessment 
were maintained, and they continue to serve as a 
valid reference for guiding risk management and 
strengthening the resilience of the portfolio exposed 
to this sector.

From a transition risk perspective, the sector

vehicles, hydrogen-based solutions, or biofuels. 
While cost reductions in these technologies facilitate 
the transition, challenges persist due to a lack of 
infrastructure, incentives, and technical capabilities,
