that maintain carbon-intensive models. Additionally, 
changes in consumer preferences and reputational 
pressure can impact demand and access to financing.
In terms of physical risks, the sector is particularly 
vulnerable to extreme weather events such as heavy 
rains, floods, landslides, droughts, and wildfires, which 
can damage road and transportation infrastructure, 
disrupt supply chains, and increase operational 
and maintenance costs. In the context of climate 
resilience testing, this sector showed the greatest 
average impact from variations in precipitation 
compared to other evaluated sectors, reinforcing 
the need to strengthen infrastructure resilience and 
the management of these risks over time.

Potential financial

To address the various identified climate risks, at 
Banco de Occidente we analyze financial products 
and services aimed at strengthening resilience and

Through these initiatives, we seek to support our 
clients in their transition toward more sustainable 
models and enhance their ability to adapt to extreme 
weather events, in line with our decarbonization 
roadmap and the TCFD recommendations.

Sustainable Financing
In 2024, at Banco de Occidente, we developed 
our Sustainable and Transition Taxonomy, using 
Colombia’s Green Taxonomy and the one designed 
by IDB Invest as references. Our goal is to capitalize 
on opportunities arising from climate change, reduce 
associated financial risks, and support our clients 
in their decarbonization process.
Our taxonomy includes eight eligibility criteria, 
focused on both climate change mitigation and 
adaptation, and we have indicators and calculation 
methodologies that allow us to adequately monitor 
our progress.

Strengthening resilience to 
climate change
We recognize the variability of information 
associated with climate change and its potential 
impacts; therefore, at Banco de Occidente, we 
have implemented a set of initiatives aimed at 
strengthening the resilience of our strategy and our 
climate risk management.
Analysis and monitoring Strengthening internal capabilities Management and response
Periodic updating of climate risk assessments using 
prioritized scenarios.
Analysis of portfolio exposure by sector and 
geography to identify the most vulnerable segments.
Periodic assessment of opportunities arising from 
climate change.
Communication of risks and opportunities to the 
responsible departments.
Awareness-raising and training sessions targeted 
at key departments.
Expert support for the review of action plans and 
internal initiatives.
Implementation of measures to avoid, prevent, or 
mitigate the most material climate risks.
Stage Description
Risk 
Identification
Identification of climate risks relevant to the Bank, considering physical and transition 
risks, as well as their relationship to the portfolio’s exposure in the short (2025), medium 
(2030), and long term (2050). 
In 2025, we updated our double materiality analysis, which assessed sustainability risks 
and opportunities, including climate-related issues. As a result of this exercise, emissions 
management and climate change were identified as material issues for the Bank. 
Risk 
Measurement
Measurement of identified climate risks through the application of climate stress scenarios, 
aimed at assessing potential impacts on financial and risk variables.
Definition of 
appetite and 
limits
Definition of climate risk appetite and operational limits.
Strategic 
and business 
alignment
Integration of climate risks into strategic planning, taking into account projections, 
strategic objectives, and business guidelines, in order to strengthen the Bank’s resilience.
Monitoring 
and analysis 
of deviations
Periodic monitoring of risk appetite, defined limits, and the evolution of climate risks, as 
well as analysis of deviations from established parameters and their potential impact on 
strategy and business.
Risk Management
Given the significance of climate risks for Banco 
de Occidente and the vulnerability of its portfolio, 
the integration of these risks into the organization’s 
risk culture has been strengthened. In this context, 
the Vice Presidency of Risk and Collections has 
been progressively involved in the different stages of 
identifying, measuring, and monitoring risks related to 
climate change, in line with the Bank’s comprehensive 
risk management model.
Climate risk management is documented in the 
Risk Appetite Framework, enabling its integration 
with strategy, decision-making, and continuous 
monitoring. This process is structured in five stages, 
which aim to ensure consistent management aligned 
with the TCFD recommendations:

Climate Change Risk 
Management Cycle
Since 2024, we have consolidated our structured 
roadmap for the identification, prioritization, 
assessment, and management of climate-related 
risks and opportunities. This roadmap remains fully 
in effect for 2025, closely aligned with Banco de 
Occidente’s comprehensive risk management model, 
which allows us to ensure constant oversight and 
an agile response to environmental challenges.

2.
Identification of risks and 
opportunities: 
Assessment and 
prioritization of risks 
and opportunities:
An initial assessment of climate-related risks and 
opportunities through 2050 was conducted based 
on a comprehensive analysis that included:
A. Analysis of market trends, regulatory frameworks, 
national commitments, and best practices in 
the financial sector.
B. Annual review of the portfolio’s sectoral profile, 
considering emissions generated, vulnerability 
levels, and loan amounts, among other factors. 
C. Analysis of the processes, roles, and 
responsibilities of the teams involved in risk 
management.
D. Alignment of the identified risks and opportunities 
with the classification proposed by the TCFD, 
distinguishing between physical and transition 
risks, as well as associated opportunities, with 
an emphasis on those aimed at mitigating GHG 
emissions and/or adapting to climate change.
The identified climate-related risks and opportunities 
were assessed and prioritized based on technical 
and financial criteria, considering:
A. The selection of prioritized climate-related 
scenarios for the analysis. At Banco de 
Occidente, we prioritized three scenarios 
proposed by the Network for Greening the 
Financial System (NGFS).

## Pagina 346

Orderly transition (Net Zero 2050): a scenario 
characterized by the early and gradual 
implementation of strict climate policies, implying 
high transition risks and low physical risks. It allows 
for limiting global temperature rise to around 1,5 °C 
by 2100 and serves as a benchmark to guide best 
business practices for mitigation and adaptation
Disorderly transition: assumes a delay in emissions 
reductions and a late and uneven implementation of 
climate policies across countries, leading to higher 
transition risks and limiting global temperature 
rise to around 1,8 °C by 2100.
Hothouse World: assumes the continuation of 
current policies, with low transition risks and high 
physical risks, and a global temperature increase 
that could reach +3 °C by the end of the century.
B. The assignment of external parameters 
associated with each risk, understood as 
variables driven by the scenarios that allow 
for the reflection of climate-related financial 
risk.
Parameter: the use of specialized sources 
such as the NGFS Scenario Explorer (IIASA) 
and the Climate Impact Explorer (Climate 
Analytics).
Financial impact: the bank’s internal financial 
metric that will be affected by climate risk.
C. The assessment of each risk using metrics that 
include:
Confidence level of the source and the 
parameter.
Scenario sensitivity.
Probability of parameter change.
Time horizon for the financial impact to 
materialize.
D. Prioritization was performed by combining two 
methodologies in a “materiality vs. certainty” 
framework, where the metric assessments are 
grouped as follows:
Materiality: simple average of the “time 
horizon” metric averaged across each climate 
scenario, for a specific parameter/variable. 
If there are multiple parameters associated 
with the same risk, materiality will be the result 
of the simple average of the “time horizon” 
metrics averaged for each parameter. 
Certainty: the simple average of the 
metrics “confidence level,” “probability,” and 
“sensitivity,” averaged across each climate 
scenario, for a specific parameter or variable. 
If there are multiple parameters associated 
with the same risk, the certainty will be the 
simple average of the metrics “confidence 
level,” “probability,” and “sensitivity” averaged 
for each parameter.

A. The adoption of a stochastic, non-deterministic 
methodology developed by Ecoacciones SAS 
BIC.
B. The identification of climate parameters 
associated with the cause or origin of each risk,

## Pagina 347

Implementation 
of SARAS
Metrics and Objectives
Since 2023, at Banco de Occidente we have 
established the Environmental and Social Risk 
Management System (SARAS) as the structured 
framework for integrating sustainability into our 
lending operations. This system brings together 
policies, tools, and processes designed to identify, 
assess, mitigate, and monitor environmental and 
social risks in the projects and economic activities 
we finance.
In 2025, we began the gradual integration of 
climate change criteria into SARAS, strengthening 
risk management within the credit process. This 
evolution is being implemented in phases, prioritizing 
sectors with greater climate exposure, such as: 
civil engineering works and building construction, 
food production, and the supply of electricity, gas, 
steam, and air conditioning, as well as activities 
related to hydrocarbons, power generation, and 
mining, among others.
We are implementing a phased approach that 
allows us to conduct a more in-depth assessment 
of clients with higher risk levels, supporting them in 
defining action and mitigation plans. In this way, we 
ensure constant monitoring of their progress, in full 
alignment with our sustainable finance guidelines 
and the Bank’s comprehensive risk management 
model.
At Banco de Occidente, we measure what we value to 
ensure compliance with our climate goals. Through 
a set of specific metrics and performance indicators, 
we analyze our portfolio’s exposure to different 
climate scenarios, which allows us to accurately 
assess the progress of our roadmap launched in 
2022. 
Measurement Methodology and 
Scope
To ensure the integrity of our data, at Banco 
de Occidente we base the measurement of our 
footprint on the standards of the Greenhouse Gas 
Protocol (GHG Protocol). We adopt an operational 
control approach that includes the quantification of 
greenhouse gases (GHGs) such as CO₂,CH₄, N₂O, 
SF₆, HFCs, and HCFCs. 
In 2022, we took a crucial step by revising our 
methodology in accordance with the Science Based 
Targets initiative (SBTi) guidelines. This has enabled 
us to project emissions trajectories across all three 
scopes:
Scopes 1 and 2: Direct and indirect emissions 
from energy consumption.
Scope 3: We include an analysis of financed 
emissions, assessing our portfolio’s exposure to 
various climate scenarios.

institutional capacity to manage environmental impact indicators. Under this framework of excellence, we 
have defined the following objectives across three time horizons to ensure our future sustainability.

Between 2021 and 2025, Banco de Occidente shows 
a sustained reduction in total GHG emissions 
intensity, falling from 2,48 to 1,03 tCO₂e per 
employee, reflecting a structural improvement in the 
environmental efficiency of operations, even amid 
external fluctuations in the national energy system.
These results confirm that the Bank’s emissions 
management strategy focuses not only on absolute 
reduction but also on progressively decoupling 
operational growth from carbon intensity.
As part of our eco-efficiency goals, we committed 
to reducing direct emissions across our Scopes 1, 2, 
and 3 by 42% by 2030, which equates to an overall 
decrease of 5,25% and an annual reduction of 1,75% 
for each scope.

Financed Emissions
At Banco de Occidente, we are making steady 
progress in measuring and managing the emissions 
associated with the loans we finance, recognizing 
their importance in understanding the carbon 
footprint of our loan portfolio and strengthening 
decision-making regarding climate management. 
In 2025, we conducted an exercise to measure 
financed emissions using data from the commercial 
and retail banking portfolios, as of December 2024, 
with the aim of obtaining a comprehensive view of the 
portfolio’s emissions profile, improving the quality of 
available data, and establishing a robust technical 
foundation for managing risks and opportunities 
associated with climate change.
This exercise was conducted in alignment with the 
Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF) 
standard, ensuring comparability, methodological 
traceability, and consistency with international best 
practices.
Financed Emissions by 
Economic Sector
The measurement of financed emissions was 
structured based on all economic sectors present 
in the Bank’s portfolio, considering Scope 1, 2, and 3 
emissions attributable to the financing provided. The 
portfolio measurement for 2024 regarding total 
financed emissions amounts to 2.245.196 tCO₂e, 
with the Corporate Banking and Retail Banking 
portfolios accounting for 98,38% of the portfolio 
under analysis.
The sectors with the highest contribution to financed 
emissions are:
The industrial sector, with 399.582,66 tCO₂e, 
associated with production processes intensive 
in energy and raw material use.
The cement sector, with 49.366,28 tCO₂e, 
associated with energy-intensive industrial 
processes and process emissions.
The steel sector, with 13.561,53 tCO₂e, linked 
to energy- and material-intensive production 
processes.
Chemical sector, with 87.069,07 tCO₂e, 
characterized by production processes intensive 
in energy and raw materials, and high exposure 
to transition risks.
AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land 
Use), with 395.368,44 tCO₂e, a sector significant 
both for its contribution to emissions and for its 
high exposure to physical risks associated with 
climate change.
Other sectors, with 386.195,68 tCO₂e, which 
include activities such as mining, personal services, 
business services, healthcare, public services, 
commerce, the public sector, telecommunications, 
transportation and logistics, hospitality, and 
tourism, reflecting a diversified contribution from 
operation- and service-intensive sectors.
The energy sector, with 284.993,34 tCO₂e,
linked to energy generation and service provision 
activities.
Oil & Gas, with 164.353,59 tCO₂e, reflecting the 
high carbon intensity associated with these types 
of activities.
Infrastructure and construction, with 162.560,28 
tCO₂e, a key sector for economic development and 
the transition toward more sustainable construction 
models.
Financial sector, with 9.022,14 tCO₂e, associated 
primarily with financial operations and services, 
with a relatively minor contribution but relevant 
for a comprehensive analysis of the portfolio.
The education sector, with 4.491,43 tCO₂e, 
accounts for a small share of total financed 
emissions but contributes to a comprehensive 
understanding of the portfolio’s sectoral profile.

## Pagina 355

Methodology for Calculating 
Financed Emissions
The measurement of financed emissions was based 
on detailed information from Retail Banking and 
Commercial Banking, applying a structured process 
of data preparation, cleansing, and validation in 
accordance with the PCAF standard.
Information sources and 
exclusion criteria
In Retail Banking, products such as credit cards, 
unsecured personal loans, and payroll loans were 
excluded due to the inability to identify the specific 
use of the funds. Likewise, auto loans were excluded 
when there was insufficient technical information to 
determine the vehicle type and assign appropriate 
emission factors.
In Commercial Banking, corporate commercial loans 
and project financing were distinguished. In both 
cases, leasing transactions—classified as leased 
assets under PCAF—were excluded, as were loans 
with undefined ISIC codes, personal loans identified 
within the commercial portfolio, and financing to 
local governments, for which the standard does not 
provide an applicable methodology.
Calculation Methodology by 
Product Type
Mortgages: Each transaction was treated as a 
housing unit classified as VIP, VIS, or non-VIS 
housing, depending on the property’s value. 
Average areas by housing type were used, assuming 
single-family homes. In the absence of complete 
information, a 100% attribution factor was applied.
Vehicle loans: Loans were classified by subcategory 
to distinguish between passenger vehicles and light 
trucks. Average annual mileage based on public 
sources was used, and the attribution factor was 
calculated as the ratio of the financed amount to 
the vehicle’s value, assuming 100% when complete 
information was unavailable.
Commercial loans and project financing: The 
ISIC classification was used to identify each client’s 
economic activity and its correspondence with the 
Exiobase sectors. Based on this relationship, the 
sectoral emission factors defined by PCAF were 
assigned.
Methodological adjustments
Since the emission factors used 
correspond to the base year 2019, 
currency conversions were performed 
using the average exchange rate 
from euros to Colombian pesos, and 
an inflation adjustment was applied 
based on values published by the 
World Bank, thereby ensuring the 
consistency and comparability of 
the results.

Action Plan for Climate 
Change Management
At Banco de Occidente, we recognize that climate 
change management requires a comprehensive, 
progressive, and cross-cutting approach that 
integrates strategic decision-making, risk 
management, business operations, and performance 
measurement. In this regard, the Climate Action 
Plan consolidates the main lines of work that guide 
the implementation of the TCFD framework at the 
Bank, strengthening our capacity for anticipation, 
response, and resilience in the face of the risks and 
opportunities associated with climate change.
This plan is structured around the four pillars of the 
TCFD—Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, 
and Metrics and Targets—and defines concrete 
actions to advance in an orderly and consistent 
manner in each of them.
1. Climate 
Governance
At Banco de Occidente, climate governance is 
a pillar subject to continuous improvement to 
ensure its relevance and operational effectiveness. 
To strengthen our capacity to respond, we are 
currently in a phase of strategically updating our 
structure, drawing on specialized advisory services 
to strengthen decision-making mechanisms and 
consolidate a leading, effective, and resilient 
governance model.
Priority lines of action:
Oversight and 
responsibilities 
in climate risk 
management
Capacity building
Alignment of 
incentives
Clear definition of responsibilities for climate risk management 
within the corporate governance model.
Integration of climate management into the Bank’s risk identification, 
assessment, and mitigation processes.
Periodic review of roles and functions to ensure their effectiveness 
and alignment with international standards.
Cross-functional coordination among key areas (Sustainability, 
Risk, Human Resources, Administration, and Commercial).
Training programs tailored to different organizational levels, aimed at 
integrating climate risk into decision-making.
Specialized workshops for key teams and areas, focused on climate 
risks, scenarios, and best management practices.
Internal forums to disseminate policies, frameworks, and lessons learned 
regarding climate issues.
Specific programs for senior management, aimed at strengthening 
strategic oversight of climate risks.
Progressive evaluation of mechanisms to integrate climate criteria into 
the Bank’s incentive and compensation schemes.
Analysis of metrics, time horizons, and indicators to track climate 
performance.
A phased approach aimed at aligning the climate strategy with value 
creation and responsible risk management.
Throughout 2025, we will continue to prioritize defining the characteristics 
and criteria of our short- and long-term incentives, ensuring they are 
fully aligned with market best practices.

progress in incorporating climate change as a 
fundamental pillar of our corporate strategy. We 
recognize that climate risks and opportunities are 
critical to the sustainability of our business, decision￾making, and value creation in the short, medium, and 
long term. In this context, our climate strategy is aimed 
at strengthening the resilience of the organization, 
our portfolio, and our operations, aligning us with 
the recommendations of the TCFD framework and

3. 4. Risk 
Management
Metrics and 
objectives
The Bank continues to make progress in the gradual incorporation of climate risk into its Integrated Risk 
Management System, recognizing its cross-cutting nature and potential financial impact. This process is 
currently in a strengthening phase, with a gradual approach aimed at enhancing methodologies, internal 
capabilities, and monitoring mechanisms, in line with the TCFD’s recommendations.
We base our climate change management on a 
robust set of metrics and targets that allow us to 
monitor performance, guide decision-making, and 
evaluate progress toward our decarbonization and 
eco-efficiency commitments. We review these 
metrics periodically and adjust them as the regulatory, 
operational, and market contexts evolve, always 
ensuring alignment with TCFD recommendations.
Between 2022 and 2025, Banco de Occidente 
has made consistent progress toward meeting its 
environmental goals, achieving the following results:
Energy: a cumulative reduction of 15,64%, resulting 
from initiatives focused on energy efficiency and 
the responsible use of resources.

## Pagina 359

General Measurement 
Approach
We measure and manage our greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions using an operational control approach, 
integrating Scopes 1 and 2—corresponding to direct 
and indirect emissions from energy consumption—as 
well as making steady progress in measuring and 
managing the impacts associated with our portfolio. 
This approach allows us to prioritize actions targeting 
the main sources of emissions and strengthen the 
traceability of our results in the short, medium, and 
long term.
Actions for the decarbonization 
of operations
Scope 1 – Direct emissions: our direct emissions 
stem primarily from fuel consumption and refrigerant 
leaks in our operations. To manage these, we have 
defined action plans focused on operational efficiency 
and the progressive reduction of emissions:
Systematic monitoring of fuel consumption by fixed 
and mobile sources, identifying critical areas and 
opportunities for reduction.
Technical evaluation for the incorporation of 
voluntary biofuel blends and lower-carbon 
alternatives.
Feasibility analysis for the gradual conversion of 
the vehicle fleet to electric or lower-environmental￾impact options.
Strengthening of environmental criteria in the 
selection of vehicle leasing and operation providers.
Preventive maintenance programs for refrigeration 
equipment, accompanied by the gradual 
replacement of conventional refrigerants with 
alternatives with lower global warming potential.
Scope 2 – Indirect emissions from energy 
consumption: Given that energy consumption 
represents one of the most significant sources in the 
emissions inventory, the Bank has prioritized actions 
aimed at energy efficiency and the transition to 
renewable sources:
Energy assessment of operational facilities, 
considering their technical conditions and usage 
patterns.
Identification of opportunities for energy savings 
and consumption optimization through operational 
and technological improvements.
Continuation of the process of converting lighting 
systems to LED technology in offices and common 
areas.
Assessment of the technical and financial feasibility 
of incorporating solar power generation solutions 
at selected facilities.
Long-term climate goals
The Bank’s climate strategy is structured around clear 
and measurable objectives, aligned with national 
and international decarbonization commitments:
Minimum annual reduction of 4,7% in Scope 1 and 
2 GHG emissions.
A cumulative 42% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG 
emissions by 2030.
Achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, as part of the 
Bank’s long-term commitment.
Operational eco￾efficiency targets for 
2030
CTo complement our emissions 
reduction targets, we have 
defined eco-efficiency goals 
that strengthen our responsible 
management of resources:
Reduce energy consumption 
at facilities by 20%.
Reduce water consumption 
by 10%.
Reduce waste generation by 
25%.
Reduce paper consumption 
by 25%.
Alignment with portfolio 
management
In addition, we are making progress in mitigating 
climate risks associated with our portfolio by 
developing sustainable financing opportunities. 
Through our credit lines, we support our clients in 
their transition toward more resilient, low-carbon 
business models. We reinforce this approach with 
continuous analysis of sectoral and geographic 
exposure, strengthening decision-making and 
comprehensive climate risk management.
